title: Rules for Billing Tenants Separately for Water and Sewer
bodyText:
If you bill tenants separately for water or sewer service you buy from a utility, the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission's rules apply on top of the statute. Your usage charges must be worked out by one of the commission's methods (actual sub-meter readings, or a reasonable allocation by unit, square footage, type of unit, number of occupants or estimated use, after deducting your own and common-area use) and may never total more than you paid.

A set-up fee may not exceed your actual administrative cost, a returned-payment fee may not exceed what your bank actually charged you, and the administrative fee may not exceed $4 a month.

Bill on a consistent schedule; give the tenant at least 17 days after sending a bill before starting collection; show on each bill the items the rules list, including the commission's phone number and website and a statement that the bill's due date is separate from the rent due date; keep utility bills and sub-bills for at least two years and give a tenant copies within three business days of asking, for at most a nominal copying fee; and correct billing errors in the tenant's favor within 90 days of learning of them, for up to one year back.

If you do not answer the commission's consumer affairs division within 15 days, or ignore its determination for 90 days, you are regulated as a public utility and may not charge tenants until you fix the problem. These rules do not apply to a flat fee that includes water without itemizing it, or to a single-unit building the utility meters directly.

title: No Late Fee Cap
bodyText: Indiana has no statute capping late fees or requiring a grace period for residential rent, and cities and counties may not regulate landlord fees. Set a fee that is a reasonable estimate of your cost of late payment; a court may refuse to enforce a fee it sees as a penalty. Whether an unpaid late fee counts as unpaid 'rent' for a 10-day nonpayment notice is not settled by statute.

title: No Application Fee Rule
bodyText: Indiana has no statute on rental application or screening fees, and cities and counties may not regulate lease applications, tenant screening or landlord fees.

title: Local Rent and Lease Regulation Preempted
bodyText:
Indiana cities, towns and counties may not regulate rents, and may not regulate tenant screening, security deposits, lease applications, lease terms, disclosures, the parties' rights or landlord fees, unless the General Assembly authorizes it; an ordinance that does is void. This does not apply to housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents.

Since July 1, 2026, a unit also may not ban or restrict using private homes as rentals, except through general health and safety rules, building and fire codes, reasonable occupancy standards and the permitted registration and inspection programs; units with such rules adopted before 2026 have until January 1, 2028, and certain short-term rental ordinances adopted before 2018 are exempt. Local governments also may not regulate landlord retaliation.

title: Local Rental Registration and Inspection Limits
bodyText:
Indiana limits local rental programs. A city, town or county may not require you to take a class or join a program in order to lease, and may require a rental permit only if it is free, lasts until the property changes hands, and is one permit for a community of five or more units. A registration fee may not exceed $5 a year.

A unit managed by a professional manager that passed a qualifying independent inspection in the past 12 months, with the report delivered on time, is exempt from routine local inspections and inspection fees, though the locality may still inspect on a complaint or reason to believe the code is violated. A penalty for a code violation requires notice and a stated reasonable time to cure first.

A political subdivision whose rental registration or inspection program was created before July 1, 1984 is exempt from the permit, inspection and registration-fee limits. A mobile home community needs a license from the Indiana Department of Health, and local governments may not license or regulate mobile home communities except to enforce the state's health and sanitation standards, apply zoning and building codes, and regulate groups of four or fewer homes.

You may pass a local fee (other than a construction fee) through to tenants (optional clause government-fee-reimbursement-in).

title: Rent Increases
bodyText: Indiana has no statute aimed specifically at rent increases. In a fixed-term lease the rent is set for the term unless the lease provides for a change (see the optional Mid-Term Rent Increase clause). A change to a rental agreement needs at least 30 days' written notice unless the written lease sets a different procedure. In a month-to-month tenancy, a landlord who wants more rent can also end the tenancy on notice equal to the rental period and offer a new one. Raising rent in response to a tenant's protected activity is retaliation, except an increase to comparable market rent at the end of the term, or during it if the lease provides for that.

title: Changing Lease Terms
bodyText: Before modifying a rental agreement, an Indiana landlord must give the tenant at least 30 days' written notice, unless a written rental agreement provides otherwise. The statute sets the notice; it does not say a landlord may change a lease without the tenant's agreement, and whether it allows that is case law. The rest of this chapter of Indiana law cannot be waived.

title: Mid-Term Rent Increases
bodyText:
An Indiana fixed-term lease can allow rent increases during the term, but only if the lease says so. Without the optional Mid-Term Rent Increase clause, the rent stays fixed until the term ends.

If you include it: (1) Retaliation: you may not raise rent because a tenant did something the statute protects, such as complaining to a code-enforcement agency, complaining to you in writing about repairs, a lockout or entry, or joining a tenant organization; but raising rent to what comparable market rentals charge is not retaliation, and an increase during the term is covered only when the lease provides for it.

An increase above comparable market rent loses that protection, which is why the clause ties the new rent to market rent instead of a number. (2) Notice: Indiana requires at least 30 days' written notice before changing a rental agreement, unless the written agreement sets something different; the clause uses 30 days. (3) Tenant's choice: the tenant may end the lease instead of paying the increase. That exit keeps the clause from locking the tenant into the term at a price you set alone.

(4) Leasing impact: tenants usually expect a fixed rent for a fixed term, so a mid-term increase clause may affect how readily applicants sign.

title: Retaliation
bodyText: Indiana bars a landlord from retaliating because a tenant complained to a code-enforcement agency about a violation materially affecting health or safety, complained to the landlord in writing about a lockout, utility shutoff or improper entry or about the landlord's repair duties, sued under the emergency-possession or landlord-duty laws, organized or joined a tenant organization, or testified against the landlord. Retaliation means raising rent, cutting or interfering with services, or bringing or threatening a possession, eviction or early-termination action. You may still decline to renew at the end of the term, raise rent to comparable market rent at the end of the term (or during it if the lease provides for it), cut services for all tenants equally, and bring a possession action where the problem was caused by the tenant or the tenant's household or guests, rent is unpaid after the cure time, code compliance requires work that displaces the tenant, the tenant's breach materially affects health or safety, the tenant holds over after a fixed term, the action was begun in good faith before the protected activity, or you in good faith want the unit back at the end of the term to live in, to renovate in a way that displaces the household, or to take off the rental market for at least six months. The rule cannot be waived.

title: Bad Check Remedies
bodyText:
For a dishonored check you may charge the writer up to $20 plus your bank's actual charge. Separately, a writer found liable under other law who stops payment without valid legal cause, or lets a check be dishonored for lack of funds, no account or a missing signature, is also liable for interest at 18% a year from the check date, court costs, attorney's fees (at least $100 if an outside attorney sues) and other collection costs.

A writer whose check was dishonored (not stopped) escapes this chapter by paying the full amount within 10 days after you give notice of nonpayment. If the writer has not paid within 30 days after you send written notice by certified mail, the court must award three times the check (if $250 or less) or the check plus $500 (if more). You must choose between this remedy and a claim under another statute the chapter names.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText: If the lease sets no interest rate, Indiana's legal rate is 8% a year until payment of judgment, running on money due under a written instrument that sets no rate from the date of settlement, or, on an account stated or closed, from the date an itemized bill was rendered and payment demanded. Indiana's limits on an agreed interest rate were not reviewed here, so check them before putting a rate in a lease.

title: No Rent Receipt Rule
bodyText: Indiana has no statute requiring a landlord to give receipts for rent, including cash rent.

title: Sales Tax on Rent
bodyText: Indiana sales tax applies to renting rooms, lodgings or accommodations for periods of less than 30 days, including transient rentals in a house, condominium or apartment. A residential lease for 30 days or more is outside that rule. Counties and cities may also impose innkeeper's taxes on short stays.

title: Accepting Late or Partial Rent
bodyText: No Indiana statute says whether accepting late or partial rent waives a default or a notice; that is case law. A nonpayment notice does not end the lease if the tenant pays the rent in full before the notice period expires.

title: Are Fees Rent?
bodyText: Under Indiana's security deposit law, and the landlord-tenant chapters that adopt its definitions, 'rent' includes every payment made to the landlord under the rental agreement except a security deposit. The 10-day nonpayment-notice statute sits outside those chapters and does not adopt that definition, so whether a late fee or other charge counts as unpaid 'rent' for that notice is not settled by statute.

title: Indiana Security Deposit Rules
bodyText:
An Indiana security deposit includes prepaid rent beyond the first full rental period and any other amount returnable when the unit is returned in the required condition. You may use it only for actual damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, rent owed (including rent due because the tenant ended the lease early), unpaid utility or sewer charges the tenant owed and you paid, and the last period's rent if agreed in writing.

Within 45 days after the tenant's occupancy ends you must mail an itemized list of damages, with the estimated repair cost of each item, and a check or money order for the balance; you are not liable under the deposit law until the tenant gives you a mailing address in writing. If you do not send the list, you are treated as agreeing that no damages are due and must return the whole deposit at once, and the tenant can recover the amount withheld plus attorney's fees and court costs. These rules cannot be waived. Deposit cases may be filed in small claims.

title: No Deposit Cap
bodyText: Indiana sets no limit on the amount of a security deposit, and cities and counties may not regulate security deposits.

title: No Interest on Deposits
bodyText: Indiana does not require a landlord to pay interest on a security deposit.

title: How Deposits Are Held
bodyText: Indiana does not require a security deposit to be kept in a separate, trust or escrow account or at a particular kind of institution.

title: Deposits Held by a Real Estate Broker Company
bodyText: Indiana's deposit law itself does not say where a security deposit must be kept. But if a licensed real estate broker company manages the property and the deposit or any other tenant money comes into its hands, Indiana's real estate licensing law requires the broker company to put it in a clearly identified trust account, keep a record of the funds held for each person, never mix it with personal or business funds, and hold any interest earned for the person the money belongs to. An owner who manages the property and holds the deposit personally is not covered by that rule.

title: Last Month's Rent and the Deposit
bodyText: In Indiana, rent you require the tenant to prepay for any period other than the first full rental period is a security deposit, so last month's rent collected at signing must be held, used and returned under the deposit rules. Unless you agree otherwise, a tenant may not apply the deposit to rent; the deposit may pay the last period's rent only if a written agreement says it will.

title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold
bodyText: The owner at the end of the tenancy is bound by Indiana's deposit-return rule. If you sell to a good-faith buyer, you are released from liability for later events once you give the tenant written notice of the sale, but for one year after that notice you remain liable for the deposit unless the buyer notifies the tenant that it has assumed your liability and you transfer the deposit to the buyer. A property manager is released for later events after written notice to the tenant that its management has ended. Either rule can be changed by agreement.

title: Selling Rented Property
bodyText: A sale of rented property is valid without the tenant's consent, and rent the tenant pays you before receiving notice of the sale is good against the buyer. Your duty to disclose the property manager and the agent for notices binds the buyer and any new manager. After a sale to a good-faith buyer, you are released for events after written notice to the tenant, subject to the deposit rule.

title: Pet Deposits and Fees
bodyText: In Indiana a refundable pet deposit is part of the security deposit, because the deposit law covers any amount returnable when the unit is returned in the required condition; it follows the same use and 45-day return rules. A nonrefundable pet fee or monthly pet rent is not returnable, so it is not a deposit, and no statute limits it. You may not charge any fee to keep an emotional support animal.

title: Move-In Condition
bodyText: Indiana does not require a move-in inspection, inventory or condition report. The only move-in writing the law requires is the tenant's acknowledgment of a functional smoke detector. At move-out, the damage list must state the estimated repair cost of each item.

title: Tenant Duties Under Indiana Law
bodyText:
Indiana tenants must follow the health and housing code duties placed on tenants; keep the areas they use reasonably clean; use the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning systems, elevators and appliances reasonably; not deface, damage, destroy or remove any part of the premises; follow reasonable rules in force at signing, and amended rules as the lease provides; keep smoke detectors working and replace batteries; and return the unit clean and proper, ordinary wear and tear excepted.

Before suing to enforce these duties you must give notice and a reasonable time to fix the problem, unless the tenancy has ended; if you repaired physical damage, your notice must list the repairs and document their cost. A winning landlord may recover actual damages, attorney's fees and court costs, an injunction or other relief. These rules cannot be waived.

title: Occupancy Limits
bodyText: Indiana's landlord-tenant law lets you refuse to rent on the basis of a reasonable occupancy standard. A standard of two people per bedroom is presumed reasonable if you do not count infants under one year old and you count a den, library, finished basement or loft that could reasonably be used for sleeping, unless that would violate state or local codes. You need not count a kitchen, dining room, living room, bathroom, hallway or closet as a sleeping area. Fair housing law still applies.

title: Tenants and City Utility Bills
bodyText: For property served by a city- or town-owned utility and occupied by someone other than the owner, the occupant applying for service must give the utility the owner's or manager's name and contact information. Charges are payable by the occupant if the utility's records show the property is occupied by a non-owner who is responsible for the bill, and they are not a lien on the property; the city may not require you to cosign or guarantee the occupant's account. This rule does not cover sewage works under the municipal sewer statutes, consolidated-city utilities or a department of public utilities. For those sewage works, a lien for unpaid fees on property occupied by someone other than the owner attaches only if the utility notifies the owner within 20 days after the fees become 60 days delinquent, unless a local ordinance provides otherwise.

title: Landlord Duties Under Indiana Law
bodyText: Indiana landlords must deliver the premises in compliance with the lease and in a safe, clean and habitable condition; comply with health and housing codes; make reasonable efforts to keep common areas clean and proper; and, if provided when the lease is signed, keep in good and safe working condition the electrical, plumbing (with a reasonable supply of hot and cold running water at all times), sanitary, heating (sufficient heat at all times), ventilating and air-conditioning systems, elevators, and appliances supplied as an inducement to the lease. These duties cannot be waived.

title: Tenant Remedies for Repairs
bodyText:
A tenant may sue to enforce your repair duties only after giving you notice and a reasonable time to repair, and must let you in to make the repairs. A winning tenant may recover actual and consequential damages, attorney's fees and court costs, an injunction or other relief; your liability for damages starts when you refuse, or fail within a reasonable time, to fix a condition you have notice or actual knowledge of. Indiana has no repair-and-deduct or rent-withholding statute.

A tenant who is locked out or has utilities cut off may seek an emergency possessory order, heard within three business days.

title: Smoke Detectors
bodyText:
Every Indiana dwelling must have at least one functional smoke detector outside each sleeping area and on each additional story, including basements, installed as the statute describes; a totally sprinkled building that met Uniform Building Code standards (an older model code) when built is exempt from the smoke detector chapter, though the move-in acknowledgment is still required.

The owner, or its manager or rental agent, must install the required detectors and repair or replace one within seven working days after written notice. When you deliver the unit you must get the tenant's written acknowledgment that it has a functional smoke detector, and the occupant must test detectors at least every six months. A landlord who violates the rule at delivery, or does not fix a hard-wired detector within seven days after certified-mail notice, commits a Class B infraction (Class A for a repeat).

These requirements cannot be waived, and local codes may be stricter. Indiana has no statute requiring carbon monoxide alarms in rentals.

title: Entering the Unit
bodyText:
In Indiana you must give the tenant reasonable written or oral notice before entering, may enter only at reasonable times, and may not abuse the right of entry or use it to harass. You may enter without notice in an emergency that threatens the occupants' safety or your property, and without consent under a court order or after the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit.

A tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply services, or show the unit to buyers, lenders, tenants, workers or contractors. These rules cannot be waived.

title: No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs
bodyText: Except under a court order, an Indiana landlord may not deny or interfere with a tenant's access to or possession of the unit, including by changing locks or adding a device to exclude the tenant, removing doors, windows, fixtures or appliances, or interrupting electricity, gas, water or other essential services (except for an emergency, good-faith repairs or necessary construction). You also may not take, remove, withhold or dispose of a tenant's belongings to enforce the lease. A tenant may get an emergency possessory order returning possession, heard within three business days. The lockout and utility rules do not apply to a unit the tenants have abandoned (rent unpaid and circumstances showing a reasonable person they surrendered possession); belongings left behind are handled under the abandoned-property rules.

title: Disability Modifications and Accommodations
bodyText: Indiana's fair housing law requires you to allow reasonable modifications of the premises at the tenant's expense when necessary for a person with a disability to fully enjoy them, and to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices and services. The Indiana text does not mention conditioning a modification on restoring the interior. You need not rent to someone whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property.

title: Emotional Support Animals
bodyText:
Under Indiana's emotional support animal law, if a person's disability is not readily apparent you may require written verification from a health service provider who treats the person (not one who only sells verification letters) that the person has a disability, has a disability-related need for the animal, and is helped by it; a person who moves from another state may provide documentation from a physician, psychiatrist, social worker or other mental health professional licensed there with whom the person has an ongoing treatment relationship.

You may evaluate the documents, but may not charge any fee to keep an emotional support animal. You may require the tenant to follow the lease and rules like other residents, pay for damage the animal causes as other pet owners would, and sign an addendum setting out the owner's responsibilities. A landlord who allows an emotional support animal as a reasonable accommodation is not liable for injuries it causes to others, subject to any other federal, state or local law. The law does not apply to dwellings exempt from Indiana's fair housing act.

title: Emotional Support Animal Misrepresentation
bodyText: In Indiana it is a Class A infraction to misrepresent to a landlord a disability or a disability-related need for an emotional support animal, to make a materially false statement to a health provider to get documentation, to give a landlord a document falsely presenting an animal as an emotional support animal, or to fit an animal with a vest or sign suggesting it is one. A health provider who verifies without adequate knowledge of the person's condition, or who only sells verification letters, commits the same infraction.

title: Guide Dogs
bodyText: Indiana law bars refusing to rent to a person with a disability because the person has a guide dog that assists with the disability.

title: Lead-Safe Work in Older Rentals
bodyText:
If you renovate, remodel or maintain target housing built before 1960 that is occupied by someone other than you or your immediate family, and the work disturbs more than 20 square feet of exterior paint, more than 2 square feet in any one room, or more than 10% of the painted surface area, Indiana bans open-flame burning, machine sanding, grinding or abrasive blasting without HEPA exhaust control, heat guns above 1,100 degrees or that char paint, and most dry scraping and dry sanding; bars volatile chemical strippers in unventilated spaces; and requires visible exterior paint chips to be cleaned up within 48 hours.

These rules do not apply to housing for the elderly or for people with disabilities where no child aged six or younger lives or is expected to live, or to a building without a bedroom. Paint is presumed to be lead-based unless a lead-based paint inspection shows otherwise. The federal lead disclosure also applies to pre-1978 housing.

title: Notice for Unpaid Rent
bodyText:
In Indiana you may end a lease for unpaid rent on at least 10 days' notice, unless the parties agreed otherwise or the tenant pays the rent in full before the notice period expires. The statute supplies a form notice to vacate within 10 days unless the rent is paid. No notice is needed where the lease expressly requires rent in advance and the tenant does not pay it.

The library's lease requires rent in advance, so it does not require you to give notice before ending the lease for unpaid rent that was due in advance. You may still give the 10-day notice first; if you do, the statute does not let you end the lease on that notice if the tenant pays the rent in full before it expires.

A notice may be served on the tenant; if the tenant cannot be found, on a person living at the premises (who must have it explained); and if no one is found, by attaching it to a conspicuous part of the premises. Because of the 'unless the parties agreed otherwise' wording, a lease could also shorten or waive the 10-day notice where it applies, but the library does not offer that clause: how courts read the phrase has not been reviewed.

It is lawful, so a landlord who still wants it can add a custom clause, after taking advice. If the property has a federally backed mortgage or takes part in a covered federal housing program, federal law may require 30 days' written notice to vacate first (see edu-cares-act-notice).

title: Ending a Tenancy
bodyText:
Indiana notice rules depend on the tenancy. A fixed-term lease ends at the end of its term without notice. A month-to-month or other periodic tenancy of three months or less ends on notice equal to the rental period (a week for week-to-week, a month for month-to-month); occupancy by the landlord's consent without other terms is month to month. A tenancy at will ends on one month's written notice and cannot exist without an express contract.

A year-to-year tenancy ends on notice at least three months before the end of the year. No notice is needed for a tenant at sufferance or a tenant at will who commits waste. Indiana supplies form notices for year-to-year tenancies and unpaid rent. If the property has a federally backed mortgage or takes part in a covered federal housing program, federal law may require 30 days' written notice to vacate first (see edu-cares-act-notice).

title: Eviction Court Process
bodyText: Indiana evictions are court cases. A possession case where the rent due when filed is $10,000 or less may be filed on a small claims docket, and filing there waives your right to a jury; the tenant may request a jury within 10 days after receiving the notice of claim. Attach a copy of a written lease to the claim. Small claims venue between landlord and tenant cannot be changed by contract. An order of possession may not be issued more than 30 days after judgment, and it lasts no more than 30 days. Before final judgment, a court may order possession only after you post a court-approved bond, and the officer may not remove occupants until 48 hours after the order is served. If the case settles before final judgment, you must move to dismiss it unless you are still seeking damages, including keeping the deposit; eviction diversion programs must be voluntary.

title: Emergency Possessory Orders
bodyText:
Indiana has a fast court track. A landlord may petition the small claims docket for an emergency possessory order if the tenant has committed or threatens waste, if the tenant or a guest committed a crime affecting the health and safety of another tenant, the landlord or the landlord's agent, or if the tenant gave materially false information to get the lease.

The court must hold a hearing within three business days, and a continuance is allowed only on clear and convincing evidence that manifest injustice would otherwise result. On a crime or false-application finding, the tenant must return possession within 7 days of the hearing. Tenants may use the same track against lockouts and utility shutoffs. The track does not override the rights of a tenant who is a crime victim.

If the property has a federally backed mortgage or takes part in a covered federal housing program, federal law may require 30 days' written notice to vacate first (see edu-cares-act-notice).

title: Eviction Record Sealing
bodyText: Indiana courts must, on their own, seal the records of an eviction case that is dismissed (including when the landlord settles or stops prosecuting), that ends in the tenant's favor, or whose judgment against the tenant is overturned on appeal. If a judgment was entered against the tenant, the tenant may move to seal the records once any money judgment is paid, or after seven years if there was no money judgment. Sealed records are open only under a court order, to law enforcement, or as the law requires. If you file an eviction and then settle, you must dismiss the case unless you still seek damages, and a case you leave idle for 180 days may be dismissed and sealed.

title: Tenant Property After Eviction
bodyText:
After a court awards you possession, you may ask the court for an order allowing removal of the tenant's property. Property not removed by the date in the order may be delivered to a warehouse or a court-approved storage facility, but only after the order and the facility's name and location are personally served on the tenant.

Medically necessary items, items used in the tenant's trade or business, and a week's seasonal clothing, blankets and items needed for the care and schooling of a minor child must be released to the tenant free; the facility has a lien on other property for its charges and may sell it if not claimed within 45 days after notice. You are not liable for loss of property a reasonable person would conclude the tenant abandoned, and a lease may not define abandonment differently.

title: Domestic Violence, Sexual Offense and Stalking Protections
bodyText: Indiana protects a tenant or applicant who is a victim (or alleged victim) of domestic or family violence, a sex offense or stalking and who has a civil protection order or criminal no-contact order. You may not terminate, refuse to renew, refuse to enter into a lease, or retaliate solely because the person or a household member is protected, or because the person ended a lease under this law. A protected tenant may end the lease with written notice at least 30 days before the termination date, with a copy of the order and, for domestic violence or sexual assault, a safety plan from an accredited program, dated within 30 days, recommending relocation. The tenant owes rent prorated to the termination date and no early-termination rent or fees, and owes nothing if the notice comes at least 14 days before the right to occupy begins. Other adult tenants stay bound. The protected tenant is entitled to deposit refunds as if the tenancy had expired, even though you otherwise need not account for the deposit until 45 days after all tenancies end; see the deposit-timing row for the safe course. These rights cannot be waived.

title: Lock Changes for Protected Tenants
bodyText: If a protected tenant gives you a written request and a copy of a protection or no-contact order, you must change the locks and give the tenant a new key within 48 hours, or within 24 hours if the restrained person lives in the same unit. In that case you may not let the restrained person in unless the order allows retrieval of property, and you are immune from liability for excluding the person under the order and for loss of property left in the unit; the excluded person stays liable for rent and damage. The tenant reimburses your actual cost. If you do not act in time, the tenant may change the locks and you must reimburse the tenant's cost, and the tenant must give you a key within 24 hours.

title: Squatter Removal
bodyText: Since July 1, 2025, an Indiana property owner may sign an affidavit, under penalty of perjury, that a person occupying the property has never had a rental agreement, the owner's permission or any other right to be there, and give it to law enforcement, which must send officers to remove the person within 48 hours unless public safety requires a delay. The track does not apply to a former or current tenant whose lease expired or who violated it, or to an invitee of the owner or of a tenant; those people must be removed through the courts. A person removed because of a knowingly false affidavit may sue the affiant.

title: No Just-Cause Requirement
bodyText: Indiana has no just-cause eviction rule: no notice is needed to end a lease for a fixed term at its end, and a periodic tenancy may be ended on the statutory notice without a reason. The limits are situational: you may not end or refuse to renew a tenancy in retaliation for protected tenant activity (non-renewal at the end of the term is allowed) or solely because the tenant is a protected victim of domestic violence, a sex offense or stalking, and fair housing law applies. In a mobile home community, state law lists the reasons an operator may eject a person (nonpayment of charges or fees, violation of law or disorderly conduct, or violation of a state or posted community rule), and closing the community takes 180 days' written notice to each home owner; whether the list of reasons is exclusive is for the courts, so the cautious course is to rely on one of them.

title: When a Tenant Dies or Is Incapacitated
bodyText:
If you know that a tenant who was the sole occupant has died, or believe a sole-occupant tenant is incapacitated and absent, Indiana law requires you to notify the tenant's representative, give the representative reasonable access to remove the tenant's belongings, and pay the representative the deposit and unearned rent the tenant would have received; you may require a signed inventory.

The representative is, in order of priority, a person the tenant named in a separate written document delivered to you, a person named in the lease, an attorney in fact, a guardian, an heir, or a person the probate court appoints, and accepts by written notice to you. If you comply you are not liable to the tenant, the estate or others; a willful violation makes you liable for actual damages. The statute does not say whether the lease ends.

title: Holdover Tenants
bodyText: Indiana has no statute setting holdover damages or double rent for a residential tenant who stays after the lease ends. A tenant who stays with your consent becomes a month-to-month tenant. Indiana needs no notice to end the tenancy of a tenant at sufferance; whether a tenant who stays without your consent is one is a question for the courts. Your damages are set by the lease or by the courts.

title: Fire and Casualty
bodyText: Indiana has no statute on what happens to a residential lease when fire or another casualty damages the unit: no statutory rent abatement and no statutory right for either side to end the lease. Your duties to keep the unit habitable and its systems working still apply and cannot be waived. Common-law rules and the lease decide the rest.

title: When the Tenant Causes Damage
bodyText: An Indiana tenant must not deface, damage, destroy, impair or remove any part of the premises. You may sue for actual damages, attorney's fees and costs after giving notice and a reasonable time to fix the problem, or at once if the tenancy has ended; if you made the repairs, your notice must list them and document the cost. Waste supports an emergency possessory order. Indiana has no casualty or rent-abatement statute that a tenant who causes damage could invoke to end the lease or stop paying rent.

title: Servicemembers
bodyText: Indiana has no state statute letting a servicemember end a residential lease; the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act governs, and Indiana treats a violation of it as a violation of state law. Indiana extends the Act's rights to members of the Indiana National Guard or another state's Guard ordered to active duty, including state active duty, for at least 30 consecutive days; for state active duty, you are not subject to the state remedies until the member or a dependent gives you documentation of Guard status and the orders. A servicemember's dependents, after giving notice to the plaintiff as applicable, have the same rights as the servicemember under the Act's Title II.

title: Re-Renting After a Tenant Leaves
bodyText: No Indiana statute says whether you must try to re-rent the unit after a tenant leaves early or how that affects the rent owed; that is case law. The deposit may be applied to rent due for the tenant's premature termination.

title: Drug Nuisance Actions
bodyText:
Using a leased house, apartment or building to commit a controlled-substance offense is a nuisance under Indiana law. The prosecutor, a city or county attorney, the Attorney General or the property owner may sue to abate it; anyone other than the owner must give each tenant and the owner 45 days' notice first.

The court must hold a hearing within 20 days and may grant an injunction, order a tenant who created the nuisance to vacate within 72 hours, and give the owner possession if the tenant disobeys, with the sheriff executing within 5 days. An owner who knew of the nuisance may be ordered to submit a plan to prevent it; other relief needs no proof that a defendant knew.

If the property has a federally backed mortgage or takes part in a covered federal housing program, federal law may require 30 days' written notice to vacate first (see edu-cares-act-notice).

title: No Landlord Lien on Belongings
bodyText: An Indiana landlord may not take, remove, withhold or dispose of a tenant's belongings to enforce the lease, and a lease term allowing it is void. You may accept, but not require, a lien on the tenant's motor vehicle as security, and only if you file or record the lien and treat it under the deposit rules. A separate writing (not the lease) may let you hold property the tenant voluntarily offers as security in exchange for not evicting.

title: Lease Terms Indiana Voids
bodyText: Indiana voids a waiver of its security deposit, tenant property, access and possession, tenant duty, landlord duty, retaliation and victim-protection rules. A lease may not define abandonment differently from the statute, and a tenant's attornment to a stranger is void without your consent or a court order. A confession-of-judgment (cognovit) term given before a claim accrues is void, and it is a Class B misdemeanor knowingly to procure the signing of a cognovit note, to keep one as its payee or holder, or to try to enforce in Indiana another jurisdiction's judgment based on one. Small claims venue cannot be waived by contract. No Indiana statute voids exculpatory or indemnity terms in residential leases; that is left to the courts.

title: Consumer Protection Act
bodyText: Indiana's Deceptive Consumer Sales Act covers leases of real property for personal or household purposes, so a landlord who regularly leases is a 'supplier'. Soliciting a tenant to sign terms that are oppressively one-sided, unduly limit remedies or set an unduly excessive price, where unequal bargaining power led the tenant to sign unwillingly or unknowingly, is an unconscionable act treated as a deceptive act; signing a written lease creates a rebuttable presumption that the tenant knew its terms. A tenant's private damages and class actions under the Act do not apply to consumer transactions in real property; how the Act is otherwise enforced was not reviewed here. The Act's list of deceptive acts has no item on leaving blanks at signing or giving a copy at signing.

title: Attorney's Fees
bodyText: Indiana statutes award attorney's fees in several landlord-tenant cases: to a tenant who recovers a wrongfully withheld deposit, to the winning landlord in a suit to enforce the tenant's statutory duties, to the winning tenant in a suit to enforce the landlord's statutory duties, and to a holder suing on a bad check. No Indiana statute makes a lease attorney-fee clause reciprocal or limits it; the shared lease clause awards fees to the prevailing party either way.

title: Written Leases and Recording
bodyText: Indiana's statute of frauds does not apply to a lease for a term of three years or less, so an oral lease of that length can be enforced. A lease for longer than three years, on paper or as an electronic record, must be in writing, signed by the landlord, and acknowledged before a notary (or proved). It must also be recorded in the county recorder's office within 45 days after signing, or it is void against a later good-faith buyer, tenant or mortgagee.

title: Which Rentals the Rules Cover
bodyText:
Indiana's residential landlord-tenant chapters apply to rental agreements for dwelling units in Indiana, but not to institutional housing (detention, medical care, maternity homes, education, counseling, religious or geriatric services), occupancy under a contract to buy the unit (except rent-to-own agreements entered into after June 30, 2008), fraternal or social organization housing, transient lodging, employee housing conditioned on employment, condominium or cooperative owners, or property used mainly for agriculture, unless the arrangement was set up to avoid the law.

Several chapters apply only to agreements made after a set date: the access chapter after June 30, 1999, the tenant- and landlord-duty chapters after June 30, 2002, and the victim-protection chapter after June 30, 2007.

title: Indiana Fair Housing Law
bodyText: Indiana's fair housing act bars refusing to rent, setting different terms, misrepresenting availability, or advertising a preference because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, disability or national origin, and requires reasonable disability modifications and accommodations. The act does not apply to an owner of no more than three single-family houses who rents one without a broker and without discriminatory advertising (one such rental in 24 months if the owner was not the last resident), or to rooms or units in an owner-occupied building for four or fewer families; federal law, not reviewed here, may still apply, including to advertising. The act does not bar discrimination based on a conviction for illegal manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance. Indiana's civil rights law also names ancestry and status as a veteran among protected traits.

title: Housing Vouchers and Source of Income
bodyText: Indiana law does not protect source of income in housing, and a city, town or county may not require a landlord to participate in the Section 8 program or a similar housing program.

title: Immigration Status
bodyText: Indiana has no statute requiring or barring immigration-status checks by landlords. Its harboring law makes concealing or shielding a person known to be unlawfully present, for gain, a crime, but expressly provides that a landlord does not violate it by renting property to an alien.

title: Towing from Rental Property
bodyText:
If you find a vehicle you believe is abandoned on rental property you own or control, Indiana lets you have an officer remove it, or arrange removal yourself by attaching a prominent notice tag with your name, address and phone number, the date and time, and a statement that the vehicle is considered abandoned and will be removed after 24 hours, that the vehicle's owner will be responsible for removal, storage and disposal costs, and that the owner may avoid the costs by removing the vehicle or parts within 24 hours; after 24 hours you may have it towed, or at once in an emergency.

An owner of commercial private property may establish a tow-away zone only with conspicuous signs posted between five and seven feet high that give contact information and say who may park; local units may set different rules.

title: Deaths and Crimes on the Property
bodyText: An Indiana owner or agent need not tell a tenant or applicant that a person died on the property, or that it was the site of a felony, criminal-organization activity, a police shooting, or the illegal manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance, and is not liable for refusing to disclose it. But you may not intentionally misrepresent those facts in answer to a direct question.

title: Former Drug Lab Sites
bodyText: Indiana has no statute requiring a landlord to tell tenants that a unit was used to make illegal drugs. After a contaminated site is demolished or remediated, the owner must file documentation with the state and local health departments that the work met the state's standards, and a qualified inspector issues a certificate of decontamination after proper remediation; the state lists such properties on a public website until 90 days after certification. A former drug lab is 'psychologically affected' property, which you need not disclose but may not misrepresent when asked directly.

title: No Radon Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Indiana has no statute requiring a landlord to test for radon or disclose radon to tenants.

title: No Mold Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Indiana has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose or remediate mold in rentals; health and housing codes, which the landlord must follow, may reach conditions that make a unit unsafe.

title: No Bed Bug Rule
bodyText: Indiana has no statute on bed bug disclosure, inspection or treatment in rentals.

title: No EV Charging Rule
bodyText: Indiana has no statute giving tenants a right to install or use electric vehicle charging.

title: Calling Police or Emergency Help
bodyText: An Indiana city, town or county may not penalize a tenant, owner or landlord, including by fines or by causing or threatening eviction, for a call for police or emergency help made by or for a victim of abuse or crime or a person in an emergency, when the caller reasonably believed help was needed or it was needed. A locality may penalize other calls, but a penalty for a tenant's call must be assessed against the tenant, not the landlord, and may not exceed $250. The statute limits local governments; no Indiana statute addresses a lease term on emergency calls.

title: Address Confidentiality Program Participants
bodyText: If a tenant gives you written notice on the state form that the tenant participates in Indiana's address confidentiality program, you may not knowingly disclose the tenant's address, and you may not display the tenant's name at the address, including on a mailbox, door or tenant directory or in a clubhouse or other common area. You may disclose with the tenant's written consent for that purpose, and may give the tenant's name to the state or a local government only in response to a specific request tied to an active code investigation or inspection or an active investigation of a law violation by the tenant.

title: Cable and Internet Providers in Multitenant Buildings
bodyText: In Indiana, the owner or operator of multitenant real estate in an area where communications providers are authorized may not prevent or interfere with a provider's installation of equipment a tenant requests, discriminate among providers, take unreasonable payments for access, or charge tenants different rent based on their provider. You may impose conditions reasonably necessary for safety, security, appearance and the convenience of others, limit installation hours, limit the number of providers if space requires it, require indemnity, require the tenant or provider to bear the full cost, and charge providers reasonable, nondiscriminatory compensation. A tenant, provider or local unit may sue, and the winner recovers attorney's fees.

title: Foreign-Adversary Land Rules
bodyText: Indiana bars a 'prohibited person' (a citizen of China, Iran, North Korea, Russia or another country the governor designates, or certain companies) from buying, leasing or acquiring land directly adjacent to a military installation, with no exception for residential leases; a violation is enforced by the Attorney General through a receivership sale. A separate ten-mile-radius ban does not apply to residential leases. A landlord who is not a prohibited person has no liability for failing to ask whether a tenant is one.

title: Manager and Agent Disclosure Consequences
bodyText: If you do not give the tenant, in writing at or before the start of the lease, the names and addresses of an Indiana resident authorized to manage the unit and an Indiana resident who can accept legal papers and notices for the owner, the person who failed to disclose becomes your agent for service, notices and your obligations, and the tenant may recover the reasonable cost of finding that information. The duty binds later owners and managers.

title: Lease Copies
bodyText: Indiana has no statute requiring a landlord to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, and the consumer protection act's list of deceptive acts does not include failing to give one. A written lease must be attached to a small claims filing based on it.

title: Foreclosure and Tenants
bodyText: No Indiana statute sets tenant protections or landlord disclosure duties when rental property is foreclosed. Federal law may protect tenants after a foreclosure sale.

title: Tenant Screening
bodyText: Indiana has no statute regulating how landlords screen tenants, and cities and counties may not regulate a landlord's screening process. Fair housing law applies, and Indiana's fair housing act does not bar refusing someone convicted of illegal manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance. A tenant who gave materially false information to get the lease can be removed through an emergency possessory order.

title: Serving Notices
bodyText: Indiana's statutory notices to end a tenancy may be served on the tenant; if the tenant cannot be found, on a person living at the premises, who must have the notice explained; and if no one is found, by attaching a copy to a conspicuous part of the premises. Indiana's electronic transactions law lists no exclusion for landlord-tenant notices, but it applies only if both parties agreed to deal electronically and it does not replace a delivery method the law specifies; see the notice method row.

title: House Rules
bodyText: An Indiana tenant must follow all reasonable rules and regulations in effect when the lease is signed. A tenant must follow amended rules only as the lease provides, so a lease without a rule-change term may not bind the tenant to rules you adopt later. Enforcing the rules in court requires notice and a reasonable time to comply.

title: Accessory Dwelling Units in Indiana
bodyText:
Indiana has no statute that requires cities or counties to allow accessory dwelling units, that sets a minimum rental term for one, or that requires the owner to live on the lot before an accessory unit can be rented.

Since July 1, 2026 state law defines an accessory dwelling unit as a self-contained living unit inside or on the same lot as a single-family home, no larger than the lesser of 75% of the home's interior habitable area or 1,000 square feet, with its own cooking, sleeping and sanitation facilities, and complying with (or exempt from) building, fire and health codes; a manufactured home regulated under the state manufactured-home zoning standards is not one.

Each county, city and town must hold a public hearing by January 1, 2027 to review its zoning and development rules with the goal of increasing housing, including by allowing accessory dwelling units, and report the result to the state by the same date; the law does not require any particular outcome, so whether you may build one is still a local zoning question.

Once a unit is lawfully there, renting it is protected in the same way as renting any home: since July 1, 2026 a locality may not prohibit or restrict using privately owned residential property as a rental, apart from general health and safety rules, building and fire codes, reasonable occupancy standards and the permitted registration and inspection programs (rules adopted before 2026 have until January 1, 2028).

Whether a local condition such as owner occupancy on renting an accessory unit survives that bar has not been decided in any case this library has reviewed, so check with the locality before relying on, or contesting, such a condition. A detached guest house or other living quarters on a single-family property counts as part of a short-term rental if you rent it for less than 30 days at a time through a booking platform, and the short-term rental rules then apply.

An association's rental restrictions are governed by its own documents. If you rent an accessory unit, the optional clause describing the unit, the shared areas and shared utilities helps avoid disputes.

title: How Notices May Be Given in Indiana, and Agreeing on Email
bodyText:
Indiana landlord-tenant law has no actual-notice standard and no provision letting you and the tenant agree that a text message or other added method counts as notice. Two sets of rules decide the question instead. First, the notices that end a tenancy or demand unpaid rent may be served on the tenant; if the tenant cannot be found, on a person living at the premises, who must have the notice explained; and if no one is found, by attaching a copy to a conspicuous part of the premises.

The statute says these methods may be used and does not say whether a lease can add others; no court decision on that was reviewed, so serve these notices only by those methods. Second, Indiana's electronic transactions law applies only when both of you have agreed to deal electronically. If you have, a law requiring information in writing is met by an electronic record the tenant can keep at the time it arrives, and you may not use a system that stops the tenant from printing or downloading it.

Where another law requires posting, display or a particular delivery method, that method still has to be used. Either of you may refuse to deal electronically in later transactions even after agreeing, and a lease cannot take that right away. Unless you agree otherwise, an email is received when it reaches an address the tenant designated or uses for that kind of message, even if no one reads it.

So an email or text can carry routine written notices, such as a 30-day notice changing the rental agreement or notice of a sale, if the lease says so; send the itemized deposit statement to the mailing address the tenant gave you in writing (an email copy can go too); and use the statutory methods for notices ending the tenancy or demanding rent. Your notice of entry may be oral, so a text or call works for it. The optional electronic notice clause sets this up.

Federal law adds two points: the federal electronic signatures law may also require the tenant's informed consent, given as that law describes, before an email can replace a written notice (whether Indiana's own electronic transactions law displaces that federal rule is unsettled and no court decision was reviewed, so the optional electronic notice clause includes the consent), and that federal law does not reach eviction notices for a tenant's primary residence.

title: Notices of Proceedings Against the Property
bodyText:
Indiana does not require you to tell your tenant about a foreclosure, tax sale, lien, condemnation or other proceeding against the property, and it does not require the tenant to tell you about papers delivered to the unit.

Some proceedings reach the tenant directly instead: in a nuisance action, every tenant or resident who may be affected by the court's order must get the notice the court orders and a chance to be heard; before the enforcement authority carries out an unsafe-building order to vacate, the order must have been served on anyone holding a present possessory interest, which includes a tenant; and a state or local agency acquiring property is to schedule its work, as far as practicable, so that a lawful occupant gets at least 90 days' written notice before having to move.

Tax sale notices, on the other hand, go only to owners and to holders of interests shown in the public records, so a tenant with an unrecorded lease usually hears nothing until the sale. Because you may not otherwise learn of papers left at the property, the library's clause requiring the tenant to forward notices received at the premises applies in Indiana leases (see the clause on notice of proceedings against the property). Telling the tenant about a proceeding that may affect the tenancy is good practice.

title: No Statutory Fee for Tampering With a Smoke Detector
bodyText:
Indiana has no statute that authorizes, sets or caps a fee for removing, disabling or tampering with a smoke detector or carbon monoxide alarm. The rules are these: no one may tamper with or remove a smoke detector except when necessary for maintenance; the tenant must keep each detector working, replace batteries as needed and not damage the premises; and you must repair or replace a required detector within seven working days after written notice, whoever caused the problem.

You may recover the actual, reasonable cost of repairing or replacing a detector the tenant's side damaged or disabled. If you have already made the repair and sue for it during the tenancy, you must first give the tenant notice describing the repair and documenting its cost. A flat fee fixed in advance is not authorized by statute, and Indiana courts decide whether such a fee is an unenforceable penalty; this library has not reviewed those cases, so it offers only an optional clause for the documented actual cost. Indiana has no statute requiring carbon monoxide alarms in rentals.

title: No Algorithmic Rent-Setting Law in Indiana; Antitrust Still Applies
bodyText: Indiana has no law on algorithmic rent-setting: no statute bans or regulates rent-pricing software, revenue management tools or shared rent data, and none names landlords in its antitrust law. Indiana's general antitrust statute still applies to landlords. It makes illegal every scheme, contract or combination in restraint of trade or to raise or lower the price of a commodity; taking part is a Class A misdemeanor, and anyone whose business or property is injured may sue for three times the damages, plus costs and reasonable attorney's fees. Whether competing landlords who feed private rent data into a common pricing tool and follow its recommendations form an illegal combination is for Indiana courts (this library has not reviewed those cases, or federal antitrust law, which also applies). The cautious course: set your own rents, do not share nonpublic rent, occupancy or lease data with competing landlords or through a tool that recommends rents for competing properties, and keep the final rent decision with you. Cities and counties may not regulate rents unless a state law allows it. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: No Indiana Duty to Provide Alternate Housing
bodyText: No Indiana statute makes a residential landlord provide, find or pay for other housing for a tenant: not while the unit is being repaired, not after a fire or other damage, not when the unit becomes unfit to live in, and not because the tenant asks. This is the same for fixed-term, month-to-month and other tenancies. Indiana answers a failure of your repair and habitability duties with a lawsuit instead. After the tenant gives you notice and a reasonable time to repair (and lets you in to do the work), a tenant who wins may recover actual and consequential damages, attorney's fees and court costs, an injunction, or any other remedy the court finds appropriate; your liability for damages begins when you refuse, or fail within a reasonable time, to fix a condition you have notice or actual knowledge of. Those duties cover rental agreements entered into after June 30, 2002 (except a rent-to-own agreement entered into before July 1, 2008) and cannot be waived. Whether a court may count a tenant's hotel or other temporary housing costs as damages is decided by Indiana courts. The cautious course, when a unit cannot be lived in, is to agree with the tenant in writing what happens to rent and to the tenancy for that period, and to keep a record of any temporary arrangement you offer. Relocation payments do exist in Indiana, but a government agency pays them, not you: a state or local agency that acquires property, or that orders people to leave a dwelling in a systematic area code-enforcement program, must pay relocation benefits to the people displaced, tenants included, among them, for an occupant of at least 90 days, a payment of up to $2,500, less a share of the displaced person's income, toward renting a replacement dwelling for up to two years (Indiana Department of Transportation payments follow federal limits instead), and an agency may not make a person move from a dwelling it is acquiring or in such a program unless it has determined that an adequate replacement dwelling is available (see `edu-eminent-domain-in`). A health officer's order to vacate a dwelling unfit for human habitation (with 5 to 15 days to leave) or a local unsafe-building order to vacate does not, by itself, make you rehouse the tenant (see `edu-condemned-premises-rent-in`). If you need a unit empty for a major remodel, you may in good faith seek possession at the end of the term to alter, remodel or demolish the unit in a way that requires the tenant's whole household to move out, even after the tenant has complained or used another protected right; no statute makes you rehouse the tenant then either. A mobile home community operator must give each home owner in the community written notice at least 180 days before the intended closure of the community (failing to is a deceptive act the attorney general or the home owner may sue over), but no statute requires the operator to pay for or find a new site. Because no statute supplies the answer, your lease should say what happens to rent and to the tenancy for any period the unit cannot be lived in (see the casualty clause, `casualty-termination-in`). Indiana law bars cities, towns and counties from regulating lease terms or the rights of the parties to a lease unless the General Assembly authorizes it. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: Animals Left Without Care in an Indiana Rental
bodyText:
No Indiana statute gives a landlord a special right to enter a rental to feed, care for or remove a tenant's animal, and none makes you the animal's owner because you fed or sheltered it for a set number of days.

The ordinary entry rules apply (they cover rental agreements entered into or renewed after June 30, 1999, and cannot be waived): you must give the tenant reasonable written or oral notice before entering and may enter only at reasonable times; you may enter without notice only in an emergency that threatens the safety of the occupants or your property; and you may enter without the tenant's consent under a court order or after the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit; otherwise the statute works through the tenant's consent, which the tenant may not unreasonably withhold for inspections, necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, necessary or agreed services, or showings to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workers or contractors.

Whether an animal in distress counts as an emergency that threatens the occupants or your property is decided by Indiana courts. Anyone without a contractual interest in the property, such as a neighbor or friend you let in, who knowingly or intentionally enters another person's dwelling without that person's consent commits criminal trespass, so a caregiver should go in only with the tenant's consent.

Indiana's animal cruelty law turns on custody, not on ownership or a day count: a person who has a vertebrate animal in the person's custody and recklessly, knowingly or intentionally abandons or neglects it commits cruelty to an animal, a Class A misdemeanor (a Level 6 felony in aggravated cases, for example if the neglect causes the animal's death).

Abandoning means deserting the animal or leaving it without provision for adequate long-term care (leaving it in a place temporarily vacated to protect human life during a disaster is not abandonment); neglect includes endangering the animal's health by failing to provide, or arrange to provide, food or drink to an animal that depends on you for them, and failing to provide adequate bedding and adequate shelter. So if you take a tenant's animal into your own care, you take on those duties while you have it.

For dog-bite liability, a dog's owner includes anyone who possesses, keeps or harbors the dog. If you take a tenant's animal to a veterinarian and it is later treated as abandoned there, the person who delivered it is liable for the veterinarian's reasonable and customary expenses. In a mobile home community, domestic animals and house pets may not be permitted to run at large or commit a nuisance within the community; that rule gives the operator no right to enter a home.

The cautious course when an animal is left alone in a unit is to try to reach the tenant and any emergency contact or tenant's representative, and to call the local animal control agency or the police: a law enforcement officer or other person with authority to impound animals who has probable cause to believe the cruelty law has been violated may take custody of the animal.

If a tenant who was the sole occupant has died, or you believe a sole-occupant tenant is incapacitated and absent, you must notify the tenant's representative and give the representative reasonable access to remove the tenant's belongings (see `edu-tenant-death-in`). Property in a unit the tenant has abandoned is handled under the abandoned-property rules (see `abandoned-property-in`).

The library offers an optional clause, `animal-care-access-in`, in which the tenant names a caregiver and consents in advance to your letting that person in after notice; these rules apply the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Which Appliances You Must Maintain
bodyText: Indiana does not presume that every appliance in a rental is yours to maintain. Your duty covers appliances supplied as an inducement to the lease, and the listed systems (electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air conditioning, and elevators) if they are on the premises when the lease is made; those must be kept in good and safe working condition, and a lease term waiving that duty is void. Whether an appliance was supplied as an inducement is a question of fact that Indiana courts decide. The clearest course is to list in the lease every appliance you supply (use the appliances clause). If you leave an item behind that you do not intend to maintain, say so in writing, but never treat a system the statute lists, such as a water heater, furnace or electrical panel, as excluded, because the statute reaches those systems whenever they are on the premises when the lease is made. You may not remove appliances during a tenancy to force a tenant out.

title: Asbestos: Work Rules, No Tenant Disclosure
bodyText: Indiana has no statute requiring you to tell tenants or applicants about asbestos in a rental or to notify them before asbestos work. Indiana regulates asbestos through its air pollution laws: the state environmental board sets rules for accrediting people who inspect, manage or abate asbestos-containing material and for licensing asbestos contractors. A contractor paid to carry out an asbestos project must hold an asbestos contractor's license, and individuals who work on the project must be accredited, unless the state waives this for a sudden emergency, or exempts an employer whose adequate asbestos safety program covers its own employees' work on premises it owns or leases. The statute directs the rules to exempt work on a private residential dwelling and on a commercial residential building with fewer than five dwelling units, so the accreditation and licensing requirements mainly reach apartment buildings with five or more units. Licensed contractors must keep project records for 30 years, and the state may stop a project that does not follow the asbestos rules. The state rules, which track the federal rules, cover every building except a residential building with four or fewer dwelling units. For a covered building, before any demolition or renovation the owner or operator must have an Indiana-licensed inspector thoroughly inspect the affected area for asbestos; the state must be notified at least 10 working days before any demolition, even if no asbestos is found, and before a renovation that will disturb at least 260 linear feet, 160 square feet or 35 cubic feet of regulated asbestos-containing material, with a fee; emission controls apply once at least 3 linear feet, 3 square feet or 0.75 cubic foot is disturbed; and only licensed persons may inspect for asbestos or work on an asbestos project. None of these rules requires notice to tenants. For a single-family rental or a building of up to four units the rules do not apply, but have suspect materials checked before renovating. Disturbing asbestos during a tenancy also bears on your duty to keep the premises safe; give tenants advance notice of any abatement work in or near their unit.

title: Association Documents and Your Tenant
bodyText:
Indiana has no statute that requires a lease of a condominium unit or of a home in a homeowners association to disclose the association's obligations, attach its documents, or contain a statement by you or the tenant about the association's rules, and a tenant is not treated as a buyer entitled to the association disclosures a seller must give.

Those seller disclosures matter if you sign a lease with an option to buy: Indiana's residential sales disclosure law (for property with four or fewer units) covers a lease with an option to buy, so the owner's disclosure form must be completed, signed and given to the tenant-buyer before the offer is accepted; and on any transfer of title to property in a homeowners association, the seller must give the purchaser, at least 10 days before closing, a disclosure that the property is in an association, a copy of the recorded governing documents, a statement of any assessments, and the names and addresses of the board members, agents or managers.

For a lease-option, the cautious course is to give the association package when the lease is signed, not only before the option closing. For an ordinary lease, giving the tenant the association's rules and recorded covenants before signing is the practical course: a condominium tenant is bound by the condominium statute and the association's declaration and bylaws in any event, and an Indiana tenant must follow reasonable rules in existence when the lease is signed, and later rules only as the lease provides.

The optional clause recording delivery of the association documents does that. Cities and counties may not require their own lease disclosures. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: No Automatic Renewal Statute in Indiana
bodyText:
Indiana has no statute on automatic renewal clauses in residential leases. No Indiana law requires a reminder notice before a lease renews, special type or a separate signed opt-in for a renewal term, or a limit on how early you may ask a tenant to commit to a renewal, and Indiana has no general consumer automatic-renewal law that reaches leases. (Since July 1, 2026, Indiana voids automatic renewal terms only in school vendor contracts, which does not reach leases.) So the lease decides.

What Indiana law does around a renewal: a fixed-term lease ends at the end of its term without notice; if the tenant stays on with your consent, the tenancy becomes month to month and ends on one month's notice; and a year-to-year tenancy ends on notice at least three months before the end of the year.

Whether a lease that renews itself year after year is treated as a year-to-year tenancy is for Indiana courts (this library has not reviewed those cases), so give at least three months' notice of non-renewal for a yearly renewal. Changing the lease, including new rent for a renewal term, needs at least 30 days' written notice unless the written lease sets a different procedure.

If the original term plus renewals could run longer than three years, sign the lease as landlord and have it acknowledged before a notary (or proved), since a lease for a term exceeding three years must be, and record the lease, or a signed and acknowledged memorandum that lists the renewal option, within 45 days of signing: an unrecorded lease longer than three years is void against a later good-faith buyer, tenant or mortgagee, and whether renewal periods count toward the three years is for the courts.

Declining to renew at the end of the term is not retaliation, but you may not refuse to renew solely because a tenant, applicant or household member is protected under Indiana's domestic violence, sex offense and stalking protections. In a mobile home community, an operator that stops renewing lot leases because it is closing the community must give each home owner written notice of the intent to close at least 180 days before the closure; failing to do so is a deceptive act under Indiana's consumer protection law.

An optional Indiana Automatic Renewal clause sets notice floors that meet the one-month, three-month and 30-day rules; it does not give the 180-day notice before a mobile home community closes, which the operator must give separately.

title: No Periodic Balcony Inspection Rule
bodyText: Indiana has no statute or state rule requiring periodic inspection of balconies, decks, porches or other exterior elevated elements at rental buildings. Balconies are built to the statewide building and residential codes when constructed or altered, and must then be maintained under the rules in effect when built; no alteration may make them unsafe under current rules. One maintenance rule reaches older buildings directly: a fire escape used as an exit, including its balconies, must support specified loads, be kept clear, operational and rust-free, and have documentation of compliance kept on site for the code official. A balcony of no more than 100 square feet may be added to an existing unsprinklered apartment building without sprinklering it. Your general duty is to deliver the unit safe, clean and habitable and to make all reasonable efforts to keep common areas in proper condition. Regular inspection of wood balconies and decks, especially for rot and loose railings, is prudent, and some local codes may require it; they are not reviewed here.

title: Bed Bugs and Pests: No Cooperation Statute
bodyText: Indiana has no statute on bed bugs, and none that requires a tenant to report pests, prepare the unit for treatment or cooperate with a pest control operator, or that sets who pays for treatment. Indiana's rat-control law is the exception for rats: anyone who owns, leases, occupies or controls a building and lets it become rat infested commits an infraction, and failing to make a good-faith effort to exterminate after knowledge or notice is a further infraction; if the person does not exterminate, state or local health officials must have the rats exterminated, and where a city or town ordered the extermination the cost is charged against the property and collected like taxes. Otherwise, rely on general duties and the lease. You must deliver the unit safe, clean and habitable and comply with applicable health and housing codes. The tenant must keep the areas the tenant uses reasonably clean, use the premises reasonably, follow reasonable rules, must not unreasonably refuse you entry to inspect or make repairs, and is responsible for damage beyond ordinary wear and tear. Write the reporting, access, preparation and cost terms into the lease or your rules; charging the tenant for treatment is safest where the tenant caused the infestation, and the cost of tenant-caused damage can be taken from the deposit.

title: Binding Arbitration Is Not Offered for Indiana Leases
bodyText: Indiana law allows arbitration agreements: a written agreement to arbitrate future disputes is valid and enforceable except on grounds that would let any contract be revoked, and the federal arbitration act reaches contracts involving interstate commerce. Indiana's arbitration act excludes consumer leases as the consumer credit code defines them, but that definition covers leases of goods, not a lease of a home, so a residential lease is not excluded. An older Indiana arbitration chapter also allows a claim to an interest in a term of years, or a term of one year or less, to be arbitrated, and the court rules preserve the parties' right to agree to arbitrate. In any arbitration under the act each party may be represented by a lawyer, and a waiver of that right made before the hearing is ineffective; no contract can change small claims venue. The library nonetheless does not offer its binding-arbitration clause for Indiana. Its rule is to offer the clause only where state law allows arbitration and no statute penalizes including or enforcing a prohibited lease term. Indiana's consumer protection act treats soliciting a tenant, through unequal bargaining power, to sign terms that unduly limit the tenant's remedies as an unconscionable act; the Attorney General may sue, a court may void or limit the clause, and a knowing violation can carry a civil penalty of up to $5,000. Whether a lease arbitration clause would be found to unduly limit a tenant's remedies is case law, so a penalty may attach and the answer turns on case law. Indiana's other penalty, the misdemeanor for procuring a confession-of-judgment note, does not reach an arbitration clause. If you want arbitration in a lease anyway, have it drafted with legal advice; keep evictions, small claims, deposit claims and emergency possessory orders in court in any case.

title: Marijuana in Indiana Rentals: No Tenant Protection; Still a Crime
bodyText:
Indiana has no medical or recreational marijuana law, and its constitution says nothing on the subject, so no Indiana law protects a tenant who uses marijuana, holds an out-of-state medical card, or wants to grow it, and no Indiana law limits a lease ban. Marijuana remains illegal: possessing it, or growing or cultivating it, is a crime, and so is knowingly letting marijuana grow on your own premises without destroying it.
