Whether a landlord who learns a tenant is growing marijuana in a rental has it growing on the landlord's premises is for Indiana courts (this library has not reviewed those cases), so act promptly.

Knowingly maintaining a building used to unlawfully use, manufacture, keep, offer for sale, sell or deliver a controlled substance is a felony (with a defense for small amounts of marijuana and a first offense), and using a rental to commit a controlled-substance offense is a nuisance that can lead to an abatement action and a court order for the tenant to leave.

Hemp, low-THC hemp extract (such as many CBD products) and smokable hemp are not marijuana under Indiana law, but possessing smokable hemp is itself a crime in Indiana; you may forbid smoking any of them, or any smoking, in the lease. You may treat marijuana use or growing as a lease violation under the library's no-criminal-activity and marijuana clauses, and end the tenancy through the normal court process; do not lock the tenant out.

title: Professional Carpet Cleaning at Move-Out
bodyText: Indiana has no statute on carpet cleaning: none lets you require professional carpet cleaning at move-out, none bars it, and none sets an age or condition test for carpet or paint charges. Two general rules decide the question. The tenant must return the unit clean and in proper condition, ordinary wear and tear excepted, and you may sue for your actual damages if the tenant does not. But you may take from the security deposit only actual damage to the unit beyond ordinary wear and tear (along with rent owed, unpaid utility or sewer charges you paid, and an agreed last period's rent), itemized with the estimated cost of each repair within 45 days, and a lease term waiving those rules is void. Whether routine carpet cleaning after normal use is damage you may take from the deposit, and whether a lease may require professional cleaning regardless of the carpet's condition, are decided by Indiana courts. For that reason the library does not offer a professional carpet cleaning clause for Indiana. The cautious course is to charge for carpet cleaning or replacement only where stains, odors, pet damage or soiling go beyond what ordinary use explains, to list each item with its cost on the 45-day notice, to deduct any carpet's age-related wear rather than charging full replacement, and to keep dated move-in and move-out photos.

title: Changing the Casualty and Re-Renting Rules by Lease
bodyText:
Indiana has no statute on what happens to a residential lease when fire or another casualty damages the home, so there is no statutory casualty rule for a lease to change, and no statute stops the lease from setting one: the lease decides whether either side may end it, and whether rent is reduced, after a casualty (the library offers an optional Indiana casualty clause for that).

One statutory limit applies: while the tenant stays, your duties to comply with health and housing codes, to make all reasonable efforts to keep common areas clean and proper, and to keep the systems you provided in good and safe working condition cannot be waived, so a casualty clause may let either side end the lease but cannot excuse you from those duties while the tenant stays. These duties cover rental agreements entered into after June 30, 2002, except a rent-to-own agreement entered into before July 1, 2008.

Mitigation is likewise not in any statute: no Indiana statute says whether you must try to re-rent after a tenant leaves early, and none says whether a lease may waive or narrow that duty; Indiana courts decide it. The deposit statute lets you apply the deposit to rent due for the tenant's premature termination.

Cautious course: do not write a clause saying you have no duty to re-rent or that the tenant owes all remaining rent regardless; make and document reasonable re-renting efforts. The library's default-by-tenant clause promises reasonable mitigation to the extent the law requires.

title: No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure in Indiana
bodyText: Indiana does not require you to show a tenant a certificate of occupancy, attach one to the lease, post it or say in the lease whether the unit has one. Whether a building or unit needs an occupancy permit before anyone lives in it is a local question: a city, town or county zoning ordinance may require an occupancy permit for the use of a structure, and units may use private providers for some inspections tied to certificates of occupancy. Make sure any required local permit is in place before a tenant moves in, because renting a unit that may not lawfully be occupied invites disputes and enforcement. Under the state law limiting local landlord-tenant rules, local governments may not add their own lease disclosure requirements for privately owned rentals unless the legislature authorizes it, and their rental registration and inspection programs are limited by separate state law (see the rental registration and inspection row). This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: Children and Occupancy in Indiana: Fair Housing and the Occupancy Standard
bodyText:
Indiana has no rule that a lease must address children, and no landlord-tenant rule on a child born or adopted during a tenancy. Fair housing law governs instead.

You may not refuse to rent, or set different terms, conditions or services, because of familial status, which covers a person who is pregnant, who lives with a child under 18 as parent or legal custodian (or with the custodian's written permission), or who is in the process of getting custody; and you may not advertise any preference or limit based on familial status (no "adults only"). Two limits apply.

Indiana's landlord-tenant law does not stop you from refusing to rent on the basis of a reasonable occupancy standard, though fair housing law still governs how you set and apply it; two people per bedroom is presumed reasonable if you do not count infants under one year old and you count a den, library, finished basement or loft that could reasonably be used for sleeping (unless codes forbid it), and reasonable local or state limits on the number of occupants still apply.

And housing for older persons (housing under an elderly program, housing solely for people 62 or older, or 55-and-older housing meeting the 80% occupancy, published-policy and verification requirements) is exempt from the familial-status rule.

Some small owners are exempt from the fair housing rental rules: an owner of no more than three single-family houses renting without a broker or discriminatory advertising (only one rental in 24 months if the owner was not the house's most recent resident), and an owner living in a building of up to four units. The single-family exemption is lost if you publish a discriminatory advertisement, and federal fair housing law may still reach an owner Indiana exempts, so do not rely on either exemption without advice. When a child joins a household mid-lease, apply the same occupancy standard you would apply to any new occupant.

title: No Cold-Weather Notice Before Vacating
bodyText: Indiana has no statute requiring a tenant who moves out in cold weather to tell you first so you can protect the unit from freezing, and no statute setting a landlord's freeze-protection duty for a vacated unit. Notice of moving out is governed by the lease and Indiana's general notice rules for ending a tenancy. A tenant must not shut off utilities if that will seriously damage the unit, and must return it in clean and proper condition except for ordinary wear and tear; damage from frozen pipes caused by the tenant's conduct can be taken from the deposit as actual damages. Once a unit is abandoned (rent unpaid and circumstances showing a reasonable person that the tenant surrendered possession), the ban on interrupting utilities and entering without consent no longer applies, so you may enter to winterize. Because winter heating-season rules let a gas or electric utility disconnect a tenant's account after 14 days' notice for nonpayment, put a lease term in place that requires the tenant to keep heat on at a stated minimum during the tenancy and to give you advance written notice of moving out between November and April, and check vacant units promptly.

title: Collection Fees and Collection Agencies
bodyText:
Indiana has no statute that caps, bars or sets terms for a fee charged to a tenant when unpaid rent or other charges are sent to collection. Federal debt-collection law, which Indiana's consumer act adopts, is what shapes the fee: a third-party debt collector may collect a fee, charge or expense on top of the debt only if the agreement creating the debt expressly authorizes it or the law permits it, and may not misstate the amount or legal status of the debt.

Residential rent and charges are consumer debts for this purpose. So if you want a collection fee passed to the tenant, the lease must say so expressly (see the optional collection fee clause), and any amount the collector adds beyond what the lease authorizes is at the collector's risk and can make the collection a deceptive act under Indiana law.

When you collect your own debt in your own name you are generally not a debt collector under the federal law, but you become one if you use a name suggesting that a third party is collecting.

In Indiana a business that collects debts owed to others must be licensed by the Secretary of State, must keep collected money in a special account and pay it over within 60 days, and commits a misdemeanor if it operates unlicensed; attorneys, licensed real estate brokers and businesses whose main work is not collection are outside that licensing law.

Within 5 days after first contacting the tenant, a debt collector must send a written notice of the debt that gives the tenant 30 days to dispute it, unless the first contact already contained that information or the tenant has paid. The cautious course is to use a licensed agency, authorize only its actual fee up to a stated ceiling, never take the fee from the security deposit, and keep it out of any notice demanding rent or possession.

title: Common Area Lighting: No Specific Rule
bodyText: Apart from mobile home communities, Indiana has no statute that sets lighting levels for the halls, stairs, entrances or parking areas of a rental, and no rule on whether a tenant may be made to pay for common-area lights wired to the tenant's own electric service. Your general duty is to make all reasonable efforts to keep common areas in a clean and proper condition (leases entered into after June 30, 2002), and to comply with applicable health and housing codes. A mobile home community must be lighted at night throughout, and the state health rules require at least 0.3 foot-candles of light on its streets and walkways, or a yard light on each lot giving at least the light of a 40-watt incandescent bulb. For buildings, the statewide codes govern lighting in new construction and alterations: the residential code for one- and two-family homes requires an artificial light at the top landing of an exterior stairway that serves emergency egress, and at the bottom landing of an exterior basement stairway; exit and egress lighting in apartment buildings comes from the model building and fire codes, which are not reviewed here, and existing lighting must be maintained as installed. If the building is submetered for electricity, common-area electricity must be your responsibility and the lease must say so. In a building that is not submetered, wiring common-area lights to a tenant's meter is not addressed by Indiana law; the cautious course is to keep common-area lighting on your own account, or, if it cannot be separated, say so plainly in the lease and adjust the rent.

title: No Communal Land Lease Approval
bodyText: Indiana has no communal, clan or native land system and no state statute that requires a government officer to approve a lease of such land before it is valid. An ordinary Indiana residential lease between private parties needs no government approval to be valid. Leases longer than three years must be recorded to protect them against later buyers and lenders (see the lease recording row). If a property is land held in trust by the United States for a tribe or a tribal member, federal law, not Indiana law, governs whether and how it may be leased; this library has not reviewed that law, so get advice before leasing such land.

title: Rent After a Vacate Order or Condemnation
bodyText: Indiana has no statute that bars you from collecting rent once a unit is condemned or ordered vacated, and none that abates rent automatically or ends the lease when that happens. Two kinds of orders can empty a rental. A local unsafe-building authority (in Indianapolis and Marion County, and in any city, town or county that has adopted the state unsafe-building law) may order an unsafe building vacated; anyone who remains in or enters the building in violation of the order commits a Class C infraction, each day a separate offense. A local board of health, county health officer or the Indiana Department of Health may order everyone to leave a dwelling unfit for human habitation within 5 to 15 days. If a court appoints a receiver for unsafe premises, the receiver, not you, collects the rents and uses them for the repairs. Your duties to deliver the unit in a safe, clean and habitable condition and to follow health and housing codes cannot be waived, and a tenant who gives you notice and a reasonable time to repair may sue for damages and other relief. Whether a tenant still owes rent for a period when the unit is condemned or under a vacate order, or may treat the lease as ended, is decided by Indiana courts. The cautious course is not to charge or sue for rent for any period the unit is under a vacate order, to refund rent and deposit amounts the tenant has prepaid for that period, to put any agreement to end or suspend the lease in writing, and not to treat the tenant's leaving under the order as abandonment or a default. In a Housing Choice Voucher tenancy, the housing agency may withhold, and then must abate, its payments for violations not corrected in time, and you may not end the family's tenancy because it did; a township paying shelter assistance will not pay the full shelter amount or a deposit for substandard housing. Local ordinances that bar rent for condemned units would generally be void (localities may not regulate rents or the parties' rights), and none was reviewed here. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: No Confession of Judgment in an Indiana Lease
bodyText: A lease term that lets you, or a lawyer or agent you choose, appear for the tenant in court, waive service of process, or confess a money judgment against the tenant without a hearing after notice, or that releases errors and appeal rights or consents to execution on such a judgment, may not be signed as part of a written contract to pay money before a claim has arisen, and such a term given before a claim accrues is void. Knowingly getting a tenant to sign one, keeping one as its holder, or trying to enforce in Indiana another state's judgment based on one is a Class B misdemeanor, and Indiana courts will not enforce such a foreign judgment or let it become a lien on real estate. The rule applies to any written contract to pay money, so it reaches leases of every type and length. Collect unpaid rent and damages by suing in the ordinary way, usually on a small claims docket. The library's general row on void lease terms covers this rule with the others.

title: Habitability: What Indiana Has and Lacks
bodyText: How Indiana compares on habitability features found in other states. Indiana has (by statute): a list of landlord duties (safe, clean and habitable delivery in compliance with the lease, health and housing code compliance, reasonable efforts on common areas, and working electrical, plumbing with hot and cold water, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning systems, elevators and inducement appliances where provided); a rule voiding any waiver of those duties; a tenant's suit after notice and a reasonable time to repair, with damages, attorney's fees and an injunction; emergency possessory orders for lockouts and utility shutoffs; smoke detector duties with a seven-working-day repair period after written notice; tenant duties of its own; and retaliation protection for repair and code complaints. Indiana lacks (we found no statute): a way to waive or trade a habitability duty for lower rent, or a separate-document procedure; a list of duties the lease may modify or shift, with or without consideration; a materiality threshold for the repair suit; any presumption about habitability, repairs or retaliation; a required habitability statement in the lease; rent withholding, rent escrow or repair and deduct, including under lead or health laws; a statutory right for you to fix a tenant's breach and bill it; a designated-repairer rule; a writing or completion-date rule for repair promises; a required form for repair requests (beyond smoke detectors); a statutory casualty rule; and a statutory mitigation rule. Where a statute is silent, Indiana courts decide, including whether an implied warranty of habitability applies. Each item has its own row.

title: Other Rules Indiana Does Not Have
bodyText: Searches across the whole 2026 Indiana Code and the 2026 session laws confirmed that Indiana has no statute on each of the following; in each case the lease, general law and Indiana case law (not reviewed in this library) decide, and the linked rows give the cautious course. (1) no early-termination right for illness, incapacity or a move to care; (2) no bar on demanding rent for a code-cited unit, and no rent escrow; (3) no hardship stay or eviction moratorium rule; (4) no end-of-term possession bond; (5) no rent-into-court or compulsory counterclaim rule; (6) no post-notice or post-judgment redemption and no relief-from-forfeiture statute; (7) no statute on minors as tenants or eviction defendants; (8) no state rule on evictions after a tenant's bankruptcy; (9) no late-benefit continuance or reinstatement; (10) no repair-cost termination right; (11) no environmental-event or declared-disaster rule ending a lease or suspending rent (the governor's disaster-emergency powers over the occupancy of premises still apply); (12) no statute on a lease's fate on an eminent domain taking. Several neighbouring points do have Indiana rules: a tenant defeats a 10-day nonpayment notice by paying the rent in full before it expires; a lockout or utility shutoff is barred except by court order; a protected victim and a servicemember may end a lease early; an owner may have a squatter removed by affidavit; and a lease must disclose a flood-plain location. Check each linked row before relying on an absence, because a later act may add a rule.

title: Rules Searched Outside the Landlord-Tenant Chapters
bodyText: These questions were checked across the whole Indiana Code, not only the landlord-tenant chapters. (1) Squatters: Indiana does have a specific remedy. Since July 1, 2025, an owner may give law enforcement a sworn affidavit that the occupant has never had a rental agreement, permission or other right to be there, and officers must be dispatched to remove the person within 48 hours unless public safety requires a delay; the affidavit is made under penalty of perjury, and a person removed on an affidavit you knowingly made materially false may sue you. It does not apply to a current or former tenant, even one whose lease expired or who broke it, or to an invitee; those people must be removed through the courts (see the squatter row). (2) Cash rent receipts: no statute requires you to give a receipt for rent, even rent paid in cash. Indiana does require a written receipt for each cash rental payment under a rent-to-own agreement, but that law covers household goods, not homes. Give a receipt anyway; in a dispute over whether rent was paid it is your evidence too. (3) Landlord registration and eviction: no state rental registry or landlord license exists, and no statute makes local registration a condition of filing an eviction or winning possession; state law limits what local registration and inspection programs may require (see the local registration row). A different filing can block a lawsuit: an out-of-state entity doing business in Indiana may not bring or keep a lawsuit until it registers with the Secretary of State (see the out-of-state owner row). (4) Duties that bind any person: anyone who has reason to believe a child is being abused or neglected, or that an adult is an endangered adult, must report it (see the law-enforcement row).

title: Construction Liens for Tenant Work in Indiana
bodyText:
Indiana's mechanic's lien law lets a contractor, subcontractor, mechanic, journeyman, laborer, equipment lessor or anyone else who performs labor or furnishes materials or machinery to build, alter, repair or remove a building or other structure (and for walks, wells, drains, sewers, cisterns and earth moving) claim a lien on the structure and on the interest of the owner of the land.

The lien reaches the land only to the extent of the right, title and interest of the owner for whose immediate use or benefit the work was done or the materials furnished. When a tenant orders work, the lien therefore reaches the tenant's leasehold; and where the owner has only a leasehold interest, the lien on buildings the lienholder put up is not lost if the lease is forfeited for unpaid rent (those buildings may be sold and removed within 90 days after the sale).

Whether a contractor the tenant hired can also reach your ownership, for example because the lease required, approved or consented to the work, is not answered by any Indiana statute; Indiana courts decide it. Indiana has no notice of nonresponsibility that an owner can post or record to keep tenant work off its interest, and no statute that lets a lease, recorded or not, keep your interest free of liens for the tenant's improvements.

The statute allows a no-lien term only in a listed set of contracts: the contract between an owner and the principal contractor to build, alter or repair a one- or two-family dwelling or townhouse, or an improvement on the same real estate that serves it, or to prepare property for that kind of residential construction (or to work on certain regulated utility property), may say that no lien may attach, and it binds subcontractors, laborers and suppliers only if it is in writing, gives the legal description of the real estate, is acknowledged like a deed and is recorded with the county recorder within 5 days after it is signed; it does not affect a lien for labor or materials supplied before it is recorded.

For other buildings (apart from that utility property), including those occupied by three or more tenants, a provision in a contract for the improvement of real estate that requires a worker or supplier to waive lien rights before being paid, or under which anyone agrees not to file a notice of intention to hold a lien, is void.

A claimant creates a lien by recording a sworn notice of intention to hold a lien in the county recorder's office within 90 days after performing the labor or furnishing the materials (60 days for a one- or two-family dwelling or townhouse); the recorder mails a copy to the owner the notice names, the lien relates back to when the work began, and the claimant must sue to foreclose within one year after recording (or after a credit expires, but only if the credit is in writing, signed by the lienholder and all owners of record, and recorded within that year) or the lien is void.

As an owner, or as anyone with an interest in the property, you may give the lienholder written notice to file a foreclosure action; if it does not file within 30 days after receiving the notice, the lien is void (the debt can still be collected in other ways), and after notice by registered or certified mail you may record an affidavit of service to clear the record.

In a foreclosure action you may file a written undertaking with surety, approved by the court, and the court must then release the property from the lien. Once the debt is paid, the lienholder must release the lien within 15 days after your demand or owe you the greater of your actual damages or $10 a day.

A lien claimant who wins recovers reasonable attorney's fees, but not against the property owner where the owner, or the party for whom the improvement was built (such as the tenant), has paid the contract price for the work. A subcontractor, laborer or equipment lessor of the tenant's contractor may also give the property owner written notice of its claim, but the owner is liable on that notice only up to what the owner owes, or comes to owe, that contractor.

The written lien notice that a supplier selling on credit must give within 30 days to the occupying owner of a one- or two-family dwelling applies only to a home its owner occupies, so it does not protect you for a home you rent out (it can reach a double you live in half of).

Because the statute leaves your exposure to case law, the cautious course is to require the tenant to get your written consent before any alteration, to say in the lease that the tenant alone is responsible for paying for its work and that your consent is not an agreement to pay, to have the tenant tell its contractors so before work starts, and to act promptly on any lien notice the recorder mails you. The library's optional clause `no-liens-ar` does this.

Its reimbursement of your costs is a payment under the lease, and because the deposit statute treats every payment under the lease other than the deposit as rent, you may apply the deposit to an unpaid enforceable reimbursement as rent in arrears. A mobile home community operator's lien on a resident's property is a different lien, like an innkeeper's lien, not a construction lien.

title: No Condominium Conversion Notice in Indiana; Ordinary Notices Apply
bodyText: Indiana has no condominium or cooperative conversion law for tenants: no notice period before conversion, no tenant right of first refusal or option to buy, no required conversion statement in the lease, and no state bar on converting rental housing to hotel or short-term use. Ordinary rules govern a conversion. A sale or conversion is valid without the tenant's agreement, and rent the tenant pays before learning of the conveyance counts against the new owner. A lease longer than three years that was not recorded within 45 days is void against a later good-faith buyer for value; whether other leases bind the buyer is for Indiana courts (this library has not reviewed those cases), so treat every lease as surviving the sale. To recover a unit you must use the normal notices: a fixed term runs to its end, a month-to-month tenancy ends on one month's notice, and a year-to-year tenancy on notice three months before the year ends. Even after a tenant's protected activity, you may in good faith take possession at the end of the term to end the property's use as a rental for at least six months. In a mobile home community, an operator closing the community must give each home owner written notice at least 180 days before closure; failing to do so is a deceptive act. Converting to short-term rentals brings the short-term rental permit and zoning rules and sales and innkeeper's taxes on stays under 30 days. When you sell, the new owner is bound by the deposit-return rules.

title: Grounds for Ending a Lease and Cure Periods
bodyText:
Indiana sets a cure period by statute for only one breach: unpaid rent. If rent is not paid when due, you may end the lease on at least 10 days' notice unless the parties agreed otherwise or the tenant pays the rent in full before the notice period runs out; no notice is needed if the lease expressly requires rent in advance and the tenant does not pay it (see the nonpayment-notice row).

For any other breach of the lease, no Indiana statute sets a notice or cure period, and no statute makes breach of a lease term, material or not, a ground for eviction. Whether a breach lets you end the lease, whether the lease may set its own cure period and notice method, and whether a lease can decide which terms are material, are left to the lease and to Indiana case law.

The cautious course is a lease that says plainly that a breach is a default, gives written notice and a fair chance to cure (as the library's default clause does), and is applied the same way to every tenant. Two statutes shape non-rent cases.

First, before you sue to enforce the duties Indiana itself imposes on tenants (following health and housing codes, keeping the unit reasonably clean, using systems and appliances reasonably, not damaging the unit, following reasonable rules, keeping smoke detectors working), you must give the tenant notice of the noncompliance and a reasonable time to fix it, unless the tenant has already moved out; give that notice before any suit, including one for possession, that rests on those duties.

Second, if the tenant has made a protected complaint (for example to a code office), you may not bring an eviction in response to it; an eviction for a non-rent breach is expressly allowed if the breach materially affects health or safety, or if another listed exception applies.

Grounds Indiana's statutes do recognize without a cure period: the end of a fixed term (no notice needed); ending a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy on notice equal to the period (no reason needed); a tenant at sufferance; waste; a crime by the tenant or a guest that affects the health and safety of another tenant, you or your agent, or materially false information given to get the lease (these support an emergency possessory order); and a drug nuisance (see the related rows).

Federal rules for assisted and federally backed housing can add notice requirements (see the federal 30-day notice row).

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure in Indiana
bodyText: Indiana has no rule requiring you to disclose defective or corrosive drywall to a tenant, and its statutes mention drywall only as construction and demolition waste and as material burned in fire-training demonstrations. If you lease a home of up to four units with an option to buy, the seller's disclosure form covers the known condition of the structure and other areas, which would include known defective drywall (see the optional lease terms row). Otherwise, if you know of a drywall problem that affects health or safety, deal with it as a repair: your duty to keep the unit safe and habitable applies (see the landlord duties row), and misstating a known condition to a tenant can be a deceptive act under Indiana's consumer protection law.

title: Pre-Set Cleaning or Repair Charges and the Deposit
bodyText: Indiana has no statute that specifically authorizes a lease to fix cleaning, carpet or repair charges in advance and take them from the security deposit, and none that specifically bars or limits a charge for professional carpet or other cleaning. The deposit law controls instead. You may use the deposit only for actual damage to the unit or its facilities beyond ordinary wear and tear, rent owed (including rent due because the tenant ended the lease early), unpaid utility or sewer charges the tenant owed and you paid, and the last period's rent if a written agreement says so. Within 45 days after the tenant's occupancy ends you must mail an itemized list giving the estimated cost of repair for each damaged item, with the balance. Those rules measure a damage deduction by the damage actually done and its repair cost, and a lease term waiving them is void. A charge fixed in the lease is a payment under the rental agreement, which the deposit law counts as rent and lets the deposit pay if unpaid, but only if the charge itself is enforceable. Separately, a tenant under a lease entered into after June 30, 2002 must hand the unit back clean and in proper condition, ordinary wear and tear excepted, and you may sue for your actual damages if the tenant does not. Whether the cost of cleaning a unit left dirty is damage you may take from the deposit, and whether a pre-set cleaning or repair charge is enforceable or is an unenforceable penalty that gets around the wear-and-tear limit, are decided by Indiana courts. The cautious course is to charge cleaning or carpet work only where the unit was left in worse shape than ordinary use explains, to list each item with its actual or estimated cost on the 45-day list, and to keep dated move-in and move-out photos. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies. Cities and counties may not regulate security deposits. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds Go to the State
bodyText: Indiana's Revised Unclaimed Property Act names a security deposit and a refund among the property it covers when held or owed in the course of a business, and a business for this purpose includes any kind of business entity, down to a sole proprietorship. So a deposit balance you owe a former tenant, or a refund check the tenant never cashes, does not become yours because the tenant cannot be found or does not respond; you hold it for the tenant. No section sets a period for deposits as such: a debt of a business is presumed abandoned three years after the obligation to pay arises, and other property three years after the owner could first demand it, counted from the tenant's last contact or other sign of interest. Once the money is presumed abandoned you must: mail the tenant a notice carrying the heading the Act prescribes, not more than 180 and not less than 60 days before you report, if you have a usable address and the amount is $50 or more; report it electronically to the Attorney General before November 1 each year, covering the 12 months before July 1; pay it over when you report; and keep the records for 10 years. A late report or payment costs interest, and the Attorney General may also impose a civil penalty of $200 a day, up to $5,000. A contract or arrangement made to evade the Act, or a willful failure to perform a duty, can cost $1,000 a day, up to $25,000, plus 25% of the amount. The Attorney General must waive the interest and penalties if it determines that you acted in good faith and without negligence, and paying over in good faith after giving the notice relieves you of later liability for the money. A lease term letting you keep an unclaimed refund does not avoid any of this: the deposit law requires the balance to be returned and voids any waiver of its rules, the Act applies even if the tenant never asks for the money, and an arrangement made to evade the Act draws the higher penalties. The Act lets a holder deduct a dormancy charge only if a valid contract with the owner authorizes it and the holder regularly imposes it, and only in an amount that is not unconscionable; this library does not offer one: such a charge would arise only after the 45-day itemized return the deposit law requires, and whether a lease may impose it on an unclaimed refund is not settled. Whether an individual renting out a single home holds the refund in the course of a business is not settled by the Act; the cautious course is to follow it. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Right to Pay the Deposit in Installments
bodyText: Indiana has no statute that gives a tenant the right to pay a security deposit in installments, and none that requires, limits or sets terms for an installment plan. You may require the whole deposit before the tenancy starts, or you may agree to take it in parts; if you agree, put the schedule in writing so both sides know when each part is due. Every part paid is part of the security deposit and follows the same use and 45-day return rules. If you spread the deposit by charging more than the average rent in some months, the extra over the average rent for the term is itself a security deposit under Indiana law, not rent, so account for it the same way. A lease term waiving the deposit rules is void. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies. Cities and counties may not regulate security deposits. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: No Move-Out Notice Condition on the Deposit Refund
bodyText: Indiana does not make a tenant's advance notice of moving out, or a formal surrender of the unit or keys, a condition of getting the security deposit back. A lease term that makes the refund depend on such a notice would cut back the deposit law, and any waiver of that law is void. The one step the law asks of the tenant is the address: you are not liable under the deposit law until the tenant gives you, in writing, a mailing address to which to send the itemized notice and the balance. Your 45 days run from the end of the tenant's occupancy, and the return section also counts them from the end of the rental agreement and delivery of possession, so send the list and refund within 45 days of whichever comes first. The library's deposit-return clause asks the tenant for that address in writing at move-out. A tenant ending a month-to-month tenancy still owes the notice the termination rules require, and rent still owed, including rent due because the tenant ended the lease early, may be taken from the deposit, but the deposit is not forfeited because the tenant gave no notice.

title: Who Makes Repairs
bodyText: No Indiana statute governs who makes repairs to a rental: none lets you require the tenant to use a repairer you designate, none sets up a list of approved repairers, and none lets the tenant hire a repairer at your expense, because Indiana has no repair-and-deduct or rent-withholding remedy. The repair duties are yours, and the tenant's remedy if you do not meet them is a lawsuit after notice and a reasonable time to repair, during which the tenant may not keep you from entering to make the repairs. So the choice of who does the work on items you are responsible for is yours, subject to the health, housing and building codes and any licensing rules for the trade. A lease may name your repair contact, say that repairs are made by you or a repairer you choose, and bar the tenant from making repairs or alterations, or deducting repair costs from rent, without your written consent; the library's no-alterations and maintenance clauses, tagged for Indiana, do this. Such terms cannot take away the tenant's statutory right to sue over your repair duties. These rules cover rental agreements entered into after June 30, 2002, except pre-July 2008 rent-to-own agreements. Cautious course: respond to repair requests promptly with your own repairers, and put any one-time permission for a tenant to arrange a repair in writing, naming the repairer and a cost limit.

title: Disaster-Displaced Guests in an Indiana Rental
bodyText: No Indiana statute lets a tenant house people displaced by a fire, flood, storm or declared disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy limits, stops you from enforcing those limits after a disaster, or places evacuees in private rentals. The lease's guest, occupancy and subletting terms keep running, for fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies alike. In a mobile home community, the operator may also eject a person for breaking a community rule that is publicly posted in the community. Indiana's emergency-management law does reach rental property during a declared disaster emergency: while it lasts the governor may control entry to and movement within the disaster area and the occupancy of premises there, make provision for temporary emergency housing, and commandeer or use private property. Compensation for property is paid only if the property was commandeered or otherwise used in coping with the emergency and its use was ordered by the governor or a member of the state's disaster emergency forces, only to the extent the use goes beyond every person's duty to manage property so as not to unreasonably detract from the emergency response, and not if the owner volunteered it; claims go through the eminent-domain procedure. A local disaster emergency, declared by a city's or county's principal executive officer, activates local disaster plans and aid; the statute gives it no power over leases. Orders issued in a particular emergency can add temporary rules; this library has not reviewed any specific order. If you voluntarily and without compensation let all or part of your property be used to shelter people during an actual or impending emergency or disaster (or a drill), you are not civilly liable for negligently causing a death, an injury or property loss because of the condition of the property or the conduct of people directing or seeking shelter; the protection is lost if you are paid, and it covers negligence only. A public housing authority that finds an acute need may make dwellings in its projects available to victims of a major disaster, and interstate evacuations are arranged between states under the emergency management compact; neither places anyone in a private rental. On occupancy, the landlord-tenant statutes do not stop you from refusing to rent on the basis of a reasonable occupancy standard, and a standard of two people per bedroom is presumed reasonable if you do not count infants under one year and you allow more people where a den, library, finished basement or loft could reasonably be used for sleeping (unless that would break state or local codes, including fire codes); that rule speaks to refusing to rent and does not itself set guest limits, and fair housing law still applies to occupancy decisions (see `edu-fair-housing-in` and `edu-occupancy-standard-in`). The cautious course, if a tenant asks to shelter displaced family or friends, is to answer in writing, naming the people, an end date and whether rent or other terms change; to change the rental agreement itself you must give at least 30 days' written notice unless the written lease provides otherwise, and whether that notice lets you change it without the tenant's agreement is decided by Indiana courts, so the cautious course is a written change you both sign. What happens to the tenancy and the rent after a disaster is covered in `edu-no-disaster-tenancy-rule-in` and `edu-casualty-in`.

title: Declared Disasters and the Lease
bodyText: Indiana has no statute that ends a residential lease or suspends rent when the governor or the President declares a disaster or emergency. Indiana's emergency management law does reach rental property in a declared disaster emergency: while it lasts the governor may control entry to and movement within the disaster area and the occupancy of premises there, assist in evacuating the area and set evacuation routes and destinations, and commandeer or use private property, with compensation only as that law allows; and every person, owners included, must manage their property so as not to unreasonably hinder the emergency response. The lease and the ordinary rules decide: your duties to comply with health and housing codes and to keep the systems you provide in good and safe working condition continue; a tenant may sue to enforce them after notice and a reasonable time; utilities may be interrupted only for an emergency, good-faith repairs or necessary construction; you may not lock a tenant out or remove the tenant without a court order; and a unit the tenant has not abandoned stays the tenant's to possess. Whether rent is owed while a unit cannot be reached or used after a disaster, and whether the lease ends, are decided by the lease and by Indiana case law; the cautious course is to include a casualty clause in the lease (see the casualty clause), to stop charging rent for any period you agree the unit cannot be used, and to put any agreement with the tenant in writing. Executive orders issued under those powers can add temporary rules; this library has not reviewed any specific order. Federal rules may also apply to federally backed or assisted housing.

title: No Double-Letting Statute in Indiana; Delivery Duty Applies
bodyText: Indiana has no double-letting statute: no rule specifically barring renting the same unit or room to two tenants for the same period, and no special rent-abatement remedy for it. The general rules cover it. You must deliver the rental premises to the tenant in compliance with the rental agreement, so if you cannot hand over a unit because someone else has it, you are in breach. After the tenant gives you notice and a reasonable time to fix it, the tenant may sue and recover actual and consequential damages, attorney's fees and court costs, an order requiring you to perform, or any other fitting remedy. That duty covers dwelling units rented under agreements made after June 30, 2002 (not rent-to-own agreements made before July 1, 2008). You may not remove the first occupant yourself to make room; only a court can order possession. The library's possession-delay clause excuses late delivery only when it is through no fault of yours, and renting the same unit twice is your fault. If you rent rooms separately in a shared home, say in each lease which room the tenant has and which areas are shared.

title: Drug-Free and Crime-Free Lease Terms in Indiana
bodyText: No Indiana statute requires, prescribes the words of, or limits a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum, and none makes the tools below depend on having one; a drug-free or criminal-activity term is an ordinary lease term. The library's optional clause `criminal-activity-in` already covers drug activity: it bars the tenant, household members and guests from crimes on or near the property that affect the health or safety of other tenants, you or your agents, and from allowing the illegal possession, manufacture, sale or distribution of a controlled substance on the property, and it makes a breach a ground to end the lease without a chance to cure. Three statutory tools work whether or not the lease says anything. First, using a leased house, building, mobile home or apartment to commit a controlled-substance offense is a nuisance: you, as owner, may sue to abate it without the 45 days' notice that a prosecutor, city or county attorney or the Attorney General must first give each tenant and the owner; the court may issue an injunction and may order a tenant who created the nuisance to vacate within 72 hours, may grant relief without proof that a defendant knew of the nuisance, and may order an owner who is a party and knew of it to submit a plan to keep it from recurring (see `edu-drug-nuisance-in`). For this purpose "tenant" does not include a person who owns a mobile home and rents a site in a mobile home community where the person lives, although the community itself is covered property. Second, you may petition the small claims docket for an emergency possessory order if a tenant or a tenant's guest has committed a crime that affects the health and safety of another tenant, you or your agent; if the court finds by a preponderance of the evidence that the crime was committed and that the victim has suffered or will suffer immediate and serious injury, loss or damage, it must order the tenant to return possession within 7 days of the hearing (see `edu-emergency-possessory-orders-in`). Third, a mobile home community owner, operator or caretaker may eject a person from the community for a violation of law or disorderly conduct, among other reasons. None of these may be used against a tenant because the tenant or a household member is a victim of domestic or family violence, sexual assault or stalking: you may not end, refuse to renew or refuse a lease, or retaliate, solely because of that, and the emergency track does not interfere with a crime victim's rights. In a Housing Choice Voucher tenancy, federal rules require the lease to make drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises by any tenant, household member or guest (or on the premises by anyone under the tenant's control) a ground for termination, and to let you evict when you determine a household member is illegally using a drug or a pattern of illegal drug use interferes with other residents' health, safety or peaceful enjoyment; the HUD tenancy addendum is added word for word and prevails over the rest of the lease. These rules apply the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies. Cities and counties may not regulate leasing terms and conditions or the rights of the parties to a lease unless the General Assembly authorizes it, so a local ordinance requiring a crime-free addendum would generally be void; this limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: Deposit Return After a Protected Tenant Ends the Lease
bodyText: Indiana lets a tenant who is a victim or alleged victim of domestic or family violence, a sex offense or stalking, and who has a civil protection order or a criminal no-contact order, end the lease with at least 30 days' written notice and the required documents (see the protected-tenant rows). Two rules then speak to the security deposit, and they point different ways. The first says the protected tenant is entitled to deposits, returns and other refunds as if the tenancy had ended by expiring under the lease, and it applies notwithstanding the rule for the tenants who stay. The second says the other adult tenants on the lease stay bound, and you need not return or account for any deposit under the lease until 45 days after every tenant's tenancy has ended. The words "notwithstanding" point toward the protected tenant's own clock, but the statute does not say how the two fit when others stay, and neither rule says how one deposit is divided among co-tenants. Indiana courts decide this. The safe course: (1) If the protected tenant was the only tenant, follow the ordinary deposit rule: within 45 days after the termination date and the return of possession, mail the itemized list of deductions, with the estimated repair cost for each damaged item, and a check or money order for the balance, to the mailing address the tenant gave you in writing. (2) If other adult tenants stay, run that same 45-day clock for the protected tenant from the protected tenant's termination date: send the protected tenant a written itemized accounting and refund the protected tenant's share of the deposit. Settle the share in writing with all the tenants when you can (the remaining tenants may replace it); without an agreement, use what the protected tenant actually paid, or an equal share if that is unknown, and tell every tenant in writing what you did. Do not ask the protected tenant to agree to wait for the others: a waiver of these protections is void. In either case you may deduct only rent accrued up to the termination date (prorated), damage beyond ordinary wear and tear that the tenant caused, and unpaid utility or sewer charges the tenant owed under the lease. You may not deduct rent or fees that would be owed only because the lease ended early. If you miss the itemized list, you must return the full deposit and can owe the amount withheld plus attorney's fees and court costs. The rule is the same for a fixed-term lease and a month-to-month tenancy. It covers rental agreements for a dwelling unit entered into or renewed after June 30, 2007.

title: No Eviction or Non-Renewal Because a Tenant Is a Protected Victim
bodyText: Indiana bars you from ending a lease, refusing to renew it, refusing to enter into it, or retaliating against a tenant solely because the tenant, an applicant, or a member of their household is a protected individual. A protected individual is a tenant or applicant who is a victim or alleged victim of a crime involving domestic or family violence, a sex offense or stalking and who has a civil order for protection or a criminal no-contact order against the perpetrator (see the qualifying-documents row). You also may not refuse to rent to, or retaliate against, someone solely because they or a household member ended an earlier lease under Indiana's protected-tenant termination right. The bar applies the same way to a fixed-term lease (ending it early or not renewing it at the end) and to a month-to-month tenancy (giving notice to end it). The word "solely" leaves your ordinary grounds in place: unpaid rent, damage, a lease breach that has nothing to do with the violence, or the end of a term for reasons unrelated to the tenant's status. Where your reason is mixed, Indiana courts decide whether the status was the sole reason; this library has not reviewed those cases, so the cautious course is to act only on a ground you would act on for any tenant, and to record it in writing. The emergency possessory order procedure for a tenant's or guest's crime does not override the rights of a tenant who is the crime victim, so do not use it against the victim for a crime committed against the victim. If the perpetrator is a co-tenant excluded under a court order, you must keep the perpetrator out (see the lock-change row), and the perpetrator stays liable with the other tenants for rent and damage; the chapter does not make you liable for what the perpetrator or a third party does. The chapter does not state what remedy a tenant has against a landlord who breaks this rule. A lease term waiving these protections is void. The rules cover rental agreements for a dwelling unit entered into or renewed after June 30, 2007. In federally assisted housing (including voucher, public housing and tax-credit units), federal law goes further: it protects a victim of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault or stalking whether or not there is a court order, treats an incident of that violence as neither a serious lease violation by the victim nor good cause to end the victim's tenancy, and lets you split the lease to evict only the abuser. A city or county also may not penalize a tenant or landlord, including by causing an eviction, over a call for police or emergency help made by or for a victim (see the emergency-call row).

title: Indiana Protection Order Citations Are Current
bodyText: Indiana has not moved its protection-order law. Indiana's protected-tenant rules (ending a lease early, lock changes, and the bar on evicting or refusing to rent because someone is a protected victim) rely on a civil order for protection issued or recognized under Indiana's protection-order chapter, or a criminal no-contact order, and on three criminal-law definitions: a crime involving domestic or family violence, a sex offense, and stalking. In the 2026 Indiana Code each of those pointers lands on live law: the protection-order chapter is in force with all its sections, and the sex-offense and stalking chapters and the domestic-violence definition are in force. If your lease, forms or notices cite those provisions, the citations are still correct. Two points to keep current: the definition of a crime involving domestic or family violence was amended effective July 1, 2026, and it now covers listed crimes by one family or household member against another, from homicide, battery, kidnapping, human and sexual trafficking and sex offenses through burglary, trespass, harassment, voyeurism, stalking, certain offenses against family and animal-cruelty crimes involving a family or household member; and an order "recognized" under the chapter includes a valid protection order from another state, a tribe or Canada, which Indiana enforces whether or not it has been registered here. Check the chapter references again whenever you update your forms.

title: Documents That Qualify a Protected Tenant
bodyText: Indiana's protections for victims of domestic or family violence, a sex offense or stalking turn on a court order, and each protection asks for different paperwork. Who qualifies at all: a tenant or applicant who is a victim or alleged victim of one of those crimes and who has received either (a) a civil order for protection issued or recognized by an Indiana court under Indiana's protection-order law that restrains the perpetrator from contact with the person, or (b) a criminal no-contact order that restrains the perpetrator from contact with the person. A police report, a victim advocate's letter or the tenant's own statement does not qualify a person under the state law. A valid protection order from another state, a tribe or Canada counts as a recognized order, whether or not it has been registered in Indiana. (1) Not evicting, not refusing to renew, not refusing to rent: the rule protects anyone who is a protected individual, and it sets no document the tenant must hand you first; if you are unsure, you may ask to see the order. (2) Lock change: the tenant gives you a written request and a copy of the court order; your 48-hour (or 24-hour, if the restrained person lives in the unit) deadline runs from when you receive the copy. No safety plan is needed. (3) Ending the lease early: the tenant gives you written notice at least 30 days before the termination date stated in it, with a copy of the order and, if the tenant is a victim of domestic violence or sexual assault, a copy of a safety plan that is dated not more than 30 days before the tenant gives you the notice, comes from an accredited domestic violence or sexual assault program, and recommends that the tenant relocate. A tenant who is a victim of stalking alone needs only the order. Time limits: the only date limit in the statute is the safety plan's 30 days, counted back from the day the notice is given. The order itself has no age limit, but each protection assumes an order that restrains the perpetrator, so a copy of an order that has expired or been dismissed should be treated with care. The statute does not define "safety plan" or say who accredits a program; if a notice is missing a document or you doubt one, tell the tenant in writing, promptly and specifically, what is missing rather than ignoring the notice. Keep the documents confidential. In federally assisted housing, federal law sets its own, wider list (a HUD certification form, a statement signed by a victim service provider, attorney or medical or mental health professional, or a police, court or agency record), lets you ask for it in writing, and gives the tenant 14 business days to provide it. These rules cover rental agreements for a dwelling unit entered into or renewed after June 30, 2007.

title: Electric Submetering: Billing, Records and Lease Statement
bodyText:
If your multi-unit building (including a mobile home community, but not a hotel or other transient lodging) gets electricity through one master meter, Indiana law lets you install a submeter for each dwelling unit and bill each tenant for the electricity used in that unit. Newer multi-unit buildings generally must be individually metered by the utility unless an exception was established with the utility before construction, so submetering is mainly for older master-metered buildings. If you submeter, the Utility Regulatory Commission's submetering rules apply to you as the owner.

Billing: all electricity you sell must be measured by meter; each bill covers the utility's billing period, read within 3 days of the master-meter reading; you may charge only for energy used in that unit, at the average cost per kilowatt-hour on your utility bill (net charges plus tax divided by total kilowatt-hours, not counting late, disconnection or similar penalties the utility charged you), and you may collect nothing beyond what the utility charged you.

Estimated bills are allowed only if the meter was tampered with or is out of order, and must be marked. Each bill must show the start and end readings and dates, kilowatt-hours, the rate, the total, the due date, the tenant's name and address, who to contact about a dispute, and a clear statement that the bill is not from the electric utility.

The lease must clearly state that the unit is submetered, that bills are based on submeter readings, that common-area electricity is your responsibility, and the dispute procedure; use the Indiana submetering clause.

You must also keep 13 months of utility bills, cost calculations, readings and test results for tenants to inspect and copy; test submeters before installation, and in service every five years or at a change of tenants, whichever is greater (the longer interval); test a tenant's submeter on written request (you may charge up to $15 if it proves accurate); refund or credit overcharges from a fast meter; register with the Commission and report annually; investigate complaints and tell the tenant in writing of the right to ask the Commission for review within 7 days.

Every unit in the building must be submetered, with the same type of meter; a unit whose current lease includes electricity in the rent may stay on that lease until it expires. The rule that makes a non-owner occupant responsible for a city- or town-owned utility's charges does not limit a qualified owner's right to submeter under the submetering statute and rules.

Indiana has no comparable rule for gas: no statute lets a landlord resell gas to tenants by meter, and whether doing so makes you a regulated utility is not settled by statute, so the cautious course is to include gas in the rent or have tenants take gas service in their own names. Water and sewer billing has its own rules; see the water and sewer billing disclosure.

title: No Emergency Contact Requirement in Indiana; Manager and Agent Disclosure Required
bodyText: Indiana does not require a lease to list an emergency or after-hours contact, a management website, or a social-services hotline. What Indiana does require is a written disclosure, at or before the start of the rental agreement, of the name and address of a person living in Indiana who is authorized to manage the unit, and of a person living in Indiana, reasonably accessible to the tenant, who is authorized to accept service of process and receive notices and demands for the owner (one person may fill both roles). If you skip it, whoever signed the rental agreement for you becomes your agent for service, notices and your obligations, the duty binds later owners and managers, and the tenant can recover reasonable expenses of finding the names and addresses. The library's Property Manager and Agent for Notices clause makes that disclosure, and an emergency phone number can be added to it. The lease may also name the tenant's chosen representative to be contacted if the tenant dies or is incapacitated. In a mobile home community, an adult attendant or caretaker you designate must be in personal charge of the community whenever homes are occupied. If you rent short-term through a platform, the local government may require you to give it an emergency contact for the rental.

title: When Rented Property Is Taken by Eminent Domain
bodyText:
No Indiana statute says whether a residential lease ends, or whether rent stops or is reduced, when the government or another body with eminent domain power takes all or part of the property; the lease decides, and where it is silent, Indiana courts do (this library has not reviewed those cases).

The condemnation procedure itself values interests separately: the court-appointed appraisers must report the fair market value of each parcel and the value of each separate estate or interest in it, so a tenant's leasehold can be valued apart from your ownership; between you and the tenant, a lease term saying who receives the award is the cautious way to settle that in advance. A condemnor that pays the appraisers' award into court may take possession.

State and local agencies must pay relocation benefits to displaced people, including tenants: moving expenses (or a scheduled moving and dislocation allowance) and, for a tenant who lawfully occupied the dwelling for at least 90 days before negotiations or code enforcement began, a payment of up to $2,500 toward renting a replacement for up to two years; agencies are to give occupants, as far as practicable, at least 90 days' written notice of the date they must move, and if an agency lets a tenant stay on after acquiring the property, the rent may not exceed the fair rental value.

Those payments belong to the tenant. The library's optional eminent-domain clause ends the lease on a total or near-total taking, reduces rent on a partial taking, gives you the award for the property including the lease's value, and leaves the tenant's relocation payments to the tenant.

title: Screening Rental Staff in Indiana
bodyText: No Indiana statute requires a residential landlord, apartment community or property manager to run background checks on its employees, maintenance workers or other staff who enter tenants' homes, and none sets a screening standard for them. Indiana requires criminal background checks in other settings, such as staff of licensed child caring institutions, home health and personal services agency workers who serve people in their homes, hospice workers, licensed residential care administrators and the managers of rent-to-own stores, but not rental-housing staff. If you do screen, Indiana's expungement law applies to you: it is unlawful discrimination for any person to refuse to employ, suspend or otherwise discriminate against someone because of a conviction or arrest record that has been expunged or sealed; an application may ask about criminal history only in terms that leave out expunged convictions and arrests (for example, asking whether the person has been arrested for or convicted of a crime that has not been expunged by a court); and a violation is a Class C infraction, may be punished as contempt and supports an injunction. An expungement order may be offered as evidence that you used due care in hiring, and an expunged conviction is not admissible in a negligent-hiring suit against an employer who relied on the order. A criminal history provider may not knowingly report records it knows are inaccurate, or, unless the person asking is required by state or federal law to get them, expunged records, records restricted by a court, or Class D or Level 6 felony convictions entered as or converted to Class A misdemeanors; a violation is a deceptive act under Indiana's consumer sales law. If you compile criminal history information yourself to judge someone's eligibility for employment or housing and then use it, you may be a criminal history provider under that law. Federal rules on consumer reports for employment purposes may also apply when a screening company prepares the report. Whether you can be liable for negligently hiring or keeping a worker who harms a tenant is decided by Indiana courts; the cautious course for staff with keys or access to occupied units is a written screening policy applied the same way to every candidate, questions that exclude expunged and sealed records, and supervision and key control. Fair employment laws also apply to hiring and were not reviewed for this row.

title: Tenant Energy Usage Data and Benchmarking
bodyText:
Indiana has no statute or Utility Regulatory Commission rule that requires or forbids a lease term letting you obtain a tenant's energy or water usage data, or that tells a utility when to release a customer's usage data to a building owner. Utilities set their own consent forms.

Indiana does forbid local mandates: after March 15, 2026, a county, city or town may not adopt or enforce an ordinance that requires a building owner or tenant, or a utility, to report a building's electric, gas, water or wastewater usage data to the local government or anyone else. A local program that only allows or encourages voluntary reporting is still permitted. So any benchmarking you do is voluntary, and getting a tenant's data depends on the tenant's consent.

If you want the data, use the optional energy usage data authorization, which has the tenant sign the utility's own release on request, limits your use of the data, and lets the tenant withdraw consent without breaching the lease.

title: Who May Appear in Court for an Entity Landlord
bodyText: Small claims court (most evictions where the rent due is $10,000 or less): an individual landlord may appear personally or through a lawyer, but not through a property manager or other agent who is not a lawyer. A sole proprietorship or partnership may appear through the owner or a partner, a lawyer, or a designated full-time employee of the business, for claims arising out of the business. A corporation, LLC, LLP or trust may appear through a lawyer, an owner, a designated full-time employee, or (for a trust) a trustee. To use a designated employee or trustee, the entity must file in each case a certificate of compliance appointing that person, backed by a board or member resolution (or a sworn document for a partnership, proprietorship or trust) saying the entity is bound by the person's acts and is liable for costs, and the person must file an affidavit that they are not disbarred or suspended. Using a designated employee or trustee gives up any claim above the $10,000 small claims limit, in that case and any other forum. An outside management company's staff are not your full-time employees, so they cannot appear for your entity under this rule unless they are lawyers. A claim you assigned to or sold to someone else can be presented by that third party only through a lawyer. A party whose representative does not follow the rules may be ordered to appear by counsel and sanctioned, including by dismissal or default. Indiana's statute also says a corporation must appear by attorney in all cases, except that corporations organized under Indiana's business, professional and nonprofit corporation laws need not do so on a small claims docket. The statute does not exempt a corporation organized in another state, and its exemption names only a small claims docket of a circuit or superior court, not the Marion County township small claims courts, so the cautious course for an out-of-state corporation, and for any corporation in a Marion County township small claims court, is to use a lawyer. Outside small claims (regular civil cases, or a case moved to the plenary docket after a jury demand), a corporation must appear by a lawyer; for an LLC or other entity, use a lawyer, since whether a non-lawyer may appear for it there is decided by Indiana courts and this library has not reviewed those cases.

title: No Lease Termination Right for Environmental Events
bodyText: No Indiana statute lets you, or the tenant, end a residential lease because of an environmental event such as a flood, a tornado, a chemical or hazardous-substance release, or contamination of the property, and none suspends or reduces rent when one happens. What does apply: your duties to deliver the unit safe, clean and habitable, to comply with health and housing codes and to keep the systems you provide in good and safe working condition continue, and a tenant may sue to enforce them after notice and a reasonable time to repair; you may interrupt utilities only for an emergency, good-faith repairs or necessary construction; and if the lowest floor of the building, including a basement, is at or below the 100-year flood elevation, the lease itself must clearly disclose that the structure is in a flood plain. Whether an event that makes the unit unusable ends the lease or the rent is decided by the lease and by Indiana case law. The cautious course is a lease clause that says what happens if the unit becomes unfit through no fault of the tenant side (see the casualty clause), and prompt written communication with the tenant after any event. Former drug-lab sites are covered in their own row.

title: Tenant Chargers at Move-Out: Lease Decides
bodyText: Indiana has no statute on what happens to a tenant-installed electric vehicle charger when the lease ends: nothing says it stays the tenant's property, nothing gives the tenant a right to remove or sell it, and nothing requires you to buy it. Decide it in the lease before installation. Choose either that the tenant removes the charger and repairs any damage the installation or removal caused, or that the charger stays and becomes yours; the optional charger-installation clause offers both choices. Without a written agreement, whether an installed charger is a fixture that stays with the property is decided by Indiana courts. If the tenant leaves damage, you may apply the security deposit only to actual damages beyond ordinary wear and tear, unpaid rent (which includes unpaid charges under the lease) and the other listed uses, with the itemized notice and return within 45 days. If the tenant leaves a removable charger behind, treat it like other property left behind (see the abandoned-property clause).

title: EV Charging at Rentals: No Tenant Right, Few Rules
bodyText:
Indiana has no statute that gives a tenant a right to install or use an electric vehicle charger at a rental, requires you to provide charging, or sets the terms on which you may allow it. Whether a tenant may install a charger is your decision under the lease; if you agree, use the optional charger-installation clause (written consent to the specific system and location, a licensed contractor, permits and codes, association rules, insurance if you choose, electricity reimbursement and what happens at move-out).

Indiana's specific EV rules are narrow. A person that owns, operates or leases EV charging equipment and makes it available to the public for compensation is not a public utility for that reason alone, and may charge by the kilowatt-hour, by time, or both, if the electricity comes from the authorized supplier for that area.

No Indiana statute addresses billing only your own tenants for charging; reimbursement of the electricity a tenant's charger uses, measured by a separate meter or a stated method, is a lease charge, and under Indiana's deposit law any money you hold to secure it is part of the security deposit. Indiana has no weights-and-measures registration rule and no special tax for electricity sold through a charger in the statutes reviewed; check with the utility and the state revenue department before charging the public.

Electric and hybrid vehicles pay a supplemental registration fee to the state, which is the owner's concern, not yours. In a homeowners association, the governing documents may not prohibit or restrict using a motor vehicle, or set different standards for different vehicles, based on fuel source (from July 1, 2026), but that does not give anyone a right to install a charger.

Local governments may not regulate lease terms, and may not adopt rules that distinguish between vehicles based on the type of energy that powers them; whether that reaches a local requirement for charger-ready parking was not resolved. The limit on regulating lease terms does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants; the limit on vehicle rules based on energy type has no such exception.

title: EV Chargers in Shared Parking: Lease Decides
bodyText: Indiana has no statute on a tenant's charger in a parking area other tenants use: no right to install one, no rule letting you charge a fee to reserve the space, and no rule on who pays for damage to the charger or the lot. All of that is for your lease. If you agree to a charger in a shared lot, assign the specific space in writing, state any reservation or parking fee as a lease charge, require installation by a licensed contractor under the codes and permits, and say who is responsible for damage from installation, use, repair and removal (the optional charger-installation clause and the assigned-parking clause cover these points). A lease binds only you and that tenant; a later tenant of the space is bound only by that tenant's own lease. A fee or reimbursement paid to you under the lease is rent under Indiana's deposit law, and money held to secure the charger obligations is part of the security deposit. In a homeowners association, the governing documents may not restrict using a vehicle based on its fuel source, but common-area chargers are governed by the association's documents and decisions. Cities and counties may not regulate lease terms or landlord fees. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: No Hardship Stay of Eviction; Local Moratoria
bodyText: Indiana has no statute that lets a court postpone an eviction because of the tenant's hardship, illness, age, the weather or the season, and no statute providing for or barring an eviction moratorium. The timing rules that do exist are procedural: in small claims cases, under the court rules, an order of possession may not be issued more than 30 days after judgment and lasts no more than 30 days, and the officer may not remove occupants until at least 48 hours after the order of possession is served (see the eviction-process row). Eviction diversion programs and settlement conferences must be voluntary for both sides, and if you settle before final judgment you must move to dismiss unless you are still seeking damages, including keeping the deposit. Local governments: a city, town or county may not regulate the rights of the parties to a lease, leasing terms and conditions, or fees, unless the General Assembly authorizes it, and an ordinance that does is void. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants. That limit does not name moratoria, but a local eviction moratorium would regulate the parties' rights; whether it falls within the bar is for the courts, and this library has not reviewed any decision. During a declared disaster emergency the governor may control the occupancy of premises in the disaster area; whether an order under that power could pause evictions is for the courts, and this library has not reviewed any order. Federal law can stop or pause an eviction: a servicemember or dependent in a home renting for no more than the federal cap may be evicted only by court order, and the court may, and on request must if military service materially affects the ability to pay, stay the case for 90 days or adjust the lease; a tenant's bankruptcy filing triggers the automatic stay with eviction-specific exceptions (see the bankruptcy row). Federal orders or programs can also impose pauses for federally backed or assisted housing.

title: Charging the Tenant for Eviction Notices or Filings
bodyText: No Indiana statute bans or limits a lease term that charges the tenant a fee for an eviction notice, for filing an eviction case, or as a penalty for being evicted, and cities, towns and counties cannot add one: local units may not regulate the fees a landlord charges or the terms of a lease, unless the General Assembly authorizes it.
