This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants. What the statutes do provide: a winning landlord in a suit to enforce the tenant's statutory duties may recover actual damages, attorney's fees and court costs; and the security deposit may be applied only to the uses the deposit statute lists; because that statute counts every payment the lease requires, other than the deposit, as rent, an eviction charge could be taken from the deposit as unpaid rent only if the charge itself is enforceable. Whether a fixed eviction charge in the lease is enforceable, or is an unenforceable penalty because it is not tied to your actual loss, is decided by Indiana courts under contract law. A charge that is unduly excessive, imposed through unequal bargaining power, can also be an unconscionable act under the consumer protection act. One related statute concerns local governments, not leases: a political subdivision may not penalize a tenant, owner or landlord, including by causing an eviction, for a call for police or emergency help made by or for a victim or a person in an emergency. Cautious course: do not put a flat eviction fee or penalty in the lease; seek actual, documented costs and attorney's fees through the court as the statutes and your lease's attorney-fee clause allow.

title: Serving Eviction Papers, Lease-Named Agents and Confidential Addresses
bodyText: In an Indiana small claims eviction, the notice of claim is the summons, and it must be served on each tenant you sue: by certified mail with return receipt, by handing it to the tenant, by leaving it at the tenant's dwelling (followed by a first-class mailed copy), or another way the court rules allow. The court rules also allow service on an agent named by a court rule, a statute or a valid agreement, again followed by a mailed copy. That could let a lease name someone to accept court papers for the tenant, but whether a term in a residential lease is a valid agreement for this purpose is for the courts, and a failed service can undo a judgment. For that reason this library does not offer a lease clause naming an agent for service; serve the tenant directly. Address confidentiality program participants: a tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, human trafficking or similar conduct may enroll in the Indiana Attorney General's address confidentiality program. Every participant designates the Attorney General's office as the participant's agent for service of process and receipt of mail. If the tenant gives you the program's written notice, you must use the designated address for all mail correspondence, may not knowingly disclose the tenant's address, and may not display the tenant's name at the address (on a mailbox, door, directory or common area), though you may require the physical address where a service could not otherwise be provided. A person may not disclose a participant's address in a court case unless the court, after notice to the participant and the Attorney General's office, finds disclosure is needed, there is no other practicable way, and the safety risk is outweighed. Because an eviction claim must describe the premises, the cautious course for a participant is: serve through the Attorney General's office as the designated agent; ask the court clerk before filing how to file the property address as a confidential record excluded from public access; and, if the court needs the address in the public record, ask the court to make the required findings rather than disclosing it yourself (see the address-confidentiality row).

title: Lease Clauses Excusing Your Liability
bodyText: No Indiana statute either voids or approves a residential lease clause that excuses you from liability for injury or property damage, or that makes the tenant hold you harmless. Whether such a clause is enforceable, and whether it can reach your own negligence, is decided by Indiana courts. Two statutory limits apply whatever the courts say. First, a clause cannot excuse what a non-waivable chapter imposes: a term releasing you from the tenant's repair action and its damages, attorney's fees and injunction, from deposit liability, or from liability for a lockout or utility shutoff is a waiver of that chapter and void. Second, a term that is oppressively one-sided or unduly limits the tenant's remedies, signed through unequal bargaining power, can be an unconscionable act under the consumer protection act. Indiana statutes do protect you in these specific situations, without any lease term: you have no liability for loss or damage to a tenant's personal property that the tenant has abandoned (the lease may not define abandonment differently); after a sole tenant dies or is incapacitated, you are not liable for property, unearned rent or the deposit you turn over by following the tenant's-representative procedure (but you are liable for actual damages if you willfully disregard it); when you change the locks under a protective order against a co-tenant, you are immune for excluding that person and for loss of use of or damage to property left in the unit, and the protected-tenant chapter does not make you liable for what the perpetrator or a third party does; and, unless otherwise agreed, after a good faith sale to a bona fide purchaser you are relieved of liability for events after written notice of the sale to the tenant, though you stay liable for the deposit for one year unless the buyer assumes it by notice to the tenant and you transfer the deposit. Cautious course: do not rely on an exculpatory clause; keep liability insurance, require renter's insurance for the tenant's own belongings if you choose, and follow the statutory procedures where an immunity depends on them.

title: No Expedited Deposit Refund Procedure
bodyText: Indiana has no procedure for an expedited or early disposition of a security deposit, and no rule letting you and the tenant agree to a different refund method or timetable in place of the statutory one. The deposit law sets the outer limit and the form: not more than 45 days after the tenant's occupancy ends, you mail the itemized list of damages, with the estimated repair cost of each item, together with a check or money order for the balance, to the mailing address the tenant gave you in writing. You may always do this sooner than 45 days. Because the statute names a check or money order, and any waiver of the deposit law is void, the cautious course is to send the balance that way even if the tenant asks for an electronic transfer. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Extended Absence Rule in Indiana; Absence Is Not Abandonment
bodyText:
Indiana has no rule on a tenant's extended absence: no statute requires a tenant to tell you before being away, sets a number of days, or gives you a right to enter while the tenant is gone. You may require notice of an absence in the lease, and the library's Extended Absence Notice clause does that.

What the lease may not do is treat an absence as abandonment on its own terms: a unit counts as abandoned only if the tenant has failed to pay or offer to pay rent due and the circumstances would lead a reasonable person to conclude the tenant has surrendered possession, and no lease may define abandonment differently. Until then the normal entry rules apply during an absence: reasonable notice and reasonable times, with entry without notice only in an emergency that threatens the occupants' safety or your property.

If you believe a tenant who lives alone is incapacitated and away from the unit, you must notify the tenant's representative, give the representative access to remove belongings, and pay the representative the deposit and unearned rent the tenant would be owed; you may require a signed inventory of what is removed.

title: Child Care in a Rented Home
bodyText: Indiana has no statute that requires you to let a tenant run a child care home, sets conditions you may impose (such as insurance or liability waivers), or requires a child care licence applicant to show your consent. Your lease decides: the residential-use clause bars it, and the optional home-business clause lets you permit it on conditions such as licensing, insurance and limits on traffic and parking. What Indiana does protect is against associations, not landlords: for governing documents adopted or amended after June 30, 2026, a homeowners association may not prohibit or restrict a person from providing child care in a detached single-family home that the person lives in and owns, rents or leases (a licensed Class I child care home holder must also live there), except in qualifying age-restricted communities. Licensing is separate. A child care home is a residence where at least 8 children, or at least 4 under 12 months, not counting the provider's own children or relatives, receive care for pay for more than 6 hours a day on 10 consecutive weekdays; it needs a state licence, and a Class I home serves up to 12 children plus 3 in at least full-day kindergarten. Smaller or unpaid care in the provider's home is outside the licensing law. If you allow child care, require the tenant to keep any required licence and give you a copy, and to carry liability insurance naming you, and remember that fair housing law protects households with children as tenants.

title: Hunting and Fishing on Leased Land
bodyText:
In Indiana no one may fish, hunt, trap or chase, shoot a firearm or bow, or gather plants or artifacts on privately owned land without the consent of the owner or the tenant of the land. Because either one's consent is enough, a tenant of farmland or other rural property can let hunters and anglers on the land unless the lease says otherwise. If you want to keep those rights, or control who comes onto the land, reserve them in the lease (the optional hunting, fishing and trapping clause does this).

Licences follow ownership and farming: a resident lessee who farms the leased farmland, with the spouse and children living with the lessee, may hunt, fish and trap on that land without a licence, as may the owner and the owner's household on land the owner owns (a nonresident owner only if the owner's home state gives Indiana owners the same right). A lease reservation does not change those licence rules, but it does control whether the tenant may hunt there at all.

For land not assessed as residential, an owner, tenant, lessee or occupant generally is not liable for injuries to people who come on the land for free (or with only government payment) to hunt, fish or trap, or for other recreation, except for malicious or illegal acts; those rules were amended effective July 1, 2026. A snare may be set only on the user's own land or with the owner's written permission.

title: Fees and Products in Place of a Security Deposit
bodyText: Indiana has no statute on fees charged in place of a security deposit, on deposit-replacement insurance or surety bonds for tenants, or on deposit-alternative programs, and none on what such a program must tell the tenant before reporting a damage claim to a credit bureau or collector. Two alternatives are in the statutes. You may accept, but may not require, a lien on a motor vehicle the tenant owns as security; to enforce it you must record the lien and follow the deposit rules. And a township trustee assisting a tenant may, instead of paying a deposit, sign an agreement with you setting aside township money for verified damage beyond normal wear and for unpaid rent; the agreement may last no more than 180 days and may not cover more than one month's rent. Otherwise a fee in place of a deposit is not regulated as such, but labels do not control: any amount paid to you and held to secure the tenant's performance, or returnable when the unit is returned in the required condition, is a security deposit under Indiana law, whatever it is called, and must be used and returned under the deposit rules. A fee that is truly nonrefundable and not held as security is not a deposit. Whether a particular program is a deposit in disguise is decided by Indiana courts. If you offer such a program, the cautious course is to make it optional with a regular deposit as the alternative, to state in writing what the fee does and does not cover, and not to treat the fee as a fund you draw damage costs from. If the product is insurance or a surety bond, Indiana insurance law, not reviewed here, governs who may sell it. Cities and counties may not regulate security deposits or landlord fees. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: No Fee Disclosure or All-In Rent Rule
bodyText: Indiana has no fee-transparency or all-in pricing law for rentals. No statute requires rent and mandatory fees to be stated as one total, fees to be listed on the lease's first page or in set words, advertised rent to include required fees, or automatically renewing leases to meet special rules, and no statute outside the landlord-tenant laws lists fees a landlord may not charge, apart from the bar on charging any fee to keep an emotional support animal, the bar on passing a local fee for building the unit on to the tenant, and the limits on separately billed water and sewer charges and returned-check charges (see the statutory caps row). Indiana's Deceptive Consumer Sales Act does reach residential leasing: a landlord who regularly leases homes for personal or household use is a supplier, and a supplier may not commit an unfair, abusive or deceptive act, omission or practice before, during or after the transaction, including misrepresenting the rights, remedies or obligations the lease involves, or claiming a price advantage that does not exist, where the landlord knows or should reasonably know the statement is false. Whether charging a fee the lease does not state, or advertising rent without its required fees, breaks that general rule is decided by the courts and in Attorney General enforcement; this library has not reviewed those decisions (see the consumer protection row for how the Act applies to leases). The one fee-disclosure rule Indiana does set for leases is for separately billed water and sewer service (see the water and sewer billing clause). Cities and counties may not regulate landlord fees, lease terms or lease disclosures. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants. The cautious course is to list every fee and its amount in the lease, to charge only fees the lease states, to change fees during a lease only as the lease and the notice rules allow, and to state required fees alongside the rent when you advertise.

title: No Specific Bar on Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: Indiana has no statute that specifically bars charging a tenant a fee for a service you do not actually provide, such as an amenity, trash, pest or package fee for a service that does not exist or has stopped. Two general rules still apply. If you bill tenants separately for water or sewer service, the total charge may not exceed what you paid the utility for the same service, less your own use, plus only the costs the statute allows. And Indiana's Deceptive Consumer Sales Act bars a landlord who regularly leases homes from any unfair, abusive or deceptive act, omission or practice before, during or after the lease, including misrepresenting what the tenant is getting; whether a particular charge for a service not provided breaks that rule is decided by the courts and in Attorney General enforcement. The cautious course is to charge a service fee only for a service the lease describes and you actually provide, and to stop or adjust the fee when the service ends. Cities and counties may not regulate landlord fees. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: Indiana's Statewide Fire and Building Codes
bodyText: Indiana has one statewide set of fire safety and building rules, adopted by the Fire Prevention and Building Safety Commission (from July 1, 2027, by the Department of Homeland Security). Which code reaches your rental depends on the building. A building used by three or more tenants (or by the public) is a Class 1 structure, governed by the Indiana Building Code (the 2012 International Building Code with Indiana amendments) and the 2014 Indiana Fire Code (the 2012 International Fire Code with Indiana amendments); a single-family home, a duplex or a qualifying townhouse is a Class 2 structure, built under the 2020 Indiana Residential Code (the 2018 International Residential Code with Indiana amendments). The fire code applies to existing conditions as well as new ones, but an existing building that was lawful when built may continue as long as it is kept in a condition equivalent to what it had when built; Indiana deleted most of the model fire code's chapter on existing buildings, including its general retrofit section, but kept Section 1104 of that chapter (amending only part of it); its text is not reviewed here, so check it with the code official. Every building and its heating, electrical, plumbing, fire detection and suppression systems must be maintained under the rules in effect when built or altered (or, for older buildings, at least as safe as when built), and no alteration may reduce existing fire protection or exits below what current rules require for new construction. Where an older building still has a fire escape used as an exit, it may not be the only or main exit, must be kept clear, operational and signed, and must meet load requirements with documentation kept on site. In buildings with three or more apartments, each apartment without immediate ground-level access to the outside must have a permanently affixed emergency sign with fire and emergency instructions; an owner who violates that rule commits a Class A infraction. Statewide rules override conflicting local rules, and cities and counties may not adopt stricter or more detailed building or fire rules, though local smoke detector ordinances may be stricter. The model codes themselves are not reviewed here; check the full codes or the local building department for specific requirements.

title: Fire Sprinklers: New Construction Only, None Required in Homes
bodyText: Indiana does not require you to add fire sprinklers to an existing rental. For single-family homes, duplexes and qualifying townhouses (Class 2 structures), sprinklers are optional by statute: no state agency, city or county may require them, and if you install one it must meet the residential code's design rules. For apartment buildings and other buildings with three or more tenants (Class 1 structures), sprinkler requirements come from the Indiana Building Code for new construction, additions and alterations; Indiana deleted the model fire code's rules that would have required sprinklers to be retrofitted into existing buildings. An existing building may continue as built if maintained, but any sprinkler system it has must be kept in working order under the rules in effect when it was installed, and no alteration may reduce existing fire protection below what current rules require for new construction. Additions and alterations must meet new-construction rules within their scope; a full rehabilitation under the existing-structures chapter of the building code requires full compliance for the work done. A small balcony (no more than 100 square feet each) may be added to an existing unsprinklered apartment building without sprinklering the balcony or the building. A totally sprinklered building that conformed to Uniform Building Code standards (an older model code) when built is exempt from Indiana's smoke detector chapter; whether the exemption reaches a building sprinklered under a later code is not settled, so the cautious course is to keep smoke detectors in every unit, and you still need the tenant's written smoke detector acknowledgment at move-in. The model building and fire codes are not reviewed here, so confirm specific sprinkler requirements for new work with the local building department.

title: Firearms in Indiana Rentals: Lease Terms, Employees and Local Preemption
bodyText: Indiana has no statute protecting a tenant's right to keep firearms in a rental, and none barring a lease term that restricts them. Indiana's handgun law says it may not be construed to stop a person who owns, leases, rents or otherwise legally controls private property from regulating or prohibiting firearms on that property, so a lease restriction is a contract term. Because the tenant also leases the unit, and the same law lets a person carry a handgun without a license in or on property the person leases or rents, how far a landlord's lease ban reaches inside a tenant's own unit is for Indiana courts (this library has not reviewed those cases); a restriction limited to common areas, or a rule on safe storage, is on firmer ground than a total ban. Indiana's parking-lot gun law protects only employees: as an employer you may not forbid your own staff from keeping a lawful firearm locked out of sight in their vehicles (with listed exceptions, including at your own residence), but the law does not cover tenants' vehicles. Cities, towns and counties may not regulate firearms, their possession, carrying or storage, so local gun rules for rentals are barred; the statute's listed exceptions include court buildings, and a court-building restriction does not reach parts occupied by residential tenants or common areas they use. Federal rules for public and assisted housing are not covered here. Apply any firearm rule evenly, and do not use it to end a tenancy without the normal court process.

title: No Duty to Tell a New Tenant About a Foreclosure
bodyText: Indiana does not require you to tell a prospective or new tenant that the property is in foreclosure, that a foreclosure complaint has been filed or that a mortgage is in default, either before the lease is signed or afterward. Telling the tenant is still the safer course. A tenant who signs without knowing and is later displaced can claim you misled them, and Indiana's consumer protection law treats misrepresentations by a landlord who regularly leases as deceptive acts. If you are buying a home from a homeowner who is facing foreclosure and leasing it back to them, Indiana's foreclosure rescue law applies (see the optional lease terms row). What happens to tenants after a foreclosure sale is covered in the foreclosure row; federal law may protect tenants after a sale.

title: No Statutory Relief From Lease Forfeiture
bodyText: Indiana has no statute that lets a court relieve a tenant from forfeiture of the lease (that is, keep the tenancy alive after a breach on terms, such as paying what is owed) once the lease has been ended. Two statutes limit forfeiture in particular cases. For unpaid rent, the tenant defeats a 10-day termination notice by paying the rent in full before the notice period runs out, unless the parties agreed otherwise (see the redemption row). For waste, a court may award damages, but it may forfeit the tenancy and evict only when the injury equals the value of the tenant's remaining term or was done in malice. For other breaches, whether a court may excuse a forfeiture is decided by Indiana courts as a matter of equity. The cautious course is to give clear written notice of the breach and a fair chance to cure before ending the lease, as the library's default clause provides, and to treat each tenant the same way.

title: Which Edition of a Code or Standard Applies
bodyText: Several Indiana rules that affect rentals point to outside codes and standards, and whether a later edition counts depends on the wording. Indiana's building and fire rules adopt specific editions of the model codes: the 2012 International Building Code and 2012 International Fire Code, and the 2018 International Residential Code, each with Indiana amendments. A newer model code edition does not apply until Indiana adopts it, though from July 1, 2027 the Department of Homeland Security must authorize compliance with a more recent version of a model code, after finding that it is not adverse to public health, safety or welfare, and identify it by notice in the Indiana Register (it may attach conditions and may later modify or end an authorization), and compliance with such an authorization is voluntary; if you choose that option, you must follow all of it. A local ordinance that refers to the state rules by their Administrative Code citation picks up later amendments unless it names a specific edition. Buildings are maintained under the rules in effect when they were built or altered. Some references are dated in a way that can surprise you: the smoke detector chapter exempts a totally sprinkled building that met Uniform Building Code standards at the time of construction (an older model code), and defines a smoke detector by the National Fire Protection Association's minimum standards without naming an edition. The electric submetering rule ties submeter accuracy to a 1982 metering standard and says later editions are not included. Where a reference is unclear, the cautious course is to meet the current edition as well as the one named.

title: Renting Furnished in Indiana
bodyText:
Indiana's landlord-tenant statutes have no special rules for furnished rentals: no required inventory, no separate furniture deposit rule and no furniture repair duty.

Your statutory upkeep duty covers the listed building systems (electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air conditioning, and elevators) if they are on the premises when the rental agreement is entered into, and appliances you supply as an inducement to the lease; whether a furnished item such as a washer or a microwave was supplied as an inducement is a question of fact, so list everything you supply.

The tenant must use the unit's facilities and appliances in a reasonable manner, must not deface, damage, destroy, impair or remove any part of the rental premises, and at the end of the occupancy must deliver the premises in a clean and proper condition, except for ordinary wear and tear expected in the normal course of living in a dwelling. Those tenant duties apply to rental agreements entered into after June 30, 2002 (except a rent-to-own agreement entered into before July 1, 2008) and cannot be waived.

When the tenancy ends, the deposit may be applied to the damages you suffer because the tenant did not comply with the law or the lease, which includes furnishings the lease lists that are missing or damaged beyond ordinary wear and tear; you must mail the itemized list, with the estimated cost of repair for each damaged item, and any balance within 45 days after the occupancy ends (your liability for missing the deadline starts once the tenant gives you a mailing address in writing).

Two older health rules reach some furnished rentals. The owner, operator or manager of a furnished apartment house, boarding house or rooming house must keep a register of the name and address of every person occupying any part of the premises and the dates and times occupied, keep it open for inspection by the Indiana Department of Health and law enforcement, maintain it for each calendar year and keep it for one year after that year; a reckless violation is a Class A misdemeanor.

And in an apartment house, rooming house or lodging house where you furnish beds and bedding for guests or lodgers, each bed must have an undersheet covering the mattress and a top sheet, changed for freshly laundered sheets after each guest or lodger leaves; a violation is a Class C infraction. Whether a single furnished unit makes a building a furnished apartment house is not defined; the cautious course for a building of furnished units is to keep the register.

Use the optional furnishings clause (`furnishings-included-la`) to list the items and their condition at move-in; Indiana does not require a move-in inspection (see `edu-no-move-in-inspection-rule-in`), but a signed inventory is your best evidence at move-out. These rules apply the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Good-Cause Eviction Law or Notice
bodyText: Indiana has no good-cause or just-cause eviction law, so there is no state notice telling tenants whether such a law covers them, and none to put in the lease. A fixed-term lease ends on its own terms, and a periodic tenancy can be ended on the statutory notice without giving a reason (see the just-cause and notice-to-quit rows); retaliation, domestic violence and fair housing protections still apply. Mobile home communities have two statutory rules of their own: the owner, operator or caretaker may eject a person for nonpayment of charges or fees, a violation of law or disorderly conduct, or a violation of a state health department rule or of a publicly posted community rule (whether that list limits other terminations is decided by Indiana courts, which this library has not reviewed, so the cautious course is to rely on a listed reason), and an operator who intends to close the community must give each home owner written notice at least 180 days before the closure. Cities, towns and counties may not adopt their own good-cause rules for private rentals, because they may not regulate lease terms or the parties' rights; that bar does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents. A federal rule does apply if the tenant has a Housing Choice Voucher: during the lease term you may end the tenancy only for a serious or repeated lease violation, a violation of law tied to the tenant's use of the unit, or other good cause (and during the first term, other good cause must rest on something the family did or failed to do); you must give the tenant written notice of the grounds at or before the start of the eviction case, give the housing agency a copy of any eviction notice, and evict only through court. Other federal programs (such as tax-credit and HUD-assisted properties, and the federal 30-day notice for federally backed properties) have their own rules; check the program documents.

title: Passing Government Fines to the Tenant
bodyText:
Indiana has no statute that bars or limits passing to the tenant a government fine, penalty or cleanup cost caused by the tenant, the tenant's household or guests, so the lease may require the tenant to reimburse you (see the optional clause on fines caused by the tenant).

Fines for conditions that are your responsibility, such as code violations you must fix, should not be shifted: your repair and code duties cannot be waived by lease, and a term shifting their cost risks being void as such a waiver (Indiana courts decide that question; this library has not reviewed those cases). Three Indiana rules shape what you may be charged.

A city, town or county may not penalize a tenant, owner or landlord for a call for police or emergency help made by or for a victim of abuse or crime or a person in an emergency; for other calls, any penalty may not exceed $250, and if the tenant made the call the penalty must be assessed against the tenant, not you. A local nuisance or code penalty may not be imposed until you or your designee have been given reasonable notice and a stated reasonable time to cure.

And if a city cleans up an ordinance violation on the property after giving at least 10 days' notice, its cost becomes a lien on the property and is billed to the owner. Government fees, as distinct from fines, are covered by the fee reimbursement clause, which excludes fees for building the unit.

title: Guarantors, Renewals and the Notice to Sue
bodyText:
Indiana has no statute that limits a lease guarantor's liability to the original term, requires a guaranty to state a maximum amount or an end date, or lets a guarantor revoke a guaranty for future rent. Whether a guarantor stays liable after a renewal, extension or month-to-month holdover, or after a rent change, therefore depends on the guaranty's own words and on Indiana case law; state the answer in the guaranty, as the library's optional guaranty clause does.

Get the guaranty in writing, signed by the guarantor: Indiana requires a signed writing to sue on a promise to answer for another person's debt, and whether that rule's exception for leases of three years or less reaches a guaranty of such a lease is decided by Indiana courts.

One Indiana statute matters after a default: a person bound as a surety on a written contract to pay money may, once the claim has accrued, give you written notice requiring you to sue right away, and if you do not sue within a reasonable time and pursue the case to judgment and collection, the surety is released from all liability. Whether a lease guarantor counts as a surety for this rule, and whether a lease can waive it, are decided by Indiana courts.

The cautious course is to treat any written demand from a guarantor that you sue as starting a short clock, and to file promptly against the tenant and guarantor together. A surety who is made to pay the tenant's debt recovers interest from the tenant at the rate the original written instrument set, and a judgment for it bears that rate, up to 10% a year.

title: No Guest-Rights Statute in Indiana; Tenants Answer for Guests
bodyText:
Indiana has no guest-rights statute: no law guarantees tenants the right to have guests, visitors, caregivers or suppliers, bars guest fees, or sets how long a guest may stay, so the lease and your house rules decide (the library's guest policy clauses do this). Guest rules must still be applied evenly under fair housing law, and an aide a tenant with a disability needs may require a reasonable accommodation. Tenants answer for their guests in two places.

If a tenant's guest commits a crime that affects the health and safety of another tenant, you or your agent, and someone has suffered or will suffer immediate and serious injury, loss or damage, you may petition for an emergency possessory order, and the court must order the tenant to return possession within seven days. And Indiana's retaliation bar does not stop you from suing for possession when a code violation was caused by the tenant's guest or invitee.

A guest who overstays is not a squatter under Indiana's squatter-removal law, which excludes invitees. Whether a person who came as a guest and stays has become an occupant you must remove through the courts, or may be asked to leave under the criminal trespass law, is for Indiana courts (this library has not reviewed those cases); the cautious course is the court process.

In a mobile home community, the operator may eject any person, including a guest, for violating a community rule that is publicly posted in the community, so post guest rules there.

title: How Serious a Repair Problem Must Be
bodyText: Indiana's repair remedy has no materiality threshold. A tenant may sue to enforce any of your statutory duties (safe, clean and habitable delivery, code compliance, common areas, and the listed systems and appliances) once the tenant has given you notice, you have had a reasonable time to repair, and you have failed or refused to fix it; the statute does not require the problem to be material, substantial or a threat to health. Your liability for damages starts when you have notice or actual knowledge and refuse, or fail within a reasonable time, to fix it. Seriousness matters in three other places. A tenant's emergency possessory order (for a lockout or utility shutoff) issues only if the tenant will suffer immediate and serious injury, loss or damage. The retaliation rule protects a tenant's complaint to a building or housing code agency only about a violation that materially affects health or safety, though a written complaint to you about your repair duties is protected whatever its size. And you may still sue for possession after a protected complaint when the tenant's own breach of the lease materially affects the health or safety of the tenant or others. The repair action covers rental agreements entered into after June 30, 2002, except a rent-to-own agreement entered into before July 1, 2008; the emergency order and retaliation rules carry no such date limit. How courts weigh a small defect, and whether an implied warranty of habitability adds a materiality test, is case law. Cautious course: treat every repair request as one the tenant can enforce, and fix it within a reasonable time.

title: What a Lease Can and Cannot Change About Your Repair Duties
bodyText: No Indiana statute lets a lease modify any of your duties as landlord, and any waiver of them, by contract or otherwise, is void. There is no list of duties a lease may shift on conditions, no exception for a property without well or utility water, and no rule letting the tenant do repairs in place of rent. What the statute itself leaves to the facts is narrower: the duty to keep electrical, plumbing (with a reasonable supply of hot and cold running water), sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning systems, elevators and inducement appliances in good and safe working condition applies to the items provided on the premises when the rental agreement is entered into. So a home rented without a given system or appliance carries no duty to maintain that item, though you must still deliver the home safe, clean and habitable and comply with the health and housing codes that apply. Who pays for electricity, gas and water is for the lease: the rule against shutting off service does not make you pay for a service you have not agreed, orally or in writing, to pay for. The tenant's own statutory duties (keeping the areas the tenant uses reasonably clean, using systems and appliances reasonably, not damaging the premises, following reasonable rules, keeping smoke detectors working) are also set by statute and cannot be waived. These rules cover rental agreements entered into after June 30, 2002, except a rent-to-own agreement entered into before July 1, 2008. Whether a lease may assign the tenant work beyond the statutory duties while you stay responsible for them is for the courts; this library has not reviewed those cases, so keep any such term limited to routine upkeep the statute does not place on you.

title: No Statutory Presumptions About Habitability
bodyText: No Indiana statute creates a presumption about habitability or repairs: none presumes a unit is uninhabitable because of a code violation, none presumes you breached your repair duty or acted in bad faith because a repair took a certain time, and none presumes that a rent increase, service cut or eviction filing after a tenant's complaint is retaliation. Each of those points is proved on the evidence. The only presumption in Indiana's residential landlord-tenant statutes is about occupancy limits: an occupancy standard of two people per bedroom, applied as the statute describes, is presumed reasonable. Separately, under the consumer protection act a person who signs a written contract is presumed, until shown otherwise, to know its terms, which matters when a tenant claims a lease term was unconscionable. Whether Indiana courts apply presumptions of their own in repair or habitability disputes is case law. Cautious course: because the tenant's case rests on notice, a reasonable time to repair and your response, keep dated records of every repair request, your reply, access attempts and the completed work, and document a legitimate reason for any rent increase, service change or filing that follows a complaint.

title: No Required Habitability Statement in the Lease
bodyText: No Indiana statute requires your lease to state that the home is, or will be delivered, fit to live in, habitable or in good repair, and none prescribes wording for such a statement. The duty applies whether or not the lease mentions it: for rental agreements entered into after June 30, 2002 (except a rent-to-own agreement entered into before July 1, 2008) you must deliver the home in compliance with the lease and in a safe, clean and habitable condition. Because the duty is to deliver the home as the lease promises, anything the lease promises about the condition or features of the home becomes part of what the tenant can enforce through the statutory repair action, so describe the home and what you supply accurately. What Indiana does require you to say in the lease is different: that the structure is in a flood plain, where its lowest floor is at or below the 100-year flood elevation (rental agreements entered into or renewed after June 30, 2009), and that the property is near a military installation, where that applies (leases entered into or renewed after June 30, 2023). Separately, you must give the tenant in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, the names and addresses of your Indiana manager and agent for notices, and get the tenant's written acknowledgment of a functional smoke detector at move-in. The library's disclosure rows cover each of these.

title: Habitability Duties Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Indiana voids any waiver of the chapter that sets your duties as landlord, whether it is written into the lease or agreed some other way. So a lease cannot remove or lower your duties to deliver the unit as the lease promises and in a safe, clean and habitable condition; to comply with the health and housing codes that apply to it; to make all reasonable efforts to keep common areas clean and proper; and to keep in good and safe working condition the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning systems, any elevators, and appliances supplied as an inducement to the lease, with a reasonable supply of hot and cold running water and adequate heat at all times. The rule covers dwelling units let for rent under a rental agreement entered into after June 30, 2002, except a rent-to-own agreement (a rental with an option to purchase) entered into before July 1, 2008. No Indiana statute lets a tenant accept a stated defect in exchange for lower rent, and none sets up a separate signed document for giving up heat or any other habitability duty, so there is no statutory way to trade these duties away. Two limits of the rule matter in practice. The system and appliance duties reach only what is on the premises when the rental agreement is entered into, so an accurate list of what you provide describes the duty's reach; it cannot relabel something you do provide as excluded. And the smoke detector rules separately cannot be waived in the lease or in a separate writing. Whether a tenant may agree to do particular work while you stay responsible for the result is for the courts (see the tenant repair agreement row), and Indiana courts also decide whether an implied warranty of habitability adds anything for leases outside the statute. Cautious course: repair conditions before move-in instead of writing them into the lease, and record minor cosmetic conditions in a move-in report rather than a waiver.

title: Contamination and Environmental Restrictive Covenants in Indiana
bodyText:
Indiana has no general rule requiring you to tell a tenant about hazardous substances, past releases or contamination on or under the property. One rule can still reach a lease.

When contaminated land is cleaned up, closed or allowed to stay in use under Indiana Department of Environmental Management oversight, the owner may record a restrictive covenant (also called an environmental covenant or environmental notice) that limits how the land may be used or requires engineering controls to be maintained; for an existing or former hazardous waste facility or a federally listed site where more than an insignificantly small amount of a hazardous substance remains, the owner must execute and record one when the Department finds it necessary.

A covenant executed after June 30, 2009 must, to qualify, require notice of the covenant to anyone who takes the land or an interest in it; the statute does not say whether a residential lease is such an interest, so treat it as one. The covenant runs with the land, binds later owners and those claiming under them, survives Indiana's marketable title rules and, if executed after June 30, 2009 in connection with a cleanup, closure or similar action the Department approved, may be enforced by the Department in court.

If such a covenant is recorded against your property, give the tenant written notice of it with the lease and make its use limits part of the lease (see the environmental covenant clause). A covenant on a former hazardous waste landfill also bars lessees from filling, grading, excavating, building, drilling or mining after closure without the Department's authorization.

For a lease with an option to buy a home of up to four units, the seller's disclosure form also covers known contamination from making controlled substances; former drug lab sites are covered in their own row.

title: Local Health Department Rules: No Copy Duty, but Orders Apply
bodyText: Indiana has no statute that requires you to give a tenant a copy of local health department rental rules, on request or otherwise, or to refer a tenant to the health department. The health rules themselves still bind you: you must comply with all health and housing codes that apply to the rental premises, and the tenant must comply with the obligations those codes put primarily on tenants. A local board of health, county health officer or the Indiana Department of Health may declare a dwelling unfit for human habitation when it is dangerous or detrimental to life or health because of want of repair, defects in drainage, plumbing, lighting, ventilation or construction, contagious disease, or an unsanitary condition likely to cause sickness. It may then order everyone living there to vacate within 5 to 15 days (stating at least one reason), declare the dwelling a public nuisance, and order it cleaned, repaired, altered or improved. The order is served on the tenant and on the owner or the owner's rental agent; it must be extended for good reason and may be revoked once the dwelling is fit again. A person aggrieved by a local order may petition the circuit or superior court within 10 days, with a bond for costs; otherwise the order becomes final. Failing to comply makes the person liable for the department's costs of carrying out the order plus attorney's fees, and a reckless violation is a Class B misdemeanor, each day a separate offense. Health officers inspecting for rats may enter a dwelling only between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. City or town building inspectors may use the same powers.

title: Heat: What Indiana Requires
bodyText: Indiana's landlord-tenant law does not set a minimum indoor temperature or require you to provide heat, but if a heating system is on the premises when the lease is made, you must provide and maintain it in good and safe working condition, and it must be sufficient to adequately supply heat at all times. This applies to leases entered into after June 30, 2002 (not to rent-to-own agreements made before July 1, 2008) and cannot be waived. You must also deliver the unit safe, clean and habitable and comply with applicable health and housing codes. Who pays for the fuel or electricity that runs the heat is up to the lease; Indiana has no rule against making the tenant pay for heat, but the shutoff ban means you may not cut heat off to a tenant, and you are not required to pay for a service you did not agree to provide, so say in the lease who pays. The tenant must use the heating system reasonably. If the heat fails, the tenant must give you notice and a reasonable time to fix it before suing; a court can award actual and consequential damages, attorney's fees and an injunction. The statewide building codes require heating equipment in new construction (based on the model codes' design temperatures, as amended in Indiana), and existing systems must be maintained under the rules in effect when installed; the model code text is not reviewed here. Local rental inspection programs may check heating systems. The state boiler rules do not regulate a heating boiler in a single-family home, duplex or qualifying townhouse, or in a residential building with fewer than seven apartments, if it runs at no more than 15 psig (steam) or 30 psig (hot water) and has a gross output of no more than 215,000 Btu per hour; ordinary domestic water heaters (up to 80 gallons and 100,000 Btu per hour input) are also outside the rules. Any other boiler, such as a larger apartment building's heating or hot water supply boiler or a larger service water heater, needs a state operating permit backed by an inspection by a licensed inspector; for low pressure steam heating boilers, hot water heating boilers, hot water supply boilers and service water heaters the permit runs two years and inspection is every 24 months (power boilers yearly). Operating a regulated boiler without a permit is an infraction for the person who controls the place where it runs, if that person can maintain it or take it out of service.

title: Renting in a Homeowners or Condominium Association
bodyText:
Indiana has no statute that requires an association to approve a lease or a tenant, caps an association approval fee, lets an association hold a deposit from your tenant, or lets an association demand rent directly from your tenant when you fall behind on assessments; the association's governing documents and your lease decide those points. If your property is in a condominium, your tenants are bound by the condominium statute and by the association's declaration and bylaws.

If the condominium association forecloses its lien for your unpaid assessments, the bylaws may require you to pay a reasonable rental for the unit during the foreclosure, and the association may ask the court for a receiver to collect it. Rental restrictions in a homeowners association come from its recorded covenants and other governing documents.

State law limits who decides them: in any homeowners association, only members who use their property as their homestead may vote on a prohibition or restriction on renting (a developer that still owns lots is exempt from that limit); this took effect when the 2026 act that added it was passed. The state bar on local rental restrictions and the short-term rental law bind local governments, not associations.

An association may assess you, as the member, a fine for a covenant violation only after its board adopts a published schedule of fines and gives you notice of the violation, amount and date (from July 1, 2026, for every homeowners association).

Your tenant also has some rights against the association: for governing documents adopted or amended after June 30, 2026, a homeowners association may not prohibit or restrict a person from providing child care in a detached single-family home the person lives in and owns, rents or leases, or from maintaining an amateur radio antenna on property the person owns, rents or leases; and for governing documents adopted or amended after June 30, 2024 it may not prohibit beekeeping on property a person owns, rents or leases if the hives are actively kept and state apiary rules are followed (it may regulate number and location, and may bar hives within 100 feet of a resident with a documented bee allergy who lived there first).

These rules bind the association, not you as landlord. The solar petition procedure belongs to the homeowner, not the tenant. If an association requires a deposit from your tenant, have the tenant pay it directly to the association: a deposit paid to you or your agent to secure the tenant's lease obligations is a security deposit under Indiana law, with its use limits and 45-day return rules. To pass association fines on to your tenant, use the association compliance clause.

title: Holding Deposits and Money Taken Before the Lease
bodyText: Indiana has no statute on holding deposits, reservation fees or other money you take to hold a unit before the lease is signed: no cap, no deadline to sign, no refund rule if either side backs out, and no rule doubling a deposit you fail to honor. The deposit law defines a security deposit as money a tenant pays to be held during the rental agreement to secure the tenant's obligations under it, and a tenant as someone who occupies a rental unit with your consent. Money taken before any agreement exists may fall outside that definition until the lease is signed, but once a lease is signed and you keep the money as security, it is a security deposit and must be used and returned under the deposit rules; money you apply to the first full rental period is rent, not a deposit. How Indiana courts treat a holding deposit that is neither applied nor returned is decided by case law. The cautious course is to put in a signed writing what the money is for, how much of it is refundable and when, what happens if you or the applicant decides not to go ahead, and whether it will become part of the security deposit or the first month's rent. If a licensed real estate broker company takes the money, the broker company must put it in a trust account, because Indiana requires broker companies to deposit all funds belonging to others in one. Cities and counties may not regulate security deposits, lease applications or landlord fees. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: Home Businesses in Indiana Rentals
bodyText:
Indiana has no statute that makes a home-based business a permitted use of a dwelling or that limits a lease term restricting business use, so your lease decides: the residential-use clause bars commercial use, and the optional home-business clause lets you permit a named business on conditions.

One state rule protects a common home business: a home based vendor may make and sell food products, other than foods that need time and temperature control for safety, made at the vendor's own primary residence (including a permanent structure on the same property), selling in person, by phone or online and delivering in person, by mail or by carrier, with labeling, sanitation and food handler requirements; those sales are exempt from food-establishment rules, and local governments may not require licensing, certification or inspection of the vendor's food.

That rule frees the vendor from food regulation; it does not give a tenant a right to run the business against your lease. Child care in a home is covered in the family child care row. Local zoning may regulate home occupations. Cities and counties may not regulate lease terms. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: Waiving the Tenant's Exemptions from Collection
bodyText: Indiana's Constitution directs the legislature to exempt a reasonable amount of a debtor's property from seizure or sale for debts, and the exemption statute protects, among other things, the real estate or personal property that is the debtor's residence, including estates or rights in that real estate, up to a dollar amount the Department of Financial Institutions updates by rule, plus other property, health aids, retirement and education savings, and earned income tax credit refunds. So a tenant who owes you a judgment keeps these exemptions when you collect it, and the residence exemption may reach a tenant's own interest in the home as well as an owner's. No Indiana statute lets a lease waive these exemptions, and no statute expressly voids such a waiver in a lease; whether Indiana courts would enforce one is case law, so the library does not offer an exemption waiver. Three statutory rules point the same way. Property a tenant leaves after an eviction that is medically necessary, used for the tenant's trade or business, or needed clothing, blankets and items for a child's care and schooling must be released from storage without payment, and a waiver of that rule by contract or otherwise is void. You may not seize, remove, lock away or dispose of a tenant's belongings to enforce the lease, except through the mobile home community lien and the deposit, abandoned-property, eviction and storage procedures; and only a writing separate from the lease may let you hold property the tenant voluntarily hands over as security in exchange for not filing an eviction. Indiana gives you no general landlord's lien on a tenant's belongings; the exceptions are a mobile home community operator's innkeeper-type lien on a resident's property, and a lien on the tenant's motor vehicle that you may accept (but not require) as security under the deposit rules. Collect a judgment through the court's ordinary process and let the court apply the exemptions.

title: No Lease Termination for Illness, Incapacity or a Move to Care
bodyText: Indiana has no statute that lets a tenant end a lease early because the tenant becomes ill, disabled or incapacitated, or moves into a nursing home, assisted living or other care, and no general rule that a tenancy ends when either party loses the capacity to contract. What does apply: (1) A month-to-month or other short periodic tenancy can be ended in the ordinary way, on notice equal to the rental period (see the notice-to-quit row); a guardian or an attorney in fact acting within that authority can give or receive that notice for the tenant. (2) A fixed-term lease is not ended by the tenant's incapacity under any Indiana statute; what the tenant then owes, and whether you must try to re-rent, are decided by the lease and by case law (see the re-renting row). (3) If you believe a tenant who lives alone is incapacitated and absent, you must notify the tenant's representative, give the representative reasonable access to remove the tenant's belongings, and pay the representative the deposit and unearned rent the tenant would have been entitled to (see the tenant-death row). (4) A servicemember who suffers a catastrophic injury or illness in service, or the member's spouse or dependent if the member lacks capacity, may end the lease under federal law within a year (see the statutory early-termination row). (5) A request from a tenant with a disability to be released early may be a request for a reasonable accommodation under fair housing law, which you must consider; whether a release is required in a given case is decided case by case (see the disability-accommodation row). If you agree to release a tenant, put the release and any final charges in writing.

title: Informal Dispute Resolution Terms in Indiana
bodyText:
No Indiana statute requires, authorizes in terms, or forbids a lease term asking the parties to try to settle a dispute informally before going to court, so a non-binding notice-and-meet term is an ordinary contract term. Indiana does set the limits such a term must respect.

Any residential eviction diversion program, meaning any pre-eviction diversion program, landlord-tenant settlement conference or similar program affecting residential evictions or possession of residential rental property, may be offered or operated only if participation is voluntary for all parties; so a lease should not make a diversion or settlement step a condition of an action for possession.

In small claims court, where most landlord-tenant cases are heard, the court may order alternative dispute resolution only when the law does not prohibit it, it is consistent with informal and speedy justice, the parties agree, and it is provided at no cost to them.

A term must also not shorten or delay a statutory notice or remedy: the 10-day nonpayment notice, the tenant's notice-and-reasonable-time step before a repair suit, the emergency possessory order track (a hearing within three business days, for lockouts and utility shutoffs, waste, crimes and materially false information given to obtain the lease), and the 45-day deposit return all run on their own terms, and the deposit and other landlord-tenant chapters cannot be waived.

Under Indiana's consumer protection act, a supplier (which can include a landlord who regularly leases) commits an unconscionable act if it solicits a tenant to sign terms that unduly limit the tenant's remedies and unequal bargaining power led the tenant to sign unwillingly or without knowing the terms (a signed contract is presumed known), so a term that blocks or delays a lawsuit could be attacked; a term that only asks for written notice and an offer to talk, leaves possession and emergency actions out, and says it does not delay or limit any legal notice, deadline or remedy is, on its words, the cautious course, because it limits no remedy; whether a court would agree is case law.

Whether a court would enforce even such a term against a party who sues first is decided by Indiana courts; this library has not reviewed those cases, so treat the term as an encouragement, not a bar. If a dispute is resolved after an eviction action is filed, the landlord must move to dismiss the action unless it is still seeking damages, including keeping the deposit.

The library's optional clause `informal-dispute-resolution-or` fits these limits; binding arbitration is not offered for Indiana (see `edu-binding-arbitration-in`). These rules apply the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Disclosing Unsafe-Building Orders
bodyText: Indiana has no general rule requiring you to tell a tenant about code violations, inspection results or condemnation orders before signing a lease. One rule may apply. Where the state unsafe-building law operates (Indianapolis and Marion County, and any city, town or county that has adopted it), a person who has been issued and has received notice of an unsafe-building order and has not complied must, before transferring or agreeing to transfer a substantial property interest in the property, supply full information about the order to the person taking that interest, and within 5 days afterward give the enforcement authority written copies of that person's full name, address and phone number and of the document making the transfer. The statute's examples of a substantial property interest are ownership, life, future, mortgage and land-contract interests; it does not say whether a lease is one, and no case on that question has been reviewed here. The cautious course is: while an unsafe-building order on the property is unmet, give any prospective tenant the full order in writing before signing, keep a signed receipt, and send the enforcement authority the tenant's name, address and phone number and a copy of the lease within 5 days. Failing to comply when the rule applies is a Class C infraction, and you can be liable to the local government for any judgment it suffers because it lacked notice. Anyone who takes an interest in property after an order is recorded takes it subject to the order. A health department order on an unfit dwelling is served on the tenant directly (see the health department row). Disclosing an outstanding order is never unlawful, and it can head off disputes. Local disclosure ordinances are generally void, because localities may not regulate disclosures about the property or lease. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: No Fixed Penalty for Entry Without Notice in Indiana; Court Remedies Apply
bodyText: Indiana sets no fixed penalty for entering without notice: no statutory fine, no set damages such as a month's rent, and no criminal penalty in the landlord-tenant laws. The tenant's remedies are court remedies. If you violate or threaten to violate the entry and possession rules, the tenant may petition the small claims court for an emergency possessory order; the court must hold a hearing within three business days, and if it finds the violation and that the tenant will suffer immediate and serious injury, loss or damage, it must order you to return possession if the tenant was shut out, to stop violating the rules, or both. The court may set a later hearing to decide damages and may make other orders it finds just, and the tenant may bring other claims arising from the tenancy. A tenant's written complaint to you about an improper entry, or a court action over it, is protected activity, so raising the rent, cutting services or starting an eviction in response is retaliation, unless an exception applies (for example a rent increase to comparable market rentals, a service cut for all tenants equally, declining to renew at the end of the term, or an eviction for rent the tenant has not paid within the time allowed). Give reasonable notice and enter at reasonable times every time; the entry rules cannot be waived.

title: Jury Trial Waivers in Indiana Leases
bodyText: Indiana's Constitution keeps the right to trial by jury in all civil cases, and no Indiana statute or court rule says whether a lease signed before any dispute can waive it. The court rules say how the right is lost in a particular case: a party waives a jury by not demanding one in time, by not appearing for trial, or by a written or in-court stipulation to a bench trial made in that case. A jury is never automatic: in an ordinary civil case a party must file a written demand within ten days after the first responsive pleading. Most evictions and deposit or damage claims are filed on a small claims docket or in a small claims court, and filing there waives the plaintiff's jury. The tenant as defendant keeps the right but must ask for a jury within ten days after receiving the notice of claim (the township small claims courts in Marion County have their own statutory timing, which the court rules override; follow the notice of claim) and pay the cost of moving the case to the regular docket; otherwise the jury is waived. So a lease jury waiver would mainly try to stop a tenant from making that request. Whether Indiana courts enforce a pre-dispute jury waiver in a residential lease, and on what showing of knowing agreement, is case law, so the library does not offer a jury-waiver clause for Indiana. Cautious course: leave jury waivers out of the lease; if the case is in small claims, the tenant's own failure to make a timely request already waives the jury.

title: No Key-Control or Staff Screening Mandate in Indiana
bodyText: Indiana has no key-control law for rental housing: no required written key policy, master-key log or rekeying between tenants, and no required background checks of employees who hold keys, at any size of complex. Two rules still shape key handling. Anyone entering a unit for you, including maintenance staff or contractors with a key, must follow the entry rules: reasonable written or oral notice, reasonable times, no harassment, and no-notice entry only in an emergency that threatens the occupants' safety or your property. And if a protection or no-contact order restrains someone from contact with a tenant, you must change the locks on the tenant's written request within 48 hours after the tenant gives you a copy of the order (24 hours if the restrained person is a co-tenant) and give the tenant a key; a restrained co-tenant gets no access unless the order allows a visit to collect belongings. Whether you are liable for a crime committed by an employee or with a lost key is for Indiana courts under ordinary negligence law (this library has not reviewed those cases), so the cautious course is to keep keys locked and logged, limit who holds master keys, rekey after a tenant leaves or a key is lost, and screen staff who hold keys.

title: Penalties for Using Prohibited Lease Terms
bodyText: Indiana's residential landlord-tenant statutes make prohibited lease terms void, but none of them adds a penalty, damages or attorney's fees for knowingly putting a void term in a lease or trying to enforce it. The tenant's protection is that the term has no effect, plus whatever remedy the underlying rule gives (for example, the deposit statute's recovery of the deposit and attorney's fees, or damages and fees in a repair suit). Two statutes outside the landlord-tenant chapters do attach consequences. Confession of judgment: it is a crime (a Class B misdemeanor) knowingly to procure someone to sign a cognovit note, to keep one as its payee or holder, or to try to enforce in Indiana a judgment from another jurisdiction based on one; a cognovit note includes any written contract to pay money, such as a lease, that authorizes a confession of judgment or a waiver of service without a court hearing. Consumer protection: soliciting a tenant to sign oppressively one-sided terms or terms that unduly limit the tenant's remedies, through unequal bargaining power, is an unconscionable act, and falsely representing that a lease involves or does not involve particular rights, remedies or obligations, when you know or should reasonably know it is false, is a deceptive act; the Attorney General may sue, and for a knowing violation a court may impose a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per violation (for real property the act speaks of enjoining patterns of incurable deceptive acts, and tenants cannot bring the act's private suit over a lease). Unlike some states, Indiana's consumer act does not list using a void lease term as a deceptive act in itself; whether insisting on a void term amounts to a false representation of the tenant's rights is case law. Cautious course: remove any term the library marks as void in Indiana, and never tell a tenant that a void term binds them.

title: What a Tenant Can Do When You Breach
bodyText: Indiana gives tenants court remedies, not self-help, when a landlord breaches. Repairs: after giving you notice and a reasonable time to repair, and while letting you in to do it, a tenant may sue to enforce your statutory duties and, on winning, recover actual and consequential damages, attorney's fees and court costs, an injunction or other appropriate relief; your liability for damages starts once you have notice or actual knowledge and refuse, or fail within a reasonable time, to fix the problem. Lockouts and shutoffs: a tenant you lock out, or whose electricity, gas, water or other essential service you cut off without a court order, may petition for an emergency possessory order, heard within three business days, and the court may order you to restore possession and stop, and later decide damages and the return of withheld property. Deposits: if you do not return the deposit with the itemized list within 45 days, the tenant may recover the deposit withheld plus reasonable attorney's fees and court costs. Disclosure: if you do not give the tenant the names and addresses of your Indiana manager and agent at the start, the person who signed for you becomes your agent for notices and for your obligations, and the tenant may recover reasonable costs of finding the information. These remedies do not limit one another. No Indiana statute lets a tenant withhold rent, pay rent into court, or repair and deduct, and no lead-paint or health statute directs rent withholding. Whether a tenant may defend an eviction on the ground of your breach, or claim an implied warranty of habitability, is case law. These rules apply to the rental agreements each chapter covers (repairs: entered into after June 30, 2002, except pre-July 2008 rent-to-own agreements; lockouts and entry: entered into or renewed after June 30, 1999).

title: No Required Landlord Liability Insurance
bodyText: Indiana has no statute that requires a residential landlord to carry liability insurance, to prove insurance to register or rent, or to disclose its insurance to tenants. Whether to insure is a business decision; a lender, an association's documents or a housing program contract may require coverage. Insurance does come up in one state rule: a professionally managed rental, or a unit in a professionally managed rental community, that passed an inspection in the past 12 months done by or for a federal or state housing agency, a financial institution or an insurance company authorized in Indiana (or by a qualified independent inspector), with the written report delivered to the locality on time, is exempt from routine local rental inspections and inspection fees, except where the locality's rental registration or inspection program was created before July 1, 1984 (the exemption rules also do not cover a mobile home community licensed and inspected by the Indiana Department of Health). Cities and counties may run registration programs but may not add conditions such as classes or program participation, and may not regulate lease terms or disclosures (a limit that does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants), so a local insurance mandate tied to registration is open to challenge. You may require tenants to carry renter's insurance under the lease (see the renter's insurance clause).

title: No State Landlord Registration; Local Registration Limits
bodyText: Indiana has no statewide registration or licensing requirement for residential landlords or rental units generally, and no rule that makes registration a condition of renting or of collecting rent. The exception is a mobile home community: it may not be operated without a license from the Indiana Department of Health (issued for four years; operating without one is a Class B misdemeanor), the operator must keep a register of the homes in the community open to the assessor and the department, and no other government body may license or regulate the community beyond enforcing the state health standards and local zoning and building codes. What Indiana does regulate is local registration. A city, town or county may run a registration program for rental units, but its annual registration fee may not exceed $5, one fee covers all the units in a rental unit community (five or more rental units on contiguous parcels not occupied only by the owner's family), and otherwise the fee is per parcel; after a change of ownership the new owner may be required to pay the fee and give updated registration information within 30 days. A locality may not require you to get a permit to lease, except a free permit that lasts until the property changes hands (one permit per rental unit community), and may not require you to take a class or join a government program as a condition of leasing. A locality whose rental registration or inspection program was created before July 1, 1984 is outside these limits; this library has not checked which localities qualify. Since July 1, 2026, a locality may not prohibit or restrict using privately owned homes as rentals, and registration or inspection rules may not be used to cap or limit rentals; a local rule adopted before January 1, 2026 that does not comply has until January 1, 2028, and a short-term rental rule adopted before 2018 under the state short-term rental law is exempt (see the single-family rental row). Separately, if you own or are buying leased property that is the subject of a final unsafe-building order, you must give the local enforcement department your name, street address (not a post office box) and phone number. Every landlord must also give the tenant, in writing at or before the start of the lease, the names and addresses of an Indiana resident who manages the unit and an Indiana resident agent for legal papers and notices (see the manager and agent rows). An out-of-state entity landlord also registers with the Indiana Secretary of State (see the out-of-state owner row).

title: Your Remedies When a Tenancy Ends or the Tenant Defaults
bodyText: In Indiana you recover possession, money, or both, through the courts; you may not lock a tenant out or cut off utilities (see the self-help row). Possession: after the lease ends (at the end of its term, on the right notice, or on a 10-day notice for unpaid rent), you sue to recover the property from the tenant in possession. A possession case in which the rent due when you file is $10,000 or less may go on a small claims docket (in Marion County, the township small claims courts have the same limit); larger cases go to circuit or superior court. Before final judgment a court may give you possession only if you post a court-approved bond, and the fast emergency-order track covers waste, a tenant's or guest's crime affecting health and safety, and false application information (see the eviction-process and emergency-order rows). Money: in the possession suit or separately, you may recover rent and other amounts owed under the lease, and in a suit to recover the property you may recover for the tenant's use and occupation up to the time it ended, for no more than six years before you sue; an occupant with no special agreement is still liable for rent. You may also recover damages for the tenant's breach of the lease or of the duties Indiana imposes on tenants; while the tenant is still in the unit, give notice of the breach and a reasonable time to fix it first, and a winning landlord in a suit to enforce those duties may recover actual damages, attorney's fees and court costs, an injunction or other appropriate relief. If a tenant commits waste, a court may award damages, and may also forfeit the tenancy and evict the tenant when the injury equals the value of the tenant's remaining term or was done in malice. A money claim of $10,000 or less may be filed on a small claims docket; but filing in small claims gives up any part of your claim above $10,000, and you cannot sue later for the rest, so file a larger claim in circuit or superior court. The security deposit may be applied only to accrued rent, damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, rent due because the tenant ended the lease early, agreed last-month rent, and unpaid utility or sewer charges, with the itemized notice within 45 days. Rent for the rest of the term after the lease ends: no Indiana statute lets you accelerate rent or says what future rent you may recover after a termination, and none requires you to re-rent; those questions turn on the lease and on case law, so the cautious course is to claim only rent that has accrued and losses you can show, and to make and document reasonable efforts to re-rent. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies, except that a month-to-month tenancy's future rent ends with the notice period.

title: Fixing a Tenant's Breach Yourself
bodyText:
Indiana has no statute giving you a right to step in, fix a tenant's failure to clean, repair or maintain, and bill the cost to the tenant as rent, the way some states' landlord-tenant acts do.

What Indiana provides instead is a lawsuit: to enforce a tenant's statutory duties (not damaging the home, using systems and appliances reasonably, keeping the tenant's areas reasonably clean, following reasonable rules, keeping smoke detectors working) you must first give the tenant notice of the problem and a reasonable time to fix it, and if the tenant's breach caused physical damage that you have repaired, your notice must specify the repairs you made and document your cost.
