Neither notice is needed once the tenancy has ended. A winning landlord recovers actual damages, attorney's fees and court costs, an injunction or other appropriate relief. The tenant-duty rules cannot be waived and cover rental agreements entered into after June 30, 2002, except a rent-to-own agreement entered into before July 1, 2008.

Any work you do inside the unit is subject to the entry rules (reasonable notice and reasonable times, except in an emergency threatening the occupants' safety or your property), and you may not use the cost as a reason to lock the tenant out, cut off utilities or keep the tenant's belongings.

Because the deposit statute counts every payment under the lease other than the deposit as rent for deposit purposes, but the nonpayment-notice statute does not adopt that definition, the library does not label a repair charge as rent. The library offers an optional clause that sets up a notice-and-cure step matching the statute; it is a contract term, not a statutory right.

title: No Late Fee Limit for Homes, Including Mobile Home Communities
bodyText: Indiana sets no cap, grace period or other limit on late fees for residential rent, and that is true for mobile home community lots as well as apartments and houses; cities and counties may not regulate landlord fees. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants. The only Indiana late-fee caps for rentals are outside housing: a self-service storage owner may charge a late fee of no more than the greater of $20 or 20% of the monthly rent for each month in default, and rent-to-own agreements for goods have their own small late-charge limits. Those caps do not apply to a lease of a home, and no statute says a dwelling late fee is or is not interest. Set your late fee as a reasonable estimate of what late payment costs you; Indiana courts decide whether a fee is an unenforceable penalty. For a mobile home community, the lien you have on a resident's home against a lender who has properly notified you is limited to actual late rent for no more than 60 days before you notify the lender that the owner has left or is behind. See the late fee row for the 10-day notice question.

title: Working With Police; Reporting Duties
bodyText: Indiana has no crime-free lease statute: nothing requires, approves or limits a crime-free or drug-free addendum, and no statute makes you give police access to a unit, hand over tenant information, or report a tenant's crime simply because you are the landlord. A lease may bar crime on the property, and Indiana gives you an emergency court track for a tenant's or guest's crime that affects the health and safety of another tenant, you or your agent (see the criminal-activity clause and the emergency-order row). Three general rules reach you as they reach anyone. (1) Child abuse or neglect: any individual who has reason to believe a child is a victim of abuse or neglect must immediately report it to the Department of Child Services or the local law enforcement agency; knowingly failing to report is a Class B misdemeanor, and a person who reports or helps with the investigation is immune from civil and criminal liability for doing so. (2) Endangered adults: any individual who believes or has reason to believe an adult is an endangered adult must report it; a good-faith reporter is immune. (3) Calls for help: a city, town or county may not penalize you or your tenant, including by forcing an eviction, over a call for police or emergency help made by or for a victim or a person in an emergency (see the emergency-call row). If a tenant is in the address confidentiality program, you may give the tenant's name to the state or a local government only in response to a specific request tied to an active code investigation or inspection or an active investigation of a law violation by that tenant (see the address-confidentiality row). Volunteer parking enforcers appointed by police may issue tickets on private property only with the owner's or property manager's permission.

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate for Rentals
bodyText: Indiana has no lead-safe or lead-free certificate, inspection certificate or lead-safe registry that a rental must have, and nothing of that kind to attach to the lease. Indiana's lead law licenses inspectors, risk assessors, clearance examiners, abatement workers and contractors, and does not require you to abate lead-based paint hazards. What applies to you: (1) the federal lead disclosure for housing built before 1978, which must be in or attached to the lease with the federal warning statement, your statement of known lead-based paint or hazards, any available records and the tenant's acknowledgment of the federal pamphlet (see the lead-based paint clause); and (2) Indiana's lead-safe work rules when you renovate, remodel or maintain a rented pre-1960 building and disturb more than small areas of paint (see the lead-safe work row). A renovator working for pay in pre-1978 housing must also give the owner and the occupants the federal lead pamphlet before work that disturbs more than two square feet of paint per component. If a local health department finds a dwelling unfit because of an unsanitary or dangerous condition, it may order repairs or vacating (see the health department row).

title: Indiana Adds No Lead Notices to the Lease
bodyText: Indiana has no lead notice, certificate, registry or information packet of its own that you must give a tenant with the lease or at renewal. The lead disclosure that goes with a lease is the federal one for housing built before 1978: the federal warning statement, your statement of any known lead-based paint or hazards, any available records, and the tenant's acknowledgment of the federal pamphlet, in or attached to the lease (see the lead-based paint clause). Indiana's lead rules come into play when work is done. If a renovator is paid to renovate pre-1978 housing and the work will disturb more than two square feet of paint per component, the renovator must give the owner and the occupants the federal pamphlet and get a written receipt or a certificate of mailing; If you do the work yourself in a rented unit, give the tenant the pamphlet too. For a lead abatement project, the licensed supervisor or project designer must prepare a written occupant protection plan before the work; the rules do not say it must be handed to the tenant, but share it. Indiana's lead-safe work practices for remodeling, renovation and maintenance of pre-1960 housing are covered in the lead-safe work row. For these rules, pre-1978 housing does not include housing for the elderly or for people with disabilities where no child aged six or younger lives or is expected to live, or a building without a bedroom. Under the state law limiting local landlord-tenant rules, cities, towns and counties may not add their own lease disclosures for privately owned rentals unless the legislature authorizes it. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: No Rule on Blank Spaces in an Indiana Lease
bodyText: Indiana has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be filled in before signing, and no rule that a lease with blanks is a violation or a material noncompliance. Indiana's consumer protection law covers residential leases by a landlord who regularly leases, but its list of deceptive acts has no item on blanks. Indiana's rent-to-own law for goods, which does address blank spaces in its agreements, does not apply to the rental purchase of a dwelling. Even so, fill in or strike every blank before anyone signs. A blank left open invites a dispute over what was agreed, and filling it in afterward without the tenant's agreement can be treated as a misrepresentation about the terms. If a term does not apply, write "N/A" or strike it, and have both sides initial any handwritten change.

title: What an Indiana Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Indiana prescribes very little that a residential lease itself must contain, and it has no rule on what goes on the first page, no rule that the start and end dates appear in a particular place, and no required lease form. The lease itself must carry: (1) a clear statement that the structure is in a flood plain, if its lowest floor (including a basement) is at or below the 100-year flood elevation on the state or federal flood maps (rental agreements entered into or renewed after June 30, 2009); and (2) the military installation statement, if the property is in a state area of interest near Naval Support Activity Crane, Lake Glendora Test Facility or Grissom Air Reserve Base (leases entered into or renewed after June 30, 2023). Other items must be given in writing but may go in the lease or in a separate document: (3) the names and addresses of an Indiana resident authorized to manage the unit and an Indiana resident agent for notices and service of process, at or before the start of the tenancy; (4) the water and sewer billing disclosure, if you bill those services separately (in the lease, the first bill or a separate signed page); and (5) the tenant's written acknowledgment, when you hand over the unit, that it has a working smoke detector. Federal law adds the lead-based paint disclosure for housing built before 1978, in or attached to the lease. A lease with an option to buy a home of up to four units also brings in Indiana's seller disclosure form. A lease for longer than three years must be in writing, signed by you, and acknowledged before a notary (or proved), and it should be recorded within 45 days. The library's Indiana clauses carry each of these items. A contract to live in a housing with services establishment (sleeping accommodations for at least five residents, with health-related or supportive services offered for a fee) has its own list of required contents, which the library does not cover.

title: No Indiana Rule Requiring Initialed Lease Clauses
bodyText: No Indiana statute requires a tenant to initial any clause of a residential lease, such as a notice requirement, a fee or a waiver, and none requires a lease term to be separately signed for it to bind the tenant. The tenant's signature on the lease is enough under state law. Some writings must still be signed or acknowledged by the tenant, though not by initials: the tenant's written acknowledgment, when you hand over the unit, that it has a working smoke detector; (if you use one) the separate signed page carrying the water and sewer billing disclosure; and, for housing built before 1978, the tenant's statement of receipt and signature on the federal lead-based paint disclosure. Initials beside an important or unusual term are still good practice. Signing a written lease raises a rebuttable presumption under Indiana's consumer protection law that the tenant knew its terms, and initials make that presumption harder to overcome for a term a tenant later says was hidden. The library's smoke detector clause includes a line for the tenant's initials for this reason.

title: Recording Long Residential Leases
bodyText: Indiana does not require an ordinary residential lease of three years or less to be recorded, and recording is not a condition of the lease being valid between you and your tenant. A lease of real estate for longer than three years must be recorded in the Miscellaneous Record of the county recorder's office where the property is located within 45 days after it is signed. If it is not, the lease is void against a later buyer, tenant or lender who acquires the property in good faith and for value; it stays good between you and the tenant and against anyone with notice of it. Instead of the whole lease you may record a memorandum signed and acknowledged by both parties that names the parties, states the term and any renewal or extension option, and describes the property (a survey or plot plan may describe part of a building); it has the same effect as recording the lease for what it contains. A lease of three years or less may also be recorded, and recorded instruments take priority in the order they are recorded. Recording does not change your duties or the tenant's rights under Indiana's landlord-tenant statutes. Whether a tenant's possession under an unrecorded lease gives a later buyer or lender notice of the lease is decided by Indiana courts; this library has not reviewed those cases, so for any lease longer than three years, record the lease or a memorandum within 45 days.

title: No Lease Term Limit in Indiana; Writing, Acknowledgment and Recording for Long Leases
bodyText: Indiana sets no maximum term for a residential lease and requires no seal. Three rules turn on length. A lease for a term exceeding three years must be in writing, signed by you as landlord, and acknowledged before a notary (or proved), and an electronic lease still needs that acknowledgment; the statute does not say what happens to a lease that lacks it, which is for Indiana courts, so always have a long lease acknowledged. To be enforced against a party, a lease for more than three years must also be signed by that party or that party's authorized agent; a lease of three years or less can be oral. And a lease for longer than three years must be recorded with the county recorder within 45 days after signing, or a later good-faith buyer, tenant or mortgagee who pays value can take free of it. Indiana requires no spouse's signature on a lease of property you own alone: by statute, a married man may lease his own real property in his own name, without his wife's joining, with the same effect as if she had signed, and a married woman has the same property rights as an unmarried woman. If you and your spouse own the property together, for example as tenants by the entireties, the statutes do not say whether one of you may lease it alone; Indiana courts decide that (this library has not reviewed those cases), so have every owner sign. Leases with an option to buy a home of up to four units carry their own disclosure rules.

title: No Lease-Type Parity Rule in Indiana
bodyText: Indiana has no rule requiring the same terms for month-to-month and fixed-term tenants. No statute bars terms that are more burdensome for one kind of tenancy, or caps a higher rent or a surcharge for a month-to-month tenancy or a short lease, so you may price and draft each type differently. The limits are the general ones: Indiana's fair housing law applies to every term; raising the rent, cutting services, or suing or threatening to sue for possession in response to a tenant's protected activity is retaliation, except declining to renew at the end of the term, raising rent to what comparable market rentals charge (at the end of the term, or during it if the lease provides for that), cutting a service for all tenants equally, and the court actions the retaliation law allows, such as an eviction for rent not paid within the time allowed or for holding over after a fixed term; and changing the rental agreement needs at least 30 days' written notice unless the written lease sets a different procedure. A month-to-month tenancy can also be ended on one month's notice and replaced with new terms; a fixed term keeps its terms until it ends unless the lease allows a change. Cities and counties may not regulate rents, lease terms or fees unless a state law allows it. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: No Minimum Type Size for an Indiana Lease
bodyText: Indiana sets no minimum type size, typeface or print format for a residential lease, and no rule that an unreadable lease is unenforceable or inadmissible. One rule reaches the lease: if you bill a tenant separately for water or sewer service and put the required disclosure in the lease, it must be printed in type no smaller than the largest type used anywhere else in the lease, which is why the library prints it on a separate signed page (see the water and sewer billing clause). The flood plain statement must be made clearly, without a type-size rule. Other Indiana print rules apply to other contracts, not to a home lease: self-storage rental agreements need a bold-type lien statement, rent-to-own agreements for goods and vehicle rental damage waivers have type-size rules, and home improvement contracts have their own format. Use type large enough to read easily. A term a tenant could not reasonably read invites a dispute over whether it was agreed, and the signing presumption under Indiana's consumer protection law (that a person who signs a written contract knows its terms) is rebuttable.

title: Deadlines to Sue for Rent and Damages
bodyText: Indiana's general limitation periods decide how long you have to sue a tenant or former tenant; no statute sets a special period for leases. Actions for the use, rents and profits of real property must be brought within six years after the claim arises, and so must actions on written contracts for the payment of money made after August 31, 1982, actions on unwritten agreements, and actions for injury to real property. Actions on other written contracts (not for the payment of money), and actions to recover possession of real estate, have ten years. Injury to personal property has two years. In a suit to recover the property, you may recover for the tenant's use and occupation for no more than six years before you sue. Which period a court applies to a particular lease claim (for example unpaid rent under a written lease, or damage to the unit) can depend on how the claim is framed; Indiana courts decide this. The cautious course is to treat six years from each missed payment or each item of damage as your deadline. Restarting the clock: an acknowledgment of the debt or a promise to pay counts only if it is in writing and signed by the person you would sue, and one co-tenant's acknowledgment does not bind another. The statute keeps whatever effect a payment has, but a note of a payment written by or for you is not enough. Whether a partial payment restarts the period is case law not reviewed here, so if a former tenant pays part, ask for a signed written acknowledgment of the balance. Limitation periods are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Damages Fixed in Advance in the Lease
bodyText:
No Indiana statute governs liquidated damages in a residential lease: none permits, voids or limits a lease term that fixes in advance what the tenant owes for a breach, such as a set charge for breaking the lease or for a late move-out. Indiana's liquidated-damages statutes cover other things (sales and leases of goods under the Uniform Commercial Code, public contracts, wage claims and the like).

Whether a lease figure is an enforceable estimate of damages or an unenforceable penalty is decided by Indiana courts under contract law. Statutes do shape the question in three ways.

The security deposit may be applied to rent due for the tenant's premature termination of the lease, among the deposit statute's listed uses, and, because the deposit statute counts every payment the lease requires, other than the deposit, as rent, a fixed early-termination charge could be taken from the deposit as unpaid rent only if the charge itself is enforceable, which is the case-law question above.

A tenant who is a protected victim of domestic violence, a sex offense or stalking and ends the lease under that statute owes rent prorated to the termination date but no other rent or fees due only because of the early termination, and nothing at all if the tenant terminates at least 14 days before first having the right to occupy. And a charge that is unduly excessive, imposed through unequal bargaining power, can be an unconscionable act under the consumer protection act.

The library's optional early-termination clause, tagged for Indiana, is an option the tenant may choose to end a fixed term for a stated fee and preserves the protected tenant's statutory right. Cautious course: tie any fixed figure to a reasonable estimate of your actual loss, and keep records of re-renting efforts and costs.

title: No Lockout for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Indiana does not allow a lockout for unpaid rent, with or without notice and whatever the lease says. Except as a court order authorizes, you may not deny or interfere with a tenant's access to or possession of the unit by any act, including changing the locks or adding a device to keep the tenant out, removing doors, windows, fixtures or appliances, or interrupting, reducing or shutting off electricity, gas, water or other essential services (you may interrupt service for an emergency, good-faith repairs or necessary construction, and you need not pay for services you did not agree to provide). A lease term permitting a lockout is void, because these rules cannot be waived, and a lease may not define abandonment differently from the statute. The only exception is a unit the tenant has abandoned: the tenant has failed to pay or offer to pay rent and the circumstances would lead a reasonable person to conclude the tenant has surrendered possession. A tenant who is locked out or has services cut off may petition for an emergency possessory order; the court must hold a hearing within three business days, rarely grants a continuance, and if it finds a violation and immediate and serious harm must order you to restore possession or stop the violation, and may later award damages and order return of the tenant's property. The lawful route for unpaid rent is the 10-day notice and an eviction case (see the nonpayment-notice and eviction-process rows). The rule applies to rental agreements entered into or renewed after June 30, 1999, fixed-term and month-to-month alike.

title: Shifting Maintenance Duties to the Tenant
bodyText:
No Indiana statute lets a lease shift any of your statutory maintenance duties to the tenant, whatever the consideration and however conspicuous the term, and none lists particular duties, such as common-area garbage removal, that may be shifted on conditions.

Your duties to deliver the home safe, clean and habitable, comply with health and housing codes, make reasonable efforts to keep common areas clean and proper, and keep the systems and inducement appliances you provide in good and safe working condition stay with you, and a waiver of them, by contract or otherwise, is void. These rules cover rental agreements entered into after June 30, 2002, except a rent-to-own agreement entered into before July 1, 2008.

What the lease can do: restate and rely on the tenant's own statutory duties (keeping the areas the tenant uses reasonably clean, using systems and appliances reasonably, not damaging the home, following reasonable rules, keeping smoke detectors working and replacing their batteries, and returning the home clean apart from ordinary wear and tear), and assign routine upkeep that the statute does not place on you, such as lawn care or snow removal at a single-family home; the library's tenant maintenance, snow removal and landscaping clauses are tagged for Indiana.

Where the line falls between routine upkeep and a statutory duty (for example, upkeep of a furnace or water heater you provided) is not settled by statute, and Indiana courts decide it. Cautious course: keep repairs to the systems and appliances you provide with you, and assign the tenant only tasks that do not touch them.

title: No Meter-Attached Energy Efficiency Charges
bodyText: Indiana has no statute or Utility Regulatory Commission rule that lets a utility place an energy-efficiency or conservation repayment charge on the meter or bill of a later customer at the same address, and none that requires you to tell a new tenant about such a charge or reduce rent for it. If a utility program you join would put a charge on the tenant's bill, the program's own terms govern; tell the tenant in writing before the lease is signed. Indiana does limit meter-related charges when you bill tenants yourself. If you sub-bill water or sewer, the bill may include only the usage charge and the listed fees (a reasonable set-up fee, an administrative fee of no more than $4 a month and a returned-payment fee), so a separate charge for the meter is not allowed; a submetered water bill must show the beginning and ending readings and dates. If you submeter electricity, you may charge only the utility's cost per kilowatt-hour with nothing added, and each bill must show the beginning and ending readings and dates.

title: Minors as Tenants and Eviction Defendants
bodyText: In Indiana a minor is a person under 18. No Indiana statute lets a person under 18 enter into a binding lease, and none bars you from renting to a minor or from naming a minor in an eviction case. Under general contract law a minor's contract can usually be undone by the minor; Indiana courts decide how that applies to a lease for housing. The exception is emancipation: a juvenile court may emancipate a child completely, in which case the child has all the rights and responsibilities of an adult, or partially, with the order listing what the child may do, which can include entering into contracts and owning property. If an applicant under 18 says they are emancipated, ask for a copy of the court order and check that it covers contracts. In court, a minor may be sued in the minor's own name, through a guardian ad litem or next friend, or through a court-appointed guardian; if the minor is not represented or not adequately represented, the court must appoint a guardian ad litem, which can slow your case. The cautious course is to have every tenant who signs the lease be at least 18 (or produce an emancipation order covering contracts), list minors as occupants rather than tenants, and, if you do rent to a minor, have an adult co-sign or guarantee the lease.

title: Nonrefundable Fees Versus Deposits
bodyText:
Indiana has no rule requiring a notice, set wording or separate signature before a deposit or fee may be nonrefundable. What decides is substance, not the label. Money you hold to secure the tenant's performance of the lease, or that is returnable when the unit comes back in the required condition, is a security deposit, whatever you call it, and must be used and returned under the deposit rules within 45 days.

Money that is truly not returnable and not held as security is not a deposit; for the deposit law it counts as rent, meaning any payment made to you under the rental agreement. Calling money "nonrefundable" does not take it out of the deposit rules if you hold it to secure the tenant's performance: a deposit is defined by what it is held for, not by whether the lease promises to return it.

No statute caps or bars nonrefundable lease fees, and cities and counties may not regulate landlord fees, but you may not charge any fee to keep an emotional support animal. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants. Whether a fee that in practice serves as security against damage is a deposit in disguise is decided by Indiana courts.

The cautious course is to name each nonrefundable fee for what it pays for and state its amount in the lease, never to call it a deposit, and to keep any money meant to cover damage in the refundable deposit. The library's optional nonrefundable-fees clause lists the fees for you.

title: No Separate Notice for Nonrefundable Amounts
bodyText: Indiana has no rule requiring a separate written notice, a separate signature or a stand-alone document before part of a deposit, or a fee, may be nonrefundable. The lease itself may state which fees are nonrefundable. Under Indiana's deposit law any amount held as security or returnable at move-out is a security deposit whatever it is called, so the safe practice is to list each nonrefundable fee and its amount in the lease and keep all security money in the refundable deposit (see the row on nonrefundable fees versus deposits). Indiana does require a disclosure, in the lease or in a separate signed writing among other places, when you bill tenants separately for water or sewer service; that is a different rule (see the water and sewer billing clause).

title: Out-of-State Owners: Indiana Agent, Registration and Service
bodyText:
**Agent and manager.** Every Indiana landlord, resident or not, must give the tenant in writing, at or before the start of the lease, the names and addresses of an Indiana resident authorized to manage the unit and an Indiana resident, reasonably accessible to the tenant, authorized to accept legal papers and notices and demands for the owner (one person may fill both roles).

If you do not, the person who failed to disclose becomes your agent for those purposes and for your obligations, and the tenant may recover the reasonable cost of finding the information (see the owner-disclosure row and the manager-and-agent clause).

That agent rule is the only nonresident-owner designation Indiana's statutes impose on landlords; no statute requires a tenant to withhold state income tax from rent paid to a nonresident owner, and the disclosure statute does not make the disclosure a condition of suing.

**Out-of-state entities.** An LLC, corporation or other entity formed in another state may not do business in Indiana until it registers with the Indiana Secretary of State, and while unregistered it may not bring or keep a lawsuit in Indiana courts (it can still defend one, and its contracts stay valid); it can also owe a civil penalty of up to $10,000.

Merely owning property, without more, is not doing business, but renting out property as a business may be; Indiana courts decide where that line falls. The cautious course is for an out-of-state entity landlord to register and keep a registered agent before it files any eviction.

**Assumed names.** An individual or general partnership renting under a name other than its real name must file an assumed-name certificate with the county recorder of each county where it has a place of business or office; an entity using a name other than its registered name files with the Secretary of State. Failing to file is a Class B infraction; the statute does not say it bars a lawsuit, but sue in your registered or real name and list the assumed name.

**Being sued.** A nonresident owner of Indiana real property is subject to Indiana courts for claims arising from that ownership, and may be served in the ways the court rules allow, including through the Indiana Secretary of State; an entity with a registered agent may be served through that agent.

title: Charging the Tenant for Serving a Notice
bodyText: Indiana has no statute that authorizes, bars or limits a lease charge for preparing, serving or posting a notice, such as the 10-day notice for unpaid rent or a notice to end a tenancy, and cities and counties may not regulate landlord fees. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants. Indiana also has no general statute, like some states have, declaring contract penalties void for leases of homes; the only codified rule on agreed damages in Indiana's commercial code applies to sales of goods. Whether a fixed notice fee in a lease is enforceable, or is an unenforceable penalty because it is not tied to your actual cost, is decided by Indiana courts; this library has not reviewed those cases, and it does not offer a notice-service fee clause for Indiana. A notice fee the lease validly imposes is a payment under the rental agreement, which the deposit law counts as rent, so if it is owed and unpaid the deposit may pay it; but if a court finds the fee an unenforceable penalty it was never owed, and withholding it from the deposit exposes you to liability for the amount withheld plus attorney's fees and court costs. The cautious course is not to charge a flat notice fee; recover your actual, documented costs, and attorney's fees where the lease and the statutes allow, through the court. A charge for a notice does not change the notice itself: the 10-day notice for unpaid rent cannot be shortened or waived in this library's leases.

title: Can the Lease Shorten or Waive the Notice to Quit?
bodyText: Indiana's notice-to-quit statutes have no sentence voiding a waiver, and only one of them lets an agreement change the notice. For unpaid rent, you may end the lease on at least 10 days' notice unless the parties otherwise agreed or the tenant pays in full within the notice period. That wording suggests a lease could change the 10-day notice, but how Indiana courts read it has not been reviewed, and the library does not offer a clause shortening or waiving it; where the lease requires rent in advance, the statute already says no notice is needed when advance rent is not paid. For ending a tenancy without fault, the statutes set the notice by tenancy type and say nothing about changing it by agreement: a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy of three months or less ends on notice equal to the rental period; a year-to-year tenancy on notice at least three months before the end of the year; a tenancy at will on one month's written notice. A fixed-term lease needs no notice to end at the end of its term, and none is needed where the lease itself fixes when the tenancy ends, for a tenant at sufferance, or for a tenant at will who commits waste. Because no statute authorizes a shorter notice for these tenancies, the cautious course is not to shorten or waive them in the lease. If a protected tenant's complaint is followed by a notice, the retaliation rules also apply. Whether a lease term shortening a periodic notice binds the tenant is case law.

title: No Special Rules While a Notice to Vacate Runs in Indiana
bodyText: Indiana has no special rules for the period after you give a notice to vacate. Nothing bars specific alterations, renovation or showings while the notice runs, and no statute adds terms to the notice itself beyond the forms Indiana supplies. The tenancy simply continues, with every ordinary rule, until the notice period ends. Without a court order you still may not change the locks, remove doors, windows, fixtures or appliances, or interrupt electricity, gas, water or other essential services; only the service interruption has an exception, for an emergency, good-faith repairs or necessary construction. You still must keep up your repair and code duties. You may enter only at reasonable times after reasonable notice (no notice in an emergency that threatens safety or your property), and you may not use entry to harass the tenant; the tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry to show the unit to new tenants or buyers, or for necessary or agreed repairs and alterations. Renovation that makes the unit unusable before the notice period ends interferes with possession; the cautious course is to wait until the tenant has left. A notice given in response to protected tenant activity can be a threat to sue for possession, which is retaliation unless an exception applies, for example declining to renew at the end of the term, rent the tenant has not paid within the time allowed, a tenant holding over after a fixed term, a code requirement to alter, remodel or demolish that would effectively deprive the tenant of the unit, or a good-faith plan at the end of the term to live there, completely remodel, or take the unit off the rental market for at least six months. If the tenant does not leave when the notice ends, only a court can remove the tenant.

title: Where Indiana Law Lets the Lease Decide, Including Options to Buy
bodyText: Several Indiana rules change only if the parties agree, some only in writing and some by any agreement. (1) Deposit as last month's rent: the deposit may pay the last rental period only if a written agreement says it will; otherwise the tenant may not apply the deposit to rent. (2) Changing the rental agreement: you must give at least 30 days' written notice before modifying it unless a written rental agreement provides otherwise; whether a lease can allow you to change terms on your own is for the courts, so the library does not offer that. (3) Utilities: you do not have to pay for electricity, gas, water or other services unless you agreed to. (4) Tenant's representative: a tenant may name, in a written lease or in a separate writing delivered to you (which ranks first), the person who may collect belongings, the deposit and unearned rent if the tenant, as the sole occupant, dies or is incapacitated and absent from the unit. (5) Sale or change of manager: the release on written notice of a sale or of a manager's departure applies unless otherwise agreed. (6) Electronic notices work only if both sides agree (see the electronic notice clause). (7) Property as security: in a writing separate from the rental agreement, you and the tenant may agree that you will hold property the tenant voluntarily hands over as security in exchange for not filing an eviction. The 10-day notice for unpaid rent can also be changed by agreement, but the library does not offer that clause. Options to buy. If you lease a home with up to four units and give the tenant an option to buy it, Indiana's seller disclosure law treats you as an owner selling the property: you must complete and sign the state seller's disclosure form and give it to the tenant before the offer is accepted; the statute treats the lease as the closing but does not say whether, for a lease-option, the form is due before the lease is signed or before the option is exercised, and no court decision was reviewed, so give it before the lease with the option is signed. Before the closing, the tenant is not bound until both of you have signed the form; if a later form discloses a defect after acceptance, the tenant may cancel within two business days and get deposits back; and at or before settlement you must disclose any material change in the property's condition or certify that it is substantially the same. If the home is in a homeowners association, the association disclosures and documents are due at least 10 days before the sale closes. The usual landlord-tenant statutes still apply to a lease with an option to purchase signed after June 30, 2008, and money paid for the option is not a security deposit unless the arrangement was meant to evade the deposit rules. Indiana has no separate rent-to-own statute for homes (no special cure period or ban on forfeiting the option payment), and its rent-to-own law for goods does not cover dwellings, so the option terms are your agreement; spell out the price, the option fee, how rent is credited and what happens on default. If you buy a homeowner's house during a foreclosure and lease it back with an option to repurchase, Indiana's foreclosure rescue law applies: you must verify the homeowner can make the lease payments and repurchase, give written notice of the homeowner's rights, complete a formal settlement, meet the surety bond requirement of Indiana's credit services organization law, and use fair lease and repurchase terms.

title: Ordnance, Demolition and Shared-Meter Disclosures in Indiana
bodyText: Ordnance and demolition: Indiana has no rule requiring you to tell a tenant that the property is near a former military ordnance site or that you have applied to demolish the building. (A separate disclosure applies near Naval Support Activity Crane, Lake Glendora Test Facility and Grissom Air Reserve Base; see the military installation clause.) If you plan to demolish or remodel so that the tenant's household must move out, you may seek possession in good faith at the end of the lease term for that purpose even if the tenant has complained about conditions, and code-required demolition that deprives the tenant of the unit is likewise not retaliation. Shared meters: two rules apply. (1) Water and sewer: if you bill tenants separately for water or sewer service you buy from a utility, your disclosure must appear in the lease, the first bill or a separate signed page, with the statute's complaint statement, and, unless the building has only one dwelling unit and the utility meters it directly, the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission's rules set what each sub-bill must show and require at least 17 days to pay a sub-bill before you start collection (see the water and sewer billing clause). (2) Electricity: in a building with more than one residential unit served through a master meter, you may install a submeter for each unit and charge each tenant for the unit's own use at the average cost per kilowatt-hour, with no extra charges; every unit in the building must then be submetered, and every rental agreement must clearly state that the unit is submetered, that electric bills will be based on submeter readings, that electricity for all common areas and common facilities is your responsibility and not the tenant's, and how disputes are handled (see the electric submetering clause and row). You must also register with the Commission and keep the required records. A building with no submeters, where electricity is in the rent, needs no meter disclosure.

title: Elevators and Garage Door Openers
bodyText: Two Indiana statutes reach building facilities a landlord may provide. Elevators: an elevator, escalator, platform lift, stairway chair lift or dumbwaiter in a rental building is a regulated lifting device unless it is in a private residence. It may not be operated without a state operating certificate, renewed yearly (and whenever the device is altered) on proof of passing safety tests; a copy of the certificate must be displayed in the car or machine room, along with the elevator's bar code where riders can scan it; and maintenance must be done by a licensed elevator mechanic. A person who controls the place where an uncertified device is operated, and has authority to maintain it or take it out of service, commits a Class C infraction. Local governments may not regulate lifting devices except through an approved state program. If an elevator is provided on the premises when the lease is made, you must also keep it in good and safe working condition. Garage door openers: anyone who regularly sells, leases or otherwise supplies goods or services to consumers and who installs, services or repairs an automatic garage door opener at a home or apartment with a garage must test that it reverses on contact with a two-inch obstacle; if it fails, the tester must attach a warning tag and the tester's employer must notify the occupant in writing within 10 working days. A knowing violation carries a $500 civil penalty. Whether a landlord counts as such a supplier is not settled, so if you or your staff install or repair openers, do the reversal test and tag any opener that fails. Cities may adopt stricter opener rules.

title: Owner Move-In in Indiana: Lease Must Reserve It
bodyText:
Indiana has no just-cause or owner move-in rule, so it neither requires nor limits an owner move-in reason. A month-to-month tenancy can be ended for any lawful reason, including your own move-in, on one month's notice (a week for a week-to-week tenancy, three months before the year's end for a year-to-year tenancy), and a fixed term ends at its end without notice.

During a fixed term you may end the lease early to move in only if the lease reserves that right; without it, a silent lease gives you no early termination for owner occupancy. The library's optional Owner Occupancy clause reserves it on written notice of at least the number of days you choose (not less than 30) to the end of a monthly rental period. Two limits apply.

Indiana's retaliation law lets you take possession in good faith at the end of the term to live in the unit yourself even after a tenant's protected activity, but a mid-term termination made in response to that activity is not covered by that exception. And you may not end a lease solely because a tenant or household member is protected under Indiana's domestic violence, sex offense and stalking protections. A tenant who will not leave must be removed through the court.

In a mobile home community, an operator closing the community must give each home owner written notice at least 180 days before closure.

title: No Parking-Rules Notice Law in Indiana; Towing Signs and Abandoned Vehicles
bodyText:
Indiana has no parking-rules notice law for rentals: no duty to deliver parking or towing rules before signing, no required heading, no limit on what vehicle information you may ask for, no rule that a parking permit last as long as the lease, and no waiting period before towing a tenant's car for expired registration. Put the parking terms, any parking fee, and the towing rules in the lease or its rules.

In a mobile home community, the state health rules require adequate parking, at least one parking space for each lot within the community and, in communities built after June 14, 1974, overflow parking of one space for every three homes, and an unlicensed or inoperative vehicle may not stay in the community more than 30 days unless stored in a designated, screened area at least 100 feet from the nearest home.

Changing those terms mid-lease follows the general rule: at least 30 days' written notice before modifying the rental agreement unless the written lease sets a different procedure. Towing has its own rules. A vehicle you believe is abandoned on your property may be towed if the owner has not moved it 24 hours after the notice-tag process, or at once in an emergency (the library's towing row has the tag details).

The owner of commercial private property who sets up a tow-away zone must post a conspicuous sign more than five and less than seven feet high saying it is a tow-away zone, giving contact information and describing who may park, and a towing company may not tow from a zone whose sign is at the wrong height; whether an apartment complex is commercial private property is not defined, so post compliant signs to be safe, and check local rules, which may differ.

A parking fee is a lease charge and counts as rent for the deposit rules, and cities and counties may not regulate your fees or lease terms unless a state law allows it. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: Tenant Rights an Indiana Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Indiana has no single rule that every tenant right is non-waivable. Instead, most chapters of its residential landlord-tenant law carry their own non-waiver sentence, and a lease term giving up those rules is void. A waiver is void for: the security deposit rules; the rules on tenant property left after an eviction (the list of exempt property and its release without payment); the rules on modifying the lease, seizing tenant property, lockouts, utility shutoffs and entry (rental agreements entered into or renewed after June 30, 1999, and this waiver is void even when made by a former tenant); the tenant duty rules and your landlord duty rules (rental agreements entered into after June 30, 2002, except a rent-to-own agreement entered into before July 1, 2008); the retaliation rules; and the protections for victims of domestic violence, sexual offenses and stalking (agreements entered into or renewed after June 30, 2007). In addition, the smoke detector rules cannot be waived in the lease or a separate writing; a lease may not define abandonment of the unit or of the tenant's belongings differently from the statute; a tenant's attornment to a stranger is void without your consent or a court order; a confession-of-judgment term signed before a claim arises is void; no contract can waive the small claims venue rule; and in an arbitration a waiver of the right to a lawyer made before the hearing is ineffective. The emergency possessory order, eviction diversion, eviction record sealing and squatter chapters have no non-waiver sentence of their own, but they set court procedures that a lease cannot change in practice. The 10-day notice for unpaid rent applies unless the parties otherwise agreed; this library does not offer a clause changing it. A lease term outside these lists can still fail as unconscionable under the consumer protection act, which Indiana courts decide case by case. No Indiana statute adds a non-waiver rule for a home sale-leaseback.

title: No No-Notice Entry for Scheduled Services in Indiana
bodyText: Indiana has no rule allowing entry without notice for regularly scheduled services, even if the lease lists them. Every entry other than an emergency needs reasonable written or oral notice of your intent to enter, and you may enter only at reasonable times; you may not use entry to harass the tenant. You may enter without notice only in an emergency that threatens the occupants' safety or your property, and without the tenant's consent only under a court order or after the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit. The tenant, for its part, may not unreasonably refuse you entry to supply necessary or agreed services, to make necessary or agreed repairs, or to inspect. These rules cannot be waived in the lease. A lease can still set a regular service schedule (for example filter changes or pest treatment) and the hours for those visits, and the tenant's agreement to the services makes refusal harder to justify, but whether a schedule in the lease is itself reasonable notice of each visit is for Indiana courts (this library has not reviewed those cases). The cautious course is to send a reminder a reasonable time before each scheduled visit, at a reasonable hour, and to knock and announce before entering.

title: No Pesticide Notice Rule for Rentals
bodyText: Indiana has no statute requiring you to notify tenants before pest control treatment or a pesticide application in or around a rental. Indiana's pesticide notification registry and advance-notice rules apply to schools, not to housing. Pesticides must be applied according to their labels, and anyone applying them for hire must be licensed by the state chemist; the state chemist's detailed pesticide rules are not reviewed here. Whenever treatment requires entering a unit, give the tenant reasonable notice of entry as Indiana requires, and it is good practice to tell tenants in advance what will be applied, any preparation steps, and how long to stay out.

title: No Pet-and-Eviction Fact Sheet to Give Indiana Tenants
bodyText: Indiana has no state fact sheet on pets and eviction that you must give a tenant who has a dog or cat, and no rule about what happens to a tenant's pets during an eviction. Your pet terms are whatever the lease says (see the pet clause and the pet deposit row), subject to the rules on guide dogs and assistance animals, which you must allow regardless of a no-pets policy (see those rows). If a tenant leaves an animal behind after moving out or being evicted, do not treat it as abandoned property to dispose of: a person who has a vertebrate animal in custody and recklessly, knowingly or intentionally abandons or neglects it commits animal cruelty, so once you take charge of the animal, feed and shelter it and contact local animal control promptly. After an eviction, the tenant's other belongings follow the court-ordered removal and storage process (see the post-eviction property row).

title: No Plain-Language Law for Indiana Leases
bodyText: Indiana has no plain-language or readability law for residential leases: no readability score, no rule that the lease be divided into captioned sections, no front-page summary and no dollar threshold. Indiana's consumer protection law does reach residential leases by a landlord who regularly leases, with no dollar limit, and it treats as unconscionable a contract with oppressively one-sided or harsh terms, terms that unduly limit the tenant's remedies or an unduly excessive price, where unequal bargaining power led the tenant to sign unwillingly or without knowing the terms. Signing a written lease raises a rebuttable presumption that the tenant knew its terms, so clear wording and headings help you keep that presumption. One narrow exception: if you operate a housing with services establishment (sleeping accommodations for at least five residents, with health-related or supportive services offered for a fee), the residency contract must set out a list of required items in clear and understandable language, and each resident gets a complete copy. Write the lease in short, plain sentences with descriptive headings in any case; a term a tenant could not reasonably read invites a dispute over whether it was agreed.

title: No Statement of Consumer Restrictions in an Indiana Lease
bodyText: Indiana does not require a residential lease to carry a statement listing the terms that favor you or every right the tenant gives up, and it has no readability test, no Attorney General preapproval of lease forms and no dollar threshold for such a rule. Indiana takes the other route: it makes the tenant's main statutory rights impossible to waive. A waiver by contract or otherwise is void for the security deposit rules, the landlord-tenant rights and obligations chapter (which also lists terms a lease may not contain), the tenant's and landlord's statutory duties, the retaliation chapter, the domestic violence and similar protections, and parts of the rules on a tenant's property after eviction. Listing such a waiver in the lease does not make it binding. Leave those waivers out rather than trying to disclose them; see the rows on terms Indiana voids and on rights an Indiana lease cannot waive.

title: Poll Takers and Candidates at Rental Buildings
bodyText: Indiana requires the proprietor or manager of a place of lodging, which includes an apartment, a residential building, a boarding or lodging house and any other place where people are lodged, to let a poll taker for a political party, or for an independent candidate for a federal or state office, enter during reasonable hours to take a poll of the residents. A condominium association of co-owners has the same duty. The poll taker carries a certificate from the party or organization stating the nature of the poll and whom it is for. The rule does not apply to a building where three or fewer people are kept as guests or lodgers, to residential mental health facilities, or to military camps or barracks. If you refuse entry, the county election board must meet, notify you by certified mail, hear evidence and, if it finds reasonable cause to believe you violated the rule, send its minutes to the county prosecutor. A building rule or lease term against solicitation does not override this duty for qualifying poll takers; you may still keep entry to reasonable hours, ask to see the certificate, and apply your ordinary security procedures. Separately, a homeowners association (other than a gated community with privately owned and maintained roads and sidewalks) may not prohibit candidates, elected officials, their spouses or their volunteers from entering association property, including members' lots, for political activity. Indiana has no other statute giving canvassers or candidates access to rental property, and no rule on tenants' own political activity at the property beyond the association sign rules (see the display row).

title: Apartment and Community Pools: Semi-Public Pool Rules
bodyText: Indiana has no statute requiring a pool safety notice in a lease or a landlord-specific pool barrier duty, but a pool at an apartment complex, condominium or mobile home park is a semi-public pool under the state health department's pool rules if it is restricted to residents and their guests. Those rules, which the state or local health department enforces, require the pool to be built, maintained and modified under the state Swimming Pool Code, which requires covered pools, including semi-public pools at apartments and condominiums, to be enclosed by a fence, wall, building or other enclosure at least six feet high. A semi-public pool with a surface area of 2,000 square feet or more must have a certified lifeguard on duty at poolside whenever it is open. When no lifeguard is on duty, signs must be posted at the entrances and inside the pool area reading "Warning-No Lifeguard on Duty" and stating that no one may swim alone and that children under 14 and nonswimmers must be accompanied by a responsible adult; other required signs include "POOL CLOSED" when closed, "No Diving" in shallow areas and the posted user health rules. Each pool must have a life pole, a ring buoy, a spine board (except spas and wading pools), a stocked first aid kit and an emergency telephone within 200 feet with emergency numbers posted, and a copy of the rules must be kept on site. The health rules do not apply to a pool at a one- or two-family dwelling kept by an individual for the household's sole use, so a pool at a single-family rental is governed by the residential code and your lease rather than these rules; whether a rented home's pool is for the household's sole use depends on the facts, so if tenants have access, treat it cautiously and set pool rules in the lease. Local codes may add requirements.

title: No Right to a Window or Portable Air Conditioner
bodyText: Indiana has no statute giving a tenant the right to install a window or portable air conditioner, requiring you to provide cooling, or requiring a lease that restricts window units to say so; there is also no comparable rule for homeowners associations. Whether a tenant may install one is up to the lease and your rules. If air conditioning is provided on the premises when the lease is made, you must keep it in good and safe working condition (leases entered into after June 30, 2002), and the tenant must use it reasonably. Local rental inspection programs may check air conditioning equipment. If you allow window units, set conditions in your rules: secure installation, no blocking of an emergency escape window, a suitable electrical circuit, and removal or repair of any damage at move-out.

title: No Tenant Right to Plug-In Solar
bodyText: Indiana has no statute that gives a tenant a right to install a plug-in, balcony or other portable solar device, and none that voids a lease term restricting solar equipment. Your lease decides; the shared no-alterations clause and your consent process apply. The homeowners association solar law gives a petition right only to a homeowner who is a member, not to a tenant. Before agreeing to a device that connects to the building's wiring, know the utility rules: for customers of an investor-owned electric utility, a generator that operates in parallel with the utility's system is a customer-generator facility that must go through the utility's interconnection review. The simplest track covers certified inverter-based systems of 10 kilowatts or less, with no application fee; the customer must sign the interconnection agreement and return it at least 10 business days before starting operation, and may not start before any inspection the utility requires. The installation must also meet local electrical codes. The customer for this purpose is whoever has agreed to pay for the electric service, so where the tenant has the account, the application is the tenant's. The rule does not say whether a small plug-in device that feeds power back through an outlet counts, so if you allow one, require the tenant to confirm with the utility first, to use only certified equipment, and to follow any utility requirements; municipal utilities and electric cooperatives have their own rules. Cities and counties may not regulate lease terms, and may not require buildings to be retrofitted with energy-producing devices. The limit on regulating lease terms does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants; the retrofit limit has no such exception.

title: Indiana Rules That Turn on How Many Units You Own
bodyText: Indiana gives no general small-landlord exemption: the deposit, landlord-tenant, repair, retaliation and eviction statutes apply whether you rent one unit or a thousand. Only a few rules turn on how many homes you own or how big the building is, and where a rule has several conditions, every one must be met. Fair housing: Indiana's fair housing act does not apply to the rental of a single-family house by an owner who owns, and has an interest in the proceeds of, no more than three single-family houses at any one time, but only if the house is rented without a licensed real estate broker, agent or salesperson (or their employees or agents) and without the services of an owner of a dwelling for five or more families, and without publishing, posting or mailing a discriminatory notice or advertisement; if you were not the most recent resident of the house, the exemption covers only one rental in 24 months. Separately, the act does not apply to rooms or units in a building for no more than four families living independently if you live in one of them. The federal Fair Housing Act has the same two exemptions, but its advertising ban still applies to exempt owners, and it counts you as in the business of renting (and not exempt) if within the past 12 months you took part as principal in three or more rentals or sales, or if you own a dwelling for five or more families (see `edu-fair-housing-in`). Licensing: no real estate license is needed to rent or manage property you own; a separate exemption covers a person whose only licensed-type activity is renting apartment units it owns and manages, up to twelve units on one parcel or contiguous parcels; renting or managing property for others for pay generally needs a license unless another exemption applies (for example, an individual employed or supervised by a licensed broker, or a full-time salaried employee of the owner). Local rental programs: a single rental permit and other limits on local registration apply to a rental unit community, meaning contiguous parcels with five or more rental units in all, not occupied only by the owner or the owner's family (see `edu-rental-registration-inspection-in`). Building size: the state fire safety rules for apartments reach buildings with three or more apartments (not an apartment with immediate ground-level access to the outside); a building used by three or more tenants is a Class 1 structure under the building code, while a building with one or two dwelling units or a townhouse is a Class 2 structure; a utility may ask a court to appoint a receiver for a multifamily property with more than four dwelling units (or a mobile home community) whose owner has not paid invoiced utility bills for more than 90 days or has missed curative payment plan amounts for at least 60 days; and when a water utility asks, the owner of a building with four or fewer dwelling units must replace the customer-owned part of a lead service line within the program's terms, while the owner of a multifamily property with more than four units may choose to join the utility's program and, if it does not answer within 45 days, must replace the line itself at its own expense. A broker's lien for commission does not reach real estate with one to four residential units. An owner who lives in a building of eight or fewer residential units may do plumbing work on its own building without a plumbing license. These thresholds apply the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No End-of-Term Possession Bond; Prejudgment Possession Bonds
bodyText: Indiana has no statute under which a tenant gives a bond, at the start or during the lease, promising to deliver possession at the end of the term, and no procedure that turns such a bond into a judgment without a hearing. A lease term in which the tenant agrees in advance that a judgment may be entered against the tenant without a court hearing after notice (a confession-of-judgment or cognovit term) is void, and knowingly getting someone to sign one, keeping one as its holder, or trying to enforce in Indiana another state's judgment based on one is a crime. The bonds Indiana does use in possession cases are court bonds during the lawsuit. If you want possession before final judgment, you may file an affidavit and ask the court for an order to show cause; the hearing may be held no earlier than five business days after service. The court may not give you possession before final judgment unless you file a written undertaking, with a surety the court approves, in an amount the court sets, to pay the tenant's damages if possession was wrongly ordered. The tenant may in turn file an undertaking, with an approved surety, to keep or recover possession until final judgment. Even with an order, the officer may not remove occupants until at least 48 hours after the order is served. After final judgment no bond is needed for possession. A security deposit is the only advance security a residential tenant gives you, and it is governed by the deposit rules.

title: Private Wells at Rentals: No Testing or Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Indiana has no statute requiring you to test a private well that serves a rental, or to give tenants well test results. If a well supplies the unit's water, your general duties still apply: deliver the unit safe, clean and habitable, comply with applicable health and housing codes, and keep plumbing provided on the premises in good and safe working condition. If your own well system has at least 15 service connections or regularly serves an average of at least 25 people daily for at least 60 days a year, it is a public water system under the federal definition that Indiana adopts, and one serving year-round residents (an apartment complex or mobile home community on its own well, for example) is a community water system. Indiana's rules require a public water system to meet the federal drinking water regulations, including their monitoring requirements; the detailed federal monitoring and notice requirements are not reviewed here, so check with the state environmental agency if your well serves 15 or more units or 25 or more people. Mobile home communities must use a public water system if one is available within 2,000 feet and otherwise a system approved by the state environmental agency. If the rental also takes water from a public water system and keeps its own well, the state's cross-connection rules let the well stay physically connected only if it is a well-water source built to protect water quality that meets drinking water standards without treatment, with an air gap or an approved backflow preventer on the service line. Testing well water at least yearly for bacteria and nitrates, and sharing results with tenants, is a prudent practice.

title: Promises to Repair or Improve
bodyText: No Indiana statute requires your promise to clean, repair or improve a rental to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be made before the lease is signed. Two statutes make a written, specific promise the safer course. First, your statutory duty is to deliver the home in compliance with the rental agreement as well as safe, clean and habitable, so a repair or improvement the lease promises becomes part of what the tenant can enforce through the statutory repair suit, with damages, attorney's fees and an injunction (rental agreements entered into after June 30, 2002, except pre-July 2008 rent-to-own agreements). Second, the consumer protection act, which covers home leases, treats some representations as deceptive acts when you know or should reasonably know they are false: that the home has characteristics or benefits it does not have, or is of a particular standard or quality; that the lease does or does not involve particular rights, remedies or obligations; and that you can complete something within a stated time when you know or should know you cannot. Where you state no time, you are presumed to have promised completion within a reasonable time. A tenant cannot bring the act's private suit over a lease, but the Attorney General can enforce it. Whether an oral promise or a promise made before signing binds you as a contract term is case law. Cautious course: put every promised repair or improvement in the lease or a signed addendum, describe it precisely, give a realistic completion date, and do not promise what you cannot deliver.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning for Indiana Rentals
bodyText: Indiana has no law like California's Proposition 65: you do not have to post or include in the lease a warning that the property may expose occupants to chemicals that cause cancer or reproductive harm, and Indiana has no formaldehyde notice for rental housing. Do not copy a California-style warning into an Indiana lease; it adds nothing the law requires and can confuse tenants. The disclosures that do bear on health are the federal lead-based paint disclosure for housing built before 1978 and, for a lease with an option to buy a home of up to four units, the seller's disclosure form, which covers known contamination from making controlled substances and known methamphetamine manufacture. Indiana also has no radon or mold disclosure rule; see those rows.

title: No Property-Tax-Share-of-Rent Statement in Indiana
bodyText: Indiana does not require you to tell a tenant what part of the rent goes to property taxes, to send an annual statement of rent paid, or to certify the rent a tenant paid to the Department of Revenue. Indiana's tax break for renters is an income tax deduction: an individual who rents a dwelling (a single-family home or a unit in a multifamily building) as a principal residence may deduct the rent paid during the year, up to $3,000 ($3,000 for a married couple filing jointly, $1,500 for a married person filing separately). The deduction is not available if the dwelling is exempt from Indiana property tax. Tenants sometimes ask for a year-end rent statement or the landlord's name and address to claim it; giving one is good service but not a legal duty. Keep accurate rent records so you can answer.

title: Questions About Protected Traits in Indiana
bodyText: Indiana's fair housing act has no separate rule that forbids asking applicants about, or keeping records of, their race, color, religion, sex, familial status, disability or national origin. It does make it unlawful to make, print or publish any notice, statement or advertisement about renting a dwelling that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on those traits, or an intention to discriminate, and to refuse to rent, set different terms or misstate availability because of them; a question on an application or in an interview can be such a statement, and asking it can be used as evidence that a later decision was discriminatory. Whether a question alone breaks the statement rule is decided by Indiana courts and the civil rights commission. Two Indiana rules do govern what you may ask. If an applicant whose disability is not readily apparent asks to keep an emotional support animal, you may require written verification from a health service provider that the person has a disability, has a disability-related need for the animal and is helped by it, and you may evaluate the documents submitted, but you may not charge a fee for the animal (see `edu-emotional-support-animals-in`). And housing for older persons that relies on the 55-and-older exemption must verify occupancy by reliable surveys and affidavits under the civil rights commission's rules, so age records are expected there. Indiana's service-animal law limits a public accommodation to two questions (whether the animal is required because of a disability and what work or task it has been trained to perform) and bars asking about the nature or extent of the disability or requiring certification; it applies to public accommodations, and whether a leasing office is one was not reviewed. The act does not apply to the small-owner and owner-occupied exemptions described in `edu-portfolio-thresholds-in`. The cautious course: do not ask about these traits, or about the nature or severity of a disability, except as needed to handle a request for a reasonable accommodation or modification; apply the same written screening criteria to everyone; and ask only for the number of occupants, not their ages or family relationships, unless you run qualifying housing for older persons. Federal fair housing law has its own rules on inquiries, which this library does not cover here. These rules apply the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Voiding a Lease for Indecent Nuisance Use in Indiana
bodyText: Indiana has one statute that lets you void a lease because of how the premises are used. If a tenant or occupant uses the building or unit for acts that create an indecent nuisance (prostitution, human trafficking, or certain sexual conduct in a public place), you may void the lease, and the statute says the right of possession reverts to you without any act of yours and that you may enter without legal process. That entry language sits beside Indiana's general bar on locking out or interfering with a tenant's possession except by court order, and how the two fit together is for Indiana courts (this library has not reviewed those cases). The cautious course is to go to court: a prosecutor or any resident of the county may sue to abate an indecent nuisance (a resident must post a bond of at least $1,000), and you may petition for an emergency possessory order when a tenant or guest commits a crime affecting the health and safety of another tenant, you or your agent; if the court also finds that someone has suffered or will suffer immediate and serious injury, loss or damage, it must order the tenant to return possession within seven days. Using a rental to commit a controlled-substance offense is a separate nuisance you may sue to abate. Apart from those statutes, Indiana does not void a lease for an improper use; the lease's use clause (residential use only, no criminal activity) and the ordinary default and notice rules govern. Local governments may limit short-term rentals used to house sex offenders, run a structured sober living home, or deal in illegal drugs or obscenity.

title: No Statutory Quiet Possession Covenant in Indiana; Possession Protections
bodyText: Indiana has no statutory covenant of quiet possession or quiet enjoyment in residential leases. Indiana's statute puts a covenant guaranteeing quiet possession into a warranty deed, not into a lease; whether a lease carries an implied covenant of quiet enjoyment is for Indiana courts (this library has not reviewed those cases), and the cautious course is to assume it does. Several statutes protect a tenant's possession directly. Without a court order you may not deny or interfere with the tenant's access to or possession of the unit by any act, including changing the locks, removing doors, windows, fixtures or appliances, or cutting off electricity, gas, water or other essential services (except for an emergency, good-faith repairs or necessary construction). You may not abuse your right of entry or use it to harass the tenant. You must deliver the premises in compliance with the rental agreement. If you interfere, the tenant can get an emergency possessory order from the small claims court, with a hearing within three business days, and the court may decide damages at a later hearing. In a mobile home community, each home must have ready and free access to the community's road. The library's No Disturbance clause handles tenants who disturb each other.

title: No Indiana Recycling Notice Duty
bodyText: No Indiana statute requires a residential landlord to provide recycling, or to tell tenants where and how to recycle at the property, whether in a lease, a posted notice or at move-in, and no 2026 act adds one. Indiana's recycling and solid-waste laws work through state agencies, solid waste management districts, local units and certain sellers (for example, a store that sells lead-acid batteries must post a notice about returning them for recycling), not through landlords. Trash service itself is a different matter. In a mobile home community, the operator must make suitable garbage containers or a garbage disposal system and trash containers available in a sanitary manner to each occupied home and must dispose of the community's garbage and trash in a manner the Indiana Department of Health approves; under the Department of Health's mobile home community rules the owner or operator is responsible for satisfactory storage, collection and disposal of refuse, in fly-tight, water-tight containers no more than 150 feet from any mobile home space, kept sanitary and with the surrounding area kept clean. Those rules say nothing about recycling. For other rentals, your duty to comply with health and housing codes includes any local trash and recycling rules that apply to the building. If you offer recycling, the cautious course is to describe it in your rules (what goes where and on what days), since a tenant must follow reasonable rules in force when the lease is signed and amended rules as the lease provides. These rules apply the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Paying Up to Stop a Nonpayment Termination
bodyText: Indiana's only redemption rule is in the 10-day nonpayment notice: if you give a tenant notice ending the lease for unpaid rent, the lease does not end on that notice if the tenant pays the rent in full before the notice period expires, unless the parties agreed otherwise. A partial payment does not stop the termination under the statute. Where the lease expressly requires rent in advance, no notice is needed to end the lease for unpaid advance rent; if you choose to give the 10-day notice anyway, the pay-in-full rule then applies to that notice (see the nonpayment-notice row). After the notice period, and after you file or win an eviction case, no Indiana statute gives the tenant a right to stop the eviction by paying what is owed, whether personally or through a charity, a government program or another third party, and none controls how such a payment may be made. You may choose to accept payment and settle; if the case is resolved before final judgment you must move to dismiss it unless you are still seeking damages, including keeping the deposit. No statute prescribes reservation wording for accepting partial rent. Whether accepting partial or late rent after a notice or a filing waives the notice or the default is decided by Indiana courts, and this library has not reviewed those cases; the cautious course is to decide before you accept, and if you accept while still intending to proceed, say so in writing at the time (see the acceptance-of-rent row). Federal programs may have their own rules for rental-assistance payments.

title: Religious and Cultural Displays
bodyText: Indiana has no statute that gives a tenant a specific right to put a religious or cultural item, such as a mezuzah, a wreath or a holiday decoration, on a door, door frame or other part of the rental, and none that limits what a lease or house rule may say about such displays. Your lease and reasonable rules decide; a tenant must follow reasonable rules in force when the lease is signed, and later rules only as the lease provides.
