Fair housing law sets the outer limit: you may not discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental, or in services or facilities, because of religion or national origin, and you may not coerce, intimidate or interfere with a tenant exercising fair housing rights. So a display rule must be content-neutral and applied the same way to everyone: a rule that allows some religions' or cultures' items but not others', or that you enforce only against one group, is risky. If you limit door or exterior displays, say what is limited (for example size, placement, damage to finishes, fire-code clearance) rather than what the display means, and consider allowing small items on the door frame. Associations' flag and political-sign rules are covered in the display row; Indiana has no association rule on religious items. Cities and counties may not add their own display rights to leases. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: No Bar on Collecting Rent for a Unit Needing Repairs
bodyText: Indiana has no statute that stops you from demanding or collecting rent, raising rent or serving a notice for unpaid rent because the unit has been cited as unsafe or substandard, and no statute sets up rent escrow or automatic rent abatement for repairs. That does not leave the tenant without remedies. You must deliver the unit safe, clean and habitable, comply with health and housing codes, and keep the listed systems working; a tenant who gives you notice and a reasonable time to repair may sue for damages, attorney's fees, an injunction and any other appropriate remedy (see the landlord-duties and repair-remedies rows). If a tenant complains to a code-enforcement office about a condition that materially affects health or safety, you may not respond by raising rent above comparable market rents, cutting services other than for all tenants equally, or bringing or threatening an eviction; you may still sue for possession if the tenant falls behind on rent and does not cure within the statutory or lease period (see the retaliation row). If a court appoints a receiver for unsafe premises in an unsafe-building case, the receiver, not you, collects the rents and uses them for repairs. Whether a tenant may lawfully withhold rent because of the unit's condition is decided by Indiana courts; this library has not reviewed those cases, so the cautious course is to fix cited conditions promptly, keep records of repair requests and work done, and not treat a tenant's withholding as either automatically lawful or automatically a default without advice. Local rental inspection programs are limited by state law (see the local registration and inspection row).

title: No Rent-Into-Court Rule; Tenant Counterclaims
bodyText: Indiana has no statute or court rule that makes a tenant pay rent into court, to the clerk or into escrow in order to defend an eviction, raise a defense, demand a jury, get a continuance or file a counterclaim, and no rule that a tenant's claims against you must be raised in the eviction or be lost. In a small claims eviction, a tenant who has a claim against you (for example for repairs or the deposit) may file a counterclaim; it must be filed in time for the court to mail it to you so that you receive it at least seven days before trial, or you may ask for a continuance. A tenant who pursues a counterclaim to decision gives up any part of it above the $10,000 small claims limit and cannot sue later for the rest. A tenant who wants a jury must make a written request within 10 days after receiving the notice of claim and pay the statutory amount to move the case to the regular docket ($70 on a small claims docket); that is a court fee, not rent. If you ask for possession before final judgment, the tenant can keep or recover possession by filing a court-approved undertaking with a surety, which secures your costs for wrongful detention; that is a bond, not rent paid to the court. Because rent is not paid into court while the case is pending, ask for a prompt trial date, keep your rent ledger current, and claim all rent accrued through the hearing in your judgment request.

title: Collecting Rent and the Duty to Maintain
bodyText: Indiana did not enact the uniform-act rule that the right to receive rent cannot be separated from the duty to maintain the premises by a lease, assignment, deed or mortgage. What Indiana has instead: for the deposit, landlord-duty, tenant-duty and retaliation laws, a "landlord" includes the owner, lessor or sublessor and anyone authorized to manage the premises, including anyone who receives rent or part of it (other than as a bona fide purchaser), so a manager or other person who collects the rent can be bound as a landlord. Your duties to deliver the unit in a safe, clean and habitable condition, follow health and housing codes, make all reasonable efforts to keep common areas clean and in proper condition, and maintain the listed systems and appliances provided when the lease was signed cannot be waived by lease. If you do not give the tenant the required written names and addresses of your Indiana manager and agent, that person becomes your agent for performing your obligations. On the other side, Indiana expressly allows rents to be assigned, mortgaged or pledged, and a lender or assignee that enforces an assignment of rents without taking possession does not take on the obligations of a mortgagee in possession; a court may also appoint a receiver to collect rents. So separating who collects the rent from who is responsible for repairs is possible in Indiana, but it does not reduce what the tenant is owed. If an assignee, manager or receiver collects the rent, make sure someone is plainly responsible for repairs and that the tenant knows whom to contact.

title: No Indiana Rent-Reporting Law; Federal Duties If You Report
bodyText: Indiana has no rent-reporting law. No Indiana statute requires you to offer positive rent reporting, sets up a state rent-reporting program, lets or forbids a lease to require a tenant to join one, or requires notice before you report late rent to a credit bureau. Whether to report is your choice, and the lease can describe it. If you report rent payments to a credit bureau, federal credit reporting law makes you a furnisher. You may not report information about a tenant that you know, or have reasonable cause to believe, is inaccurate; if you clearly give the tenant an address for notices of errors, that rule gives way to a narrower one, under which you may not report information the tenant has told you at that address is inaccurate if it is in fact inaccurate. If you report regularly and learn that something you reported is incomplete or inaccurate, you must promptly correct it with the bureau. If a tenant disputes the accuracy of what you reported, you may not report it again without noting that it is disputed. When a bureau sends you a tenant's dispute, you must investigate and report the result before the bureau's deadline, and fix, delete or block the item if it is wrong or cannot be verified; federal rules also require you to investigate some disputes a tenant sends you directly. A federal rule that requires a written notice before or within 30 days after first reporting negative information applies to financial institutions that extend credit; whether a landlord is one is a federal question this library has not settled, so the cautious course is to tell the tenant in writing before you first report a late payment. A collection agency you hire has its own federal duties.

title: Requiring Renter's Insurance in Indiana
bodyText:
No Indiana statute regulates a residential landlord's requirement that a tenant carry renter's insurance. Indiana does not require you to let the tenant choose the insurer, does not set a deadline before you may buy coverage and charge it to the tenant, does not cap an administrative fee for doing so, and does not require a written statement that your insurance will not cover the tenant's belongings or a renter's-insurance notice before signing.

So a requirement to carry renter's insurance, with a liability minimum and proof on request, is an ordinary lease term (the library's clause `tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca` is already marked for Indiana). Three general points still apply.

First, if the lease lets you buy a policy and charge the tenant, that charge is a payment under the lease; Indiana's deposit statute counts every payment under the lease other than the deposit as rent, so an unpaid enforceable charge may be taken from the deposit as rent in arrears, but no Indiana statute caps it, so state the amount or how it is figured in the lease (see `edu-no-required-fees-rule-in`).

Third, a different Indiana disclosure does reach some rentals: if the lowest floor of the structure, including a basement, is at or below the 100-year flood elevation on the state, FEMA or approved local maps, you must clearly disclose in the rental agreement that the structure is in a flood plain (rental agreements entered into or renewed after June 30, 2009; see `flood-disclosure-in`).

Whether a court would enforce a particular insurance term, or award a landlord the cost of a policy bought for a tenant, is decided by Indiana courts. These rules apply the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Right to End a Lease Because Repairs Cost Too Much
bodyText: No Indiana statute lets you refuse a needed repair because it would cost too much and end the lease instead, and no statute lets a tenant end the lease because repairs were not made. Your duties continue whatever the cost: deliver the unit safe, clean and habitable, comply with health and housing codes, make all reasonable efforts to keep common areas clean and proper, and keep the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning systems, elevators and inducement appliances that were there when the lease began in good and safe working order. A tenant who gives you notice and a reasonable time to repair may sue for damages, attorney's fees, an injunction or other appropriate relief. These duties cannot be waived. Your ways out are the ordinary ones: let a fixed term expire, or end a month-to-month tenancy with the notice the law requires; non-renewal at the end of the term is not retaliation even after a code complaint. Two retaliation exceptions bear on major work: you may bring a possession action, even after a tenant's code complaint, if complying with the building or housing code requires alteration, remodeling or demolition that would effectively deprive the tenant of use of the unit, or if at the end of the term you in good faith want possession to alter, remodel or demolish in a way that requires the household to move out entirely. You may interrupt utilities only for an emergency, good-faith repairs or necessary construction. For fire or other casualty, see the casualty rows; Indiana has no casualty statute, so the lease decides.

title: No Rent Escrow for Repairs, So No Exemption Notice
bodyText: Indiana has no statutory rent escrow remedy for repairs: no statute lets a tenant deposit rent with a court clerk or into escrow because you have not made repairs, and so there is no small-landlord exemption from such a remedy and no exemption notice to put in the lease. A tenant who wants repairs must give you notice and a reasonable time to fix the problem, and may then sue for damages, attorney's fees, an injunction or any other remedy the court finds appropriate (see the tenant repair remedies row); this library has not reviewed whether a court has ordered rent paid into court as such a remedy. Do not copy another state's exemption notice into an Indiana lease. Withholding rent is not an Indiana statutory remedy either; a tenant who stops paying risks a nonpayment termination, and the bar on retaliation does not stop an action for possession when the tenant is in default on rent and has not cured it within the notice period.

title: Repair Requests and Notice
bodyText: Indiana's repair statute requires the tenant to give you notice of the problem, and a reasonable time to fix it, before suing, but it does not say the notice must be written or sent a particular way. Your liability for damages starts when you have notice or actual knowledge of the problem and then refuse, or fail within a reasonable time, to fix it, so a problem you know about counts even if the tenant never sent a formal request. A lease may tell the tenant where and how to report repairs (a phone line, portal or address), and doing so helps prove when you were told; but a term making written notice the only way you can become responsible, or excusing you for problems you actually knew about, would be a waiver of the repair chapter and void. Two statutes do use written notice. Smoke detectors: you must repair or replace a required detector within seven working days after written notification, and failing to fix a hard-wired detector within seven days after written notice by certified mail, return receipt requested, is an infraction; the tenant must use that notice for a hard-wired detector the tenant believes is not working. Retaliation: a tenant's written complaint to you about lockouts, shutoffs or your repair duties is protected activity, so take written requests seriously. These rules cover rental agreements entered into after June 30, 2002 (repairs) and after June 30, 1999 (lockouts and entry), with the usual rent-to-own exception. Cautious course: name a repair contact in the lease, accept requests by any reasonable means, log the date you learn of each problem, and respond within a reasonable time.

title: Every Disclosure an Indiana Lease May Need
bodyText:
Indiana has no single required lease form, no rule that a state form be the first page, and no notice about just-cause or rent-increase laws, because Indiana has none. These are the disclosures an Indiana residential lease may need, each in its own clause or row.

Always: (1) the names and addresses of an Indiana resident authorized to manage the unit and an Indiana resident agent for notices and service of process, in writing at or before the start of the tenancy; (2) the tenant's written acknowledgment at move-in that the unit has a working smoke detector.

When the condition applies: (3) a clear statement in the lease that the structure is in a flood plain; (4) the military installation statement for property near Naval Support Activity Crane, Lake Glendora Test Facility or Grissom Air Reserve Base; (5) the water and sewer billing disclosure if you bill those services separately; (6) the electric submetering statement if you submeter electricity from a master meter; (7) the federal lead-based paint disclosure for housing built before 1978; (8) notice of a recorded environmental restrictive covenant; (9) if you, or an owner of the property, hold an Indiana real estate broker license, a written disclosure of that ownership interest and of the license.

Special leases: (10) a lease with an option to buy a home of up to four units brings in Indiana's seller disclosure form, due before the offer is accepted, which the library treats as before the lease-option is signed because the statute does not say (Indiana has no other lease-option statute); (11) if you buy a homeowner's house during a foreclosure and lease it back, you must give written notice of the homeowner's rights and follow Indiana's foreclosure rescue law; (12) a housing with services establishment contract has its own required contents; (13) if you operate a mobile home community, a community rule must be publicly posted in the community before you can eject someone for breaking it, and closing the community takes 180 days' written notice to each home owner (see the written notices row).

If a licensed broker represents you, the broker must also tell a prospective tenant about adverse material facts or risks the broker actually knows concerning the physical condition of the property, and facts required by law to be disclosed, that a reasonable and timely inspection would not reveal. Indiana does not require you to disclose deaths or crimes on the property, sex offender information, foreclosure, radon, mold or code variances.

Under the state law limiting local landlord-tenant rules, cities, towns and counties may not add their own lease disclosure requirements for privately owned rentals unless the legislature authorizes it. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: No Rule That Every Fee Be in the Lease
bodyText:
Indiana has no statute requiring every fee, fine, interest or other charge to be stated in the written lease, no required total of rent plus fees, no general cap on a markup of a service a third party bills, and no ban on a fee for maintaining common areas. Your right to collect a fee rests on the lease or another legal basis, so state every fee you intend to charge, with its amount or how it is figured and when it is due. Two specific rules apply.

To change the lease during its term, including adding a fee, you must give at least 30 days' written notice unless the written lease provides otherwise; whether that lets you add a fee without the tenant's agreement is decided by Indiana courts.

And if you bill tenants separately for water or sewer service, you may charge no more than you paid the utility, less your own and common-area use, plus only the small fees the statute and the Utility Regulatory Commission's rules allow; electric submetering likewise may not exceed the master-meter bill. A fee a city, town or county assesses on the rental unit may be passed to the tenant, except fees for building the unit. Cities and counties may not regulate landlord fees.

This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants. The library's optional fee-list clause lists the fees for you.

title: No Tenant Rights Guide to Hand Out
bodyText: Indiana has no state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights and responsibilities that you must give a tenant before signing or at renewal, and no required acknowledgment of one. No state statute requires a written summary of the landlord-tenant laws in or with the lease. Cities, towns and counties may not fill the gap: they may not require disclosures about the property, the lease or the rights and responsibilities of the parties, and any ordinance that does is void (housing receiving government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents is outside that bar). The disclosures Indiana does require are specific ones, such as the names and addresses of the manager and the agent for notices, a flood-plain location, a nearby military installation and water or sewer billing; see those rows. A federally assisted program may require its own tenant materials; follow the program documents.

title: Code Variances Need Not Be Given to Indiana Tenants
bodyText: Apart from the state health department's health and sanitation rules for mobile home communities (whose only waiver is the state's power to license a temporary community for six months and waive the chapter's requirements, with no notice to residents), Indiana has no state sanitary code for rentals, and it has no rule requiring you to give a tenant, or attach to the lease, a copy of a variance or exception from a building, fire, health or housing code. State building and fire safety rules can be varied: the state may grant a variance where compliance would impose an undue hardship (or prevent preserving an architecturally or historically significant part of a building) and the alternative will not be adverse to public health, safety or welfare. The variance is conditioned on meeting the approved alternative standard, and it overrides conflicting state agency rules and local ordinances. A local variance from fire safety or building laws is not effective until the state approves it. Applications are posted on a public portal, but there is no notice to tenants. Until June 30, 2027 the state building and fire safety commission or its department grants these variances; from July 1, 2027 the department alone does. If your building operates under a variance, keep a copy and meet its conditions: the alternative standard is what your repair and safety duties are measured against. Local health department orders about unfit dwellings are covered in the health department row.

title: No Seasonal Tenancy Category in Indiana
bodyText: Indiana has no seasonal tenancy category: no rule that a summer or other seasonal let ends by itself, skips the usual notices, or falls outside the landlord-tenant laws. Indiana's residential landlord-tenant laws apply to rental agreements for dwelling units in Indiana, so a seasonal rental of a home or apartment is an ordinary tenancy. They do not apply to transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or other lodging, unless the arrangement was set up to avoid those laws; whether a particular vacation stay is transient occupancy is for Indiana courts (this library has not reviewed those cases), so treat a stay of a month or more under a rental agreement as a tenancy. State exact start and end dates. A fixed term ends on its last day without notice; a rental by the week or month with no end date is a periodic tenancy that ends on notice equal to the rental period; and an occupant who stays on after the term without your consent should be removed only through the courts (whether that occupant is a tenant at sufferance is for Indiana courts; this library has not reviewed those cases). Short stays bring separate rules. A short-term rental is a home or a dwelling unit rented for terms of less than 30 days at a time through a short-term rental platform. Where that state law applies (it does not reach a city, town or county that adopted short-term rental rules before January 1, 2018), the local government may require a permit, rental without a required permit is a Class C infraction, and an owner-occupied short-term rental is a permitted residential use; homeowners, condominium and lake associations may still restrict short-term rentals. Rooms or lodging rented for less than 30 days, including transient housing in a house, condominium or apartment, are subject to Indiana sales tax, and you may be liable to collect it and any county or city innkeeper's tax if the guest does not pay through a booking platform that collects it. Housing for five or more adult seasonal or temporary farm workers is an agricultural labor camp, which needs a state health department permit before it operates.

title: Deposit Rules Cannot Be Waived
bodyText:
Any waiver of Indiana's security deposit rules by you or the tenant is void.

A lease therefore cannot lengthen the 45 days you have to return the deposit with an itemized list of deductions, add uses for the deposit beyond the statutory list (accrued rent and rent due for the tenant's premature termination, actual damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, and unpaid utility or sewer charges the lease makes the tenant's), excuse the itemized list, or limit the tenant's recovery of the deposit and attorney's fees when you do not comply.

Two points the statute itself leaves to agreement: the tenant may apply the deposit to rent only if you agree, and the deposit may serve as the last rent payment only if a written agreement between you and the tenant says so. You are not liable under the deposit rules until the tenant gives you a mailing address in writing; a lease may ask for it, but cannot excuse your duties.

The deposit rules use a broad definition: a deposit includes any required prepayment of rent other than the first full rental period, rent charged above the average rent for the term, and any other money or property returnable if the unit is returned in the required condition, however the payment is labeled.

The rules do not cover rental agreements entered into before July 1, 1989, or the arrangements the residential landlord-tenant statutes exclude (such as transient lodging, institutional housing and employee housing conditioned on employment).

title: No Rule on Posting Deposit Standards
bodyText: Indiana has no statute requiring you to post, or give applicants before signing, the standards you use to set security deposit amounts, and no rule about using different standards for different units or properties, however many units you own. Indiana also sets no limit on the amount of a deposit. You may therefore set deposits as you choose, but Indiana's fair housing law bars different terms or conditions of rental because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, disability or national origin, so a deposit standard must not vary on any of those grounds (see the fair housing row for who the law covers). Applying one written standard to everyone, and keeping it on file, is the cautious course. Cities and counties may not regulate security deposits or lease applications. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: No Required Locks, Deadbolts or Rekeying
bodyText:
Indiana has no statute or state rule requiring you to install deadbolts, door viewers, window or sliding-door locks or other security devices in a rental, or to rekey locks between tenants. Rekeying at turnover is a sound practice and you may set key and lock terms in the lease.

Indiana's only lock-change duty is for tenants protected by a court order against a perpetrator: on the tenant's written request with a copy of the order, you must change the locks and give the tenant a key within 48 hours, or within 24 hours if the restrained perpetrator lives in the same unit (and then you may not let the perpetrator in unless the order allows it).

The tenant reimburses your actual cost; if you miss the deadline, the tenant may change the locks and you reimburse the tenant, who must give you a key within 24 hours. These rules apply to leases entered into or renewed after June 30, 2007. Separately, you may never change the locks or add a device to keep a tenant out without a court order. Local codes may have their own requirements; they are not reviewed here.

title: No Work Cards for Senior Housing Staff in Indiana
bodyText: No Indiana statute requires employees of senior apartments, 55-and-older communities or other age-restricted rental housing to hold a work card, permit or registration, and none requires the landlord to screen them because the housing serves older residents. Ordinary age-restricted rental housing is treated like any other rental for staffing. Different rules apply if what you run is a licensed care setting rather than housing: home health and personal services agencies may not use workers with certain convictions to serve people in their homes, and residential care administrators must be licensed and pass a national criminal history background check (see `edu-no-employee-screening-rule-in`). If you screen staff anyway, the expungement and criminal-history-report limits in that row apply. Housing that relies on the 55-and-older exemption from the familial-status rules must meet its own occupancy, policy and verification requirements (see `edu-no-protected-class-inquiry-ban-in`).

title: No Duty to Disclose Sex Offender Registry Information
bodyText: Indiana does not require you to tell a tenant whether a registered sex or violent offender lives in or near the property, and it does not require a lease notice pointing tenants to the registry. The sheriffs keep a public Indiana sex and violent offender registry website, updated at least daily, that shows each registered offender's name, photograph, offense and principal residence address, so a tenant can check it directly. You may mention the registry in the lease or a move-in packet if you wish; if you do, state only that the website exists and that you make no statement about who is listed, and never misstate what you know if a tenant asks you directly. Two related points: an offender who rents from you must register the rented address, and a person you rent to may be an offender against children who commits a crime by knowingly or intentionally living (more than three nights in any 30 days) within 1,000 feet of school property (not a college's), a youth program center, a public park or a licensed day care center, or where a child care provider gives child care, or by establishing a residence within one mile of the victim's residence; that residency rule is the offender's duty, not yours. Fair housing and screening rules on criminal records are covered in the screening rows.

title: Sex Offenders as Occupants in Indiana
bodyText: No Indiana statute makes a landlord responsible for where a registered sex or violent offender lives: there is no duty to check the registry before renting, no duty to refuse a unit near a school, park or day care, no ban or fine for renting to two or more registered offenders who live together, and no lease-statement safe harbor. Indiana's residency restriction binds the offender, not you: an offender against children (a registered offender who is a sexually violent predator or was convicted of child molesting, child exploitation, child solicitation, child seduction, or kidnapping a child who is not the offender's own) who knowingly or intentionally resides (spends more than three nights in any 30-day period) within 1,000 feet of school property (not including college property), a youth program center, a public park or a licensed day care center, establishes a residence within one mile of the victim's residence, or resides where a child care provider provides child care, commits a Level 6 felony. That section was amended by a 2026 act effective July 1, 2026; the rule stated here is the version in force. The restriction applies to every offender against children. An offender against children may petition a court, not earlier than ten years after release from incarceration or parole (or from probation, if never incarcerated) and not more than once a year, to stop being treated as one, but an offender with two or more unrelated qualifying convictions may not petition. A registered offender who rents from you must register the rented address as the offender's principal residence, which includes a residence leased by another person where the offender spends the most time. Whether you may screen out or evict applicants and tenants because of a conviction is covered in the screening rows; the registry and disclosure point is in `edu-no-sex-offender-disclosure-in`. Indiana law bars cities, towns and counties from regulating tenant screening, leasing terms or the rights of the parties to a lease unless the General Assembly authorizes it. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: No Single-Family Occupancy Disclosure in Indiana
bodyText: Indiana has no rule requiring a lease of a single-family home to carry an occupancy disclosure, and no rule on where a disclosure must sit in the lease (such as the first page) or how large it must be relative to the rest of the lease. The disclosures that do apply to a rented house are the same as for any rental: the flood plain and military installation statements where they apply, the manager and agent for notices, any separate water or sewer billing, the smoke detector acknowledgment and, for housing built before 1978, the federal lead disclosure. The only type-size rule that reaches a lease is the water and sewer billing disclosure (see the type-size row). If you rent a single-family home for short stays, a local short-term rental permit can ask you to report the advertised occupancy limits to the city or county, but that is a report to the government, not a disclosure to the tenant; that state permit framework does not apply in a city or county that already regulated short-term rentals by ordinance before January 1, 2018, unless it later repealed that ordinance. Under the state law limiting local landlord-tenant rules, cities, towns and counties may not regulate lease terms or disclosures for privately owned rentals unless the legislature authorizes it (see the local preemption and single-family rental rows). This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: No Shoreline or Water Access Disclosure in Indiana
bodyText: Indiana has no rule requiring you to tell a tenant about public access to a shoreline, a lake, a stream or a beach near the property, or about riparian rights that come with it. If the lease gives the tenant use of a lake, a pier or a waterfront, say in the lease what the tenant may use and on what terms; Indiana law does not supply those terms for a residential lease. One statute limits a waterfront owner's exposure: where the state designates a stream as a recreational stream, that use does not put a duty on the riparian landowner or tenant to provide for the safe use of the stream. Flood plain location is a separate, required disclosure (see the flood plain clause).

title: Notice for Showings Cannot Be Waived
bodyText:
Indiana sets no fixed entry-notice period. Before any entry, including one to show the unit to prospective tenants, buyers, lenders, workers or contractors, you must give the tenant reasonable written or oral notice, enter only at reasonable times, and not use entry to harass. The tenant may not unreasonably refuse consent to a showing.

You may enter without notice only in an emergency that threatens the occupants' safety or your property, and without consent only under a court order or after the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit. A waiver of these rules, in the lease or otherwise, is void, and the rule covers rental agreements entered into or renewed after June 30, 1999.

Because there is no statutory number of hours, there is nothing a tenant can sign away to shorten notice, and no Indiana statute sets up a separate signed document for showings. A lease term that sets a shorter notice for showings does not change the legal test: if a court finds that notice was not reasonable on the facts, the term does not protect you. The library therefore does not offer a shortened-showing-notice clause for Indiana; its standard entry clause gives at least 24 hours' notice.

What counts as reasonable notice is case law. Cautious course: give written notice at least a day ahead for showings, schedule them at reasonable hours, and get the tenant's agreement in writing for any shorter notice on a particular occasion.

title: No Indiana Shutdown Rent Protection
bodyText: No Indiana statute delays rent, bars late fees or stops an eviction for a federal, state or other government employee who goes unpaid or is furloughed during a government shutdown, and no 2026 act adds one. The ordinary rules apply: if a tenant does not pay rent when due, you may end the lease on at least 10 days' notice unless the parties agreed otherwise or the tenant pays in full before the notice period ends (see `edu-nonpayment-notice-in`), and Indiana sets no statewide cap on late fees (see `edu-no-late-fee-limit-in`). Retaliation protections, fair housing rules and the federal protections for servicemembers on active duty are separate and are not shutdown rules. Because nothing in Indiana law requires it, any accommodation for a tenant affected by a shutdown is your choice; the cautious course is to put a payment plan or deferral in writing, say whether late fees are waived, and keep the tenant's other lease duties unchanged, so the agreement cannot later be read as a waiver of rent. These rules apply the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Renting Homes in Single-Family Areas
bodyText: Indiana has no statute that limits renting a home in a single-family zone or requires the owner to live on the lot, and since July 1, 2026 state law works the other way. A local government (a county, municipality or township) may not adopt or enforce any ordinance, regulation, policy or rule that prohibits or restricts an owner of privately owned residential property from using it as a rental, or that has that effect. It may still enforce generally applicable health and safety rules, building and fire codes, reasonable occupancy standards and the registration and inspection programs state law permits, as long as those programs do not cap or limit rentals. A local rule adopted before January 1, 2026 that does not comply has until January 1, 2028 to come into line, and a short-term rental ordinance adopted before January 1, 2018 under the state short-term rental law is exempt. Short-term rentals (under 30 days at a time through a booking platform) have their own rules, except in a locality that adopted an ordinance regulating short-term rentals before January 1, 2018, where the state short-term rental law does not apply: renting your own primary residence that way is a permitted residential use in any zone that allows residential use, and for other short-term rentals a locality may require a special exception or variance but may not use it to prohibit or unreasonably restrict them; a locality may require a permit (up to $150 for the first one, free to renew). A locality also may not regulate rents through zoning. None of these limits bind a homeowners, condominium or similar association: its properly adopted rental restrictions are governed by its own documents and association law (see the association rows). Whether a particular local rule was adopted before 2026 or before 2018 was not checked.

title: No Smart-Access Law in Indiana; Lockout and Lock-Change Rules Apply
bodyText: Indiana has no law on smart locks, keyless entry or app-based access in rentals, and no law letting a domestic violence survivor make a landlord or device-account manager cut off another person's access to a connected device. The general rules apply to electronic access as they do to keys. You may not deny or interfere with a tenant's access to or possession of the unit without a court order, by any act, including changing the locks or adding a device to exclude the tenant; turning off a tenant's code, fob or app access to force them out falls within that ban. An electronic entry log does not replace notice: every non-emergency entry needs reasonable written or oral notice and must be at a reasonable time. For a tenant protected by a court order, you must change the locks on the tenant's written request within 48 hours after receiving a copy of the order (24 hours if the restrained person is a co-tenant), give the tenant a key, and, where the restrained person is a co-tenant, give that person no access unless the order allows a visit to collect belongings; the tenant reimburses your actual cost, and if you miss the deadline the tenant may change the locks and you reimburse the tenant. Whether reprogramming an electronic lock counts as changing the locks is for Indiana courts (this library has not reviewed those cases); the cautious course is to issue new credentials to the protected tenant and revoke every credential the restrained person could use, within the same deadline, and to change physical keys too.

title: Smoke Drift and Common-Area Smoking
bodyText:
No Indiana statute addresses tobacco smoke drifting from one unit into another, or a lease clause in which the tenant gives up claims about drifting smoke. Indiana's smoke-free air law does not ban smoking inside a tenant's own home. It bans smoking in a public place (an enclosed area of a structure where the public is invited or permitted), in a place of employment (an enclosed area of a structure that is a place of employment), and within eight feet of a public entrance to either.

In an apartment building those words can reach a leasing office, an enclosed lobby or other enclosed common area open to visitors, and enclosed hallways, laundry or maintenance areas where your employees or contractors work; the statute does not say more precisely how it applies to residential common areas, and how the Alcohol and Tobacco Commission and the courts apply it was not reviewed.

Where it applies, the owner, operator or manager must remove ashtrays from no-smoking areas, post signs at each public entrance about the eight-foot rule, and, for a public place, post no-smoking signs, ask a person smoking in violation to stop and have the person removed if they do not; failing to comply is a Class B infraction (Class A after three prior infractions), and the person smoking also commits an infraction. Cities, towns and counties may adopt stricter smoking ordinances.

Your lease may ban smoking anywhere on the property; the library's smoking policy clause, tagged for Indiana, does so. Whether a tenant harmed by drifting smoke has a claim against you, and whether a lease waiver of that claim is enforceable, is case law. Cautious course: treat enclosed common areas as smoke-free, post the required signs, and use the lease's smoking ban rather than a waiver.

title: No Late-Benefit Defense; Voucher Payment Delays
bodyText: Indiana has no statute that requires a court to continue an eviction, or reinstate a tenancy, because the tenant's Social Security, other public benefit or rental-assistance payment arrived late. In small claims, either side may ask for a continuance for good cause, usually only once, for as short a time as possible and with the court's approval; whether a late benefit check is good cause is up to the judge. Under the 10-day nonpayment notice the tenant can still stop the termination by paying the rent in full before the notice period runs out (see the nonpayment-notice row). Federal voucher rules go further for Housing Choice Voucher tenancies: the family is not responsible for the part of the rent the housing assistance payment covers, the housing agency's failure to pay that part is not a lease violation, and you may not end the tenancy during the lease for the agency's nonpayment. You also may not end a voucher tenancy because the agency withheld or abated assistance over housing-quality problems. Pursue the agency's share with the agency under your contract with it, and sue the tenant only for the tenant's own share.

title: No Special-District Statement in Indiana Leases
bodyText: Indiana has no statute that requires a lease to say that the property lies in a special taxing, assessment, conservancy, economic improvement, sewer or other special district, or that requires the tenant to acknowledge a district's charges, rules or plans. Special assessments and district charges are the owner's obligation and are collected from the property. You may pass costs to a tenant only as the lease provides; Indiana separately lets an owner require tenants to reimburse fees a political subdivision assesses on the rental unit (other than construction fees such as building permits), but whether a special assessment counts as such a fee is not settled, so state any pass-through in the lease as a specific charge. If you distribute water or sewer service to tenants, the water and sewer billing rules apply (see that row). Cities and counties may not require their own lease disclosures. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure or Retrofit Incentive
bodyText: Indiana has no statute or rule requiring you to tell a tenant or applicant whether the building has fire sprinklers, and no state grant, loan or tax credit program for adding sprinklers to a rental. The only sprinkler disclosure in Indiana law is for nursing homes, which the state health department lists in its consumer guide as fully, partially or not sprinklered. Sprinklers are not required in existing rentals or in single-family homes and duplexes (see the fire sprinkler duty row). If the building is totally sprinklered and conformed to Uniform Building Code standards (an older model code) when built, it is exempt from Indiana's smoke detector chapter (whether a building sprinklered under a later code qualifies is not settled), but the lease must still include the tenant's written acknowledgment that the unit has a functional smoke detector. If you choose to tell tenants about sprinklers, keep the statement accurate and tell tenants not to hang anything from or paint sprinkler heads.

title: Dollar Caps That Apply to Indiana Landlords
bodyText: Indiana sets few figure limits on residential landlords. These are the ones this library located. Charges you collect from a tenant: (1) For a check, draft or similar instrument that is dishonored or returned unpaid, you may charge no more than $20 plus your bank's actual charge for the returned item. (2) If you bill tenants separately for water or sewer service bought from a utility, the usage charges may not total more than you paid the utility for the same service, less your own use; the only extra charges allowed are a set-up fee no larger than your actual administrative cost, an administrative fee of no more than $4 a month, and a returned-payment fee no larger than what your bank actually charged you; you may charge only a nominal fee to copy billing records; and you must give the tenant at least 17 days after sending the bill before starting collection. These sub-billing rules do not apply to a flat fee that includes water without itemizing it, or to a single-unit building the utility meters directly. (3) If you submeter electricity, you may not charge more than the master-meter bill, and if a tenant asks you to test a submeter that proves accurate, you may charge up to $15. (4) You may not charge any fee to keep an emotional support animal. Amounts charged to you: (5) A local rental registration fee may not exceed $5 a year, and a local rental permit must be free, except in a locality whose rental registration or inspection program was created before July 1, 1984. (6) A local penalty for a non-emergency police or emergency call from a rental may not exceed $250, and if the tenant made the call it must be charged to the tenant, not to you. (7) A city sewer deposit may not exceed the estimated average bill for three months. Other limits: (8) A township trustee's agreement setting aside money in place of a deposit may last no more than 180 days and cover no more than one month's rent. (9) In a mobile home community, your lien against a lender who has notified you is limited to actual late rent for no more than 60 days. (10) Small claims dockets hear money claims up to $10,000 and possession cases where the rent due is not more than $10,000. (11) Federal law bars evicting a servicemember or dependents without a court order where the monthly rent is not more than $2,400 as adjusted for inflation each year. Where a lease sets no interest rate, Indiana's legal rate is 8% a year, and a bad-check claim under Indiana's check statute carries 18% interest and set damages. Indiana sets no cap on security deposits, late fees, application fees, pet fees or rent, and cities and counties may not regulate rent or landlord fees. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: When a Tenant May End a Lease Early by Law
bodyText:
Indiana law gives a tenant only two ways to end a lease early without your agreement, and a lease cannot take either away. (1) Protected victims. A tenant who is a victim or alleged victim of domestic or family violence, a sex offense or stalking, and who has a civil protection order or a criminal no-contact order, may end the lease with written notice at least 30 days before the termination date, with a copy of the order and, for domestic violence or sexual assault, a recent safety plan recommending relocation.

The tenant owes rent prorated to the termination date and no rent or fees that are owed only because of the early end, and owes nothing at all if the notice comes at least 14 days before the tenant first had the right to move in (see the protected-tenant rows). (2) Servicemembers.

Federal law lets a servicemember end a residential lease signed before entering military service, or signed while in service if the member then receives permanent-change-of-station orders or orders to deploy for at least 90 days (or signed on such orders and then blocked by a stop-movement order of at least 30 days or of indefinite length), by giving you written notice and a copy of the orders. For a lease with monthly rent, the termination takes effect 30 days after the next rent due date following the notice.

You may not charge an early-termination fee; the member owes prorated rent up to the effective date and other charges due under the lease, such as reasonable charges for excess wear. Refund rent paid in advance for any period after the effective date within 30 days. Knowingly holding a servicemember's deposit or belongings to cover rent for the period after a lawful termination is a federal crime.

The member's spouse or dependent may end the lease within a year after the member dies in service, and a member who suffers a catastrophic injury or illness in service (or the spouse or dependent, if the member lacks capacity) may end it within a year.

Indiana extends these federal rights to members of the Indiana National Guard or another state's Guard ordered to active duty, including state active duty, for at least 30 consecutive days, and it treats a violation of the federal act as a violation of Indiana law (see the servicemember row).

No other Indiana statute gives a tenant an early-termination right: there is none for a landlord's misrepresentation or fraud, none for a tenant's death or illness, and no rule that leaving a statement out of the lease lets the tenant leave or wipes out rent owed. A tenant whose landlord fails to keep up the unit may sue for damages, an injunction and other relief after notice and a reasonable time to repair; whether a court will treat that as ending the lease is case law.

Fraud or misrepresentation claims are decided under general law. On your side, a tenant's materially false information given to get the lease is a ground for an emergency possessory order. Outside these rights, a fixed-term tenant may leave early only on terms you agree to (for example an early-termination clause); a month-to-month tenant simply gives the notice the law and the lease require.

title: Forms and Wording Indiana Supplies
bodyText: Indiana has no statutory lease form and no wording that every residential lease must repeat. State law supplies wording in only a few places. (1) Two optional notice forms: a notice ending a year-to-year tenancy at the end of the current year, and a notice to vacate within 10 days unless the unpaid rent is paid. The statute says these forms may be used, so other wording that meets the notice rules also works (see the notice-to-quit and unpaid-rent rows). (2) If you bill a tenant separately for water or sewer service you buy from a utility, your disclosure must include the statute's complaint statement word for word, in type no smaller than the largest type in the document that carries it (see the water and sewer billing clause). (3) If the property is near one of the listed military installations, the lease must say that the property is near a military installation, may be affected by its operations and may be subject to local limits on use and development (see the military installation clause). (4) If the lowest floor of the structure, including a basement, is at or below the 100-year flood elevation on the state or federal flood maps, the lease must clearly say that the structure is in a flood plain, but the statute gives no set words (see the flood plain clause). (5) If you lease a home of up to four units with an option to buy, the seller's disclosure form adopted by the Indiana Real Estate Commission applies, and that form carries two notices to the buyer in substantially the statute's words (see the optional lease terms row). Under the state law limiting local landlord-tenant rules, cities, towns and counties may not add their own required lease wording or disclosures for privately owned rentals unless the legislature authorizes it. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants. The federal lead-based paint disclosure for housing built before 1978 has its own required warning statement (see the lead-based paint clause).

title: No Radiator Cover Rule
bodyText: Indiana has no statute or state rule requiring you to provide steam radiator covers or guards, on request or otherwise, and no required lease rider about them. If the unit has steam or hot-water radiators, they are part of the heating system you must keep in good and safe working condition, and the heating system must adequately supply heat at all times. Where young children live in a unit with hot exposed radiators, offering covers is a sensible safety step.

title: No Duty to Supply a Stove or Refrigerator
bodyText: Indiana has no statute or state rule requiring you to supply a stove, oven, refrigerator or other cooking appliance in a rental. If you supply appliances as an inducement to the lease, you must keep them in good and safe working condition (leases entered into after June 30, 2002), and that duty cannot be waived. List the appliances you supply in the lease so it is clear which ones you must maintain; anything a tenant brings is the tenant's to maintain. During a tenancy you may not remove appliances to force a tenant out. Local housing codes may require cooking or refrigeration facilities; they are not reviewed here.

title: Student Housing in Indiana
bodyText: Indiana has no student-housing statute for private landlords: no rule on student leases, parental guarantors, roommate turnover or academic-year terms. A student renting from you is an ordinary tenant with the same rights as any other. The one student-housing rule cuts the other way. Indiana's residential landlord-tenant laws (deposits, tenant rights, repair duties, retaliation, domestic violence protections and the related chapters) do not apply to residence at a rental unit owned or operated by an institution directly related to education, unless the arrangement was set up to avoid those laws. Laws outside that group, such as the general notice-to-quit rules and fair housing law, still apply. Indiana's test is owned or operated, not both, so a building a college runs may be outside those laws even if a private company owns it; a privately owned and privately run building that simply rents to students is covered. Whether a building master-leased to a college, or managed for it, is operated by the college is for Indiana courts (this library has not reviewed those cases), so treat your tenants as covered unless the school itself runs the housing. Where a private developer or user manages and operates housing on or next to a state university campus under the state's campus-facilities law, the project's specifications must require that it be generally available without discrimination at reasonable charges that the university's trustees review. If a parent guarantees a student's rent, get the guaranty in writing and signed, since a promise to answer for another person's debt must be. Cities and counties may not regulate your screening, deposits, applications, lease terms, disclosures, the parties' rights or your fees unless a state law allows it. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants. Colleges must also let registered student poll takers knock on doors in campus student housing near the end of each voter registration period.

title: Inspections in Subsidized Units: No Indiana Refusal Rule
bodyText: Indiana has no statute on what happens when a tenant in subsidized or voucher housing refuses an inspection, and no special eviction procedure for that refusal. The general rules apply. A tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to inspect the unit, make necessary or agreed repairs, supply services or show the unit (see the entry row for notice and timing); a tenant's refusal is a lease matter you handle under the lease and the ordinary eviction process. Where a local unsafe-building department operates (Indianapolis and Marion County, and any city, town or county that has adopted the state unsafe-building law), its inspector may get a court inspection warrant, valid for 48 hours, if the owner or the person in possession refuses an inspection. If the unit is under the federal Housing Choice Voucher program, federal rules govern the inspection itself: you must keep the unit in compliance with federal Housing Quality Standards, correct a life-threatening deficiency within 24 hours of notice and others within 30 days (or an approved extension), and the housing agency may withhold, and then must abate, its payments if you do not; the family may be held responsible for breaches it causes, such as damage beyond ordinary wear and tear by a household member or guest. These are the federal rules for assistance contracts signed on or after, or renewed after, June 6, 2024; older contracts follow the earlier version. You may not end the family's tenancy because the agency withheld or abated its payments. The family's own program duty to allow agency inspections is a federal program rule this library has not reviewed, so follow the agency's instructions and keep a written record of any refused appointment. Indiana's ban on local regulation of lease terms does not apply to housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents, so a local rule for subsidized housing is not barred by it; local inspection programs are still limited by state law (see the local registration and inspection row).

title: Subsidized Rent When a Unit Fails Inspection in Indiana
bodyText: No Indiana statute prorates or reduces a subsidized tenant's share of the rent, or the subsidy, when a unit becomes uninhabitable. The rules that do apply come from the program paying the subsidy. In a Housing Choice Voucher tenancy under a HAP contract executed on or after, or renewed after, June 6, 2024 (a contract is renewed when it continues beyond the lease's initial term), you must keep the unit to federal Housing Quality Standards and fix a life-threatening deficiency within 24 hours of notice and any other within 30 days (or a reasonable extension the housing agency approves). Once the agency notifies you in writing of deficiencies it may withhold its payments; if you repair within the cure period it must resume and pay what it withheld, but if you do not, it must abate its payments, including the withheld amounts, and it does not pay you later for the abated period; if the unit still fails 60 days (or a longer period the agency sets) after the notice of abatement, the agency must end the HAP contract. You may not end the family's tenancy because the agency withheld or abated its payments, the family is not responsible for the agency's share, and the agency's failure to pay is not a lease violation by the family; during an abatement the family may end the tenancy by notifying you and the agency. If the agency finds the family caused a deficiency beyond ordinary use, it may waive your responsibility, and then its payments may not be withheld or abated. Older HAP contracts follow the version of the rule in effect on June 6, 2024, which this library does not hold. The tenant's own share of the rent is set by the lease; whether a tenant owes it for a period the unit could not be lived in is decided by Indiana courts, which this library has not reviewed, so the cautious course is not to charge the tenant's share for a period you agree the unit was not habitable and to put that in writing. Township assistance has its own rule: substandard housing that does not meet minimum standards of health, safety and construction is not eligible for the maximum level of township shelter payments or for damage or security deposits paid from or encumbered by township funds, and when a unit is substantially below those standards the township trustee, when necessary, must help the applicant find other shelter. Your own duties to deliver the unit safe, clean and habitable and to comply with health and housing codes continue for every tenant (see `edu-condemned-premises-rent-in`). These rules apply the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Late Fees for Subsidized and Voucher Tenants
bodyText: Indiana has no statute that limits a late fee for a subsidized or Housing Choice Voucher tenant, for example to a share of only the tenant's portion of the rent; Indiana's general rule of no late fee cap applies. The state bar on local regulation of landlord fees does not apply to privately owned housing that receives government funds or benefits for the express purpose of providing reduced rents to low or moderate income tenants, so a local rule may reach such housing. Federal voucher rules do limit what the tenant owes: the family is not responsible for the part of the rent the housing assistance payment covers, and the housing agency's failure to pay that part is not a violation of the lease. So a late fee may be based only on the tenant's own late payment of the tenant's share, and should not be charged because the agency paid late. Under the voucher program the federal tenancy addendum is added to your lease word for word and controls over any conflicting lease term, and the housing agency may refuse to approve a lease that breaks state or local law. Other federal programs, such as public housing and project-based assistance, have their own lease rules that this library has not reviewed; follow your program's rules and any agency-approved lease. Set any late fee as a reasonable estimate of your cost of late payment.

title: Unsafe-Building Orders and Receivership
bodyText: Indiana's unsafe-building law applies in Indianapolis and Marion County and in any city, town or county that adopts it by ordinance. It covers any building that is structurally unsafe, a fire hazard, a public-health hazard, a public nuisance, dangerous because it violates a building-condition or maintenance law, or vacant or blighted and not fit for habitation, together with its lot. It is not limited to buildings of a certain size; one rented house is covered. The local enforcement authority may order the building vacated, sealed, exterminated, cleaned of trash or hazards, repaired or rehabilitated to habitability standards, or demolished. The order must give you at least 10 and not more than 60 days to act (with a substantial start within 30 days if longer than 30 days are allowed). Repair, sealing, extermination and clean-up orders become final 10 days after notice unless an owner, mortgagee or contract buyer asks for a hearing; other orders require a hearing. For a willful failure to comply the hearing authority may impose civil penalties of up to $5,000 each, and for an unheeded repair order without a hearing the enforcement authority may impose up to $2,500 and then up to $1,000 every 90 days. If you do not comply, the authority may do the work itself or by contract and charge every owner, life tenant and contract buyer jointly for the cost plus an average processing expense; unpaid costs become a court judgment and lien or are added to the property-tax bill. The department, its designee or a qualifying neighborhood organization may sue (the organization must first give 60 days' certified-mail notice to the owner and to the tenants), and the court may order an injunction, a performance bond, a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per defendant, and treble damages for a second judgment within two years. The court may also appoint a receiver, which takes possession, collects the rents (ahead of any earlier assignment of rents) and uses them for the ordered repairs, may borrow against the property with notes that take priority over existing mortgages, and may sell the property if it holds a lien; instead, the court may let the owner or a mortgagee rehabilitate within 60 days under a bonded schedule. If the property is also found abandoned, a receiver may take it, rehabilitate it and sell it at auction. Separately, a court may appoint a receiver at a utility's request for a mobile home community or a multifamily property with more than four units whose owner has not paid utility bills for more than 90 days. When an order on a building you lease to others becomes final (no hearing was requested or the order was affirmed, and it is not under court review or the court ruled against you), you must give the department your name, street address and phone number. Whether your locality has adopted the unsafe-building law, and its local code, were not reviewed.

title: Tenancy at Will in Indiana
bodyText: Indiana recognizes a tenancy at will but makes it hard to create one by accident. A tenancy at will cannot arise or be created without an express contract. Someone you simply let move in, with your consent and no other terms agreed, is a month-to-month tenant, not a tenant at will (that month-to-month rule does not apply to agricultural land). If you do expressly agree to a tenancy at will, you end it with one month's written notice delivered to the tenant. You need no notice if a tenant at will commits waste (serious damage to the property). The statute sets only your notice to the tenant; it sets no notice the tenant must give you, so put the tenant's notice in the agreement. Indiana's general notice rules let a notice be served on the tenant, or, if the tenant cannot be found, on a person living at the property (who must have the notice explained), or by posting it on a conspicuous part of the property if no one is there; because the at-will rule says the notice is delivered to the tenant, the cautious course is to hand it to the tenant and keep proof. The deposit, landlord-tenant rights, repair-duty and retaliation rules turn on a residential tenant occupying a rental unit with your consent for agreed rent under an agreement, not on the length of the tenancy, so treat an at-will tenant as covered by them. Compared with the other tenancies: a fixed term ends at its end without notice, a month-to-month tenancy ends on one month's notice, a week-to-week tenancy on a week's notice, and a year-to-year tenancy on notice at least three months before the end of the year. For most rentals a fixed term or month-to-month tenancy is clearer than a tenancy at will. In a mobile home community, the operator may also eject a person for nonpayment of charges or fees for accommodations, violation of law or disorderly conduct, or violation of a state health department rule or a publicly posted community rule, and must give each home owner written notice at least 180 days before closing the community. Whether those ejection grounds also limit how a lot tenancy may be ended is for Indiana courts (this library has not reviewed those cases), so the cautious course in a community is to end a lot tenancy through the court process and, where you can, on one of those grounds.

title: When a Tenant Files for Bankruptcy
bodyText: Indiana has no statute on what happens to an eviction or an order of possession when the tenant files for bankruptcy, so federal bankruptcy law controls. A bankruptcy filing automatically stops most acts to collect pre-filing debts or to obtain possession of the debtor's property, including starting or continuing an eviction case, unless an exception applies or the bankruptcy court lifts the stay. Two exceptions matter for residential evictions. (1) Judgment already entered: if you obtained a judgment for possession before the tenant filed, the stay does not stop you from completing the eviction, unless the tenant, with the petition, certifies that state law lets the tenant cure the entire monetary default after the judgment and deposits with the bankruptcy clerk the rent due for the next 30 days; even then the exception applies after 30 days unless the tenant also certifies that the whole default has been cured. You may object, and the court must hold a hearing within 10 days. Indiana law gives no statutory right to cure after a judgment for possession, and this library has not reviewed Indiana case law on the point. (2) Endangerment or drugs: if your eviction is based on the tenant endangering the property or illegally using, or allowing the use of, controlled substances there in the last 30 days, you may file and serve a certification under penalty of perjury; the exception takes effect 15 days later unless the tenant objects, and then the court must hold a hearing within 10 days. In other cases, do not file, continue, or enforce an eviction, or collect pre-filing rent, without first getting relief from the stay from the bankruptcy court. The lease itself: in a Chapter 7 case, a residential lease the trustee does not assume within 60 days after the order for relief (or a longer time the court sets) is treated as rejected; in Chapter 11, 12 or 13 cases it may be assumed or rejected up to plan confirmation, and a lease in default can be assumed only if the default is cured or adequately assured. Rent coming due after the filing is generally handled differently from pre-filing rent; get bankruptcy advice before acting.

title: Keeping Tenant Information Confidential in Indiana
bodyText: Indiana has no general statute that bars a landlord from sharing a tenant's or applicant's information or that requires the tenant's consent before you do. Four narrower rules apply. First, address confidentiality: if a tenant enrolled in the Attorney General's address confidentiality program gives you written notice on the program's form, you may not knowingly disclose the tenant's address, and you may not display the tenant's name at the address; in a multifamily building or complex, you may not display it at the unit, building or complex, including on a mailbox, a door, a tenant directory, the clubhouse or another common area. You may disclose the address with the tenant's written consent, only for the purpose consented to, and you may give the tenant's name to the state or a local government only in response to a specific request connected with an active investigation or inspection of a health, building or fire code violation or an active investigation of a violation of law the tenant allegedly committed. You must accept the program's designated address as the tenant's address and use it for all mail, although you may ask for the physical address where a service would be impossible without it (see `edu-address-confidentiality-in`). Second, data security: if you own or license computerized data that includes a person's Social Security number, or a name with a driver's license number, state ID number, credit card number, or financial account or debit card number together with the code that opens the account, you must implement and maintain reasonable procedures to protect it from unlawful use or disclosure, and you may not throw away records with that unencrypted, unredacted information without shredding, burning, erasing or otherwise making it unreadable; those two duties do not apply if you maintain your own data security procedures under a privacy, security or compliance plan under one of the listed federal laws (such as the Fair Credit Reporting Act) that requires reasonable procedures, and you follow it. After a breach that you know, should know or should have known could result in identity deception, identity theft or fraud, you must notify the affected Indiana residents and the Attorney General without unreasonable delay and within 45 days of discovery (with limited reasons for delay), and also the consumer reporting agencies if more than 1,000 people are notified. Only the Attorney General enforces these duties: a knowing or intentional failure to keep reasonable security procedures or to dispose of records properly is a deceptive act with a civil penalty of up to $5,000, and a failure to give breach notice is a deceptive act with a civil penalty of up to $150,000 per deceptive act. Discarding a customer's unencrypted, unredacted personal information in a public place, including the trash, without shredding or similar treatment is also a Class C infraction (Class A for more than 100 customers or a repeat). Third, Indiana's consumer data protection law reaches only businesses that control or process the personal data of at least 100,000 Indiana consumers in a year (or at least 25,000 if more than half their gross revenue comes from selling personal data), and it does not apply to nonprofit organizations; most landlords fall outside it. Fourth, a real estate licensee who represents a tenant may not disclose the tenant's confidential information without the tenant's informed written consent, except where the law requires disclosure or failing to disclose would be fraud or dishonest dealing, while a licensee who represents you owes the tenant honesty and must disclose adverse material facts or risks it actually knows about the property's physical condition, and facts required by law to be disclosed, that a reasonable and timely inspection would not reveal. Separately, a tenant may ask a court to keep eviction records from public view in some cases (court records, not your files), and criminal history reports are limited as described in `edu-no-employee-screening-rule-in`. Because nothing else limits sharing, the cautious course is to share a tenant's information only with the tenant's written consent or as the law requires (for example, to answer a subpoena or a housing agency in a voucher tenancy), and to state your practice in the application or lease. These rules apply the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Flags, Signs and Antennas: What Indiana Protects
bodyText: Indiana has no statute that gives a tenant a right, against you as landlord, to display a flag, a political or religious sign, or other items, and none that limits what your lease or house rules may say about displays. Your lease and your reasonable rules decide; a tenant must follow reasonable rules in force when the lease is signed, and later rules only as the lease provides. Cities and counties may not create their own display rights for tenants, because they may not regulate lease terms or the parties' rights. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants. Two sets of rules do reach displays. First, associations: a homeowners association may not prohibit a member from displaying a political sign (for a candidate, a party or a ballot question) on the member's property from 30 days before through 5 days after the election, though it may reasonably limit size, number and location (it may not bar a sign in a window or on the ground); and since July 1, 2026 a homeowners, condominium, cooperative or similar association may not prohibit or restrict a member from displaying the United States flag or the Indiana flag, including from a flagpole, subject to reasonable rules on flag etiquette, flagpole construction, size, number, location, lighting and noise (at least one front-yard flagpole of up to 20 feet, or one attached to the member's home, must be allowed). These protections are written for the association's members (owners); whether a tenant can claim them is not settled, and they never bind you as landlord. Second, antennas: a federal rule bars a lease provision that unreasonably restricts a tenant's installation or use of a satellite dish or similar antenna one meter or less across, or a TV antenna, on property within the tenant's exclusive use or control, such as a private balcony or patio, except for clearly defined safety or historic-preservation needs. You may still keep antennas off common areas, roofs and exterior walls that the tenant does not exclusively control. For association governing documents adopted or amended after June 30, 2026, an association also may not prohibit a person who rents from maintaining an amateur radio antenna. If you want display rules, put them in the lease or the house rules, keep them content-neutral, and apply them evenly.

title: Housing Your Own Employees in Indiana
bodyText: Indiana's residential landlord-tenant statutes (the deposit, abandoned-property, tenant-rights, emergency-possessory-order, tenant-duty, landlord-duty, retaliation, domestic-violence, eviction-diversion and eviction-record chapters) do not apply to occupancy by your employee whose right to occupy is conditional upon employment in or about the premises, such as a resident manager or maintenance worker living on site, unless the arrangement was created to avoid those statutes. No Indiana statute requires a signed disclosure of the employee's occupancy and move-out conditions, requires you to offer a rental agreement when the job ends, or expressly names caretakers or others you placed on the property in the eviction statute. Other laws still reach the arrangement, because the exclusion does not limit statutes outside those chapters: the general notice-to-quit rules may still apply, and the court action to recover possession remains available (a person with a right to possession may sue the tenant in possession, or if there is no tenant, the person claiming the property). Because the lockout and utility-shutoff ban sits in one of the excluded chapters, whether self-help is lawful against an excluded employee is decided by Indiana courts; the cautious course is to recover possession only through the courts. If the employee also pays rent or the occupancy does not depend on the job, the ordinary statutes apply. Whether a particular on-site worker's occupancy is conditional upon employment, which notice applies when the job ends, and whether the arrangement was created to avoid the statutes are decided by Indiana courts; this library has not reviewed those cases, so the cautious course is a written occupancy agreement stating that the right to occupy ends with the job, how long the person has to leave, what happens to any deposit, and that you will recover possession only through the courts. Rent cannot simply be taken from wages: Indiana's wage-assignment statute lists the purposes for which an employee may assign wages, and rent or housing is not among them in either version of the section effective July 1, 2026; whether housing may be treated as part of wages is a wage-law question this library has not reviewed. If you house five or more adult seasonal or temporary agricultural workers, the housing is an agricultural labor camp: you need an Indiana Department of Health permit, posted in the camp, before anyone moves in, with an annual inspection within the 60 days before first occupancy, and you must meet the Department's construction, sanitation, equipment and operation rules; violations can bring compliance orders and civil penalties of up to $500 per violation per day. Sponsored guest workers are not the subject of any Indiana landlord rule.

title: Claims Against a Tenant After a Fire in Indiana
