bodyText: No Indiana statute bars you, or your property insurer suing in your name after paying a claim, from recovering from a tenant for fire or other damage the tenant caused, and none excuses a tenant from liability for an accidental fire. Indiana also has no statute that makes a tenant an implied co-insured under your policy or that addresses waivers of subrogation in residential leases. The statutory starting point is the tenant's duty to refrain from defacing, damaging, destroying, impairing or removing any part of the rental premises and to return the premises in a clean and proper condition, except for ordinary wear and tear (for rental agreements entered into after June 30, 2002, other than a rent-to-own agreement entered into before July 1, 2008). Before suing on those statutory duties during the tenancy, you must give the tenant notice and a reasonable time to fix the problem, and if you have repaired physical damage, your notice must list the repairs and document their cost; no notice is needed once the tenant's occupancy has ended. Whether a tenant who negligently causes a fire is liable to you or to your insurer, and whether a lease clause on insurance or a waiver of subrogation changes that, are decided by Indiana courts. The cautious course is to say in the lease which party insures what, whether your property insurance is for your benefit only, and whether either party waives claims to the extent insurance pays, and to check any such clause with your insurer, because a waiver in the lease can affect the insurer's rights under the policy. These rules apply the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies; see also the casualty clause (`casualty-termination-in`) and `edu-no-renters-insurance-rules-in`.

title: No Tenant Portal Law in Indiana; Electronic Transactions Limits
bodyText: Indiana has no tenant-portal law: no statute lets or forbids you to require rent payments, signatures, maintenance requests or notices through an online portal, and none caps a portal or convenience fee. The lease may name the payment methods you accept. Indiana's electronic transactions law sets the limits. It applies only between parties who have each agreed to deal electronically, judged from the context and their conduct. A tenant who agrees to use the portal for one transaction may still refuse to deal electronically in other transactions, and a lease cannot take that right away, so a term requiring every future signature or document to go through the portal is not fully binding; keep a paper or in-person alternative. Where a law requires something in writing, an electronic record counts only if the parties agreed to deal electronically and the tenant can keep the record when received, and a portal may not block printing or downloading. A lease for a term over three years signed through a portal must still be signed by you as landlord and acknowledged before a notary (or proved). Where a law requires a notice to be sent or served a certain way, such as the eviction-related notices, use that method; posting it in the portal is not enough. A portal or payment fee is a lease charge: it counts as rent for the security deposit rules, so you may take an unpaid fee from the deposit if the fee is enforceable, and cities and counties may not regulate your fees unless a state law allows it. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants.

title: Tenant Records and Rent Ledgers in Indiana
bodyText: No Indiana statute requires a residential landlord to keep a rent ledger, to give a tenant a statement of account or payment history on request, to include a ledger with a nonpayment notice, or to let a tenant inspect or copy the landlord's records about the tenancy; Indiana also has no rent-receipt requirement (see `edu-no-rent-receipt-rule-in`). The records duties that do exist are these. When the tenancy ends, the deposit statute requires you to mail the tenant, within 45 days after the occupancy ends, an itemized list of damages claimed with the estimated cost of repair for each damaged item and the amounts and lease on which you intend to assess the tenant, together with the balance of the deposit; you are not liable under that statute until the tenant gives you a mailing address in writing. You must also give the tenant, in writing, the name and address of the manager and of an Indiana agent for notices (see `edu-required-disclosures-in`). Two health-law registers reach some rentals. The owner, operator, manager or person in charge of a furnished apartment house, boarding house or rooming house must keep a register of the name and address of every person occupying any part of the premises and the dates and times occupied, keep it open for inspection by the Indiana Department of Health and law enforcement, maintain it for each calendar year and keep it for one year after that year; a reckless violation is a Class A misdemeanor (see `edu-furnishings-included-in`). A mobile home community operator must keep a register open for inspection by the township or county assessor and the Indiana Department of Health; entries made after 2019 list each home's owner as shown on its title and its vehicle identification number, and from October 1, 2020 a copy of the title (entries made before 2020 listed the names and ages of all occupants). Indiana's data-security statute does reach landlords: if you own or license computerized data containing an applicant's or tenant's Social Security number, or a name with a driver's license, state ID, credit card or financial account number and its access code, you must implement and maintain reasonable procedures to protect it, must not dispose of it without shredding or similar treatment, and must give breach notice within 45 days of discovery; the details and exceptions are in `edu-tenant-confidential-information-in`. Because nothing else sets a standard, the cautious course is to keep a dated ledger of every charge and payment for each tenant (you will need it to prove rent in arrears or to itemize the deposit), to give a copy when a tenant asks, and to keep records at least until any claim about the tenancy could no longer be brought. Court records of an eviction are a separate subject (see `edu-eviction-sealing-in`). These rules apply the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Agreements for the Tenant to Make Repairs
bodyText: No Indiana statute authorizes an agreement for the tenant to take over your repair duties, whether in the lease or in a separate writing, in good faith or for a rent reduction, at a single-family home or an apartment. Your statutory duties (safe, clean and habitable delivery, code compliance, common areas, and the systems and inducement appliances you provide) cannot be waived by contract or otherwise, so any agreement that moves one of them to the tenant, or excuses you if the tenant does not do the work, is void to that extent. The library therefore does not offer a tenant repair agreement clause for Indiana. Three things remain open. First, the tenant has statutory duties of its own (not damaging the home, using systems and appliances reasonably, keeping its areas reasonably clean, keeping smoke detectors working), and when the tenant's breach causes physical damage you have repaired, you may sue for your cost after giving the tenant notice that specifies the repairs and documents what they cost (no notice is needed once the tenant has moved out); the library's tenant-caused damage clause covers this. Second, a particular repair the tenant agrees to do, while you stay responsible for the result, is a contract question Indiana courts decide. Third, the tenant may not unreasonably refuse you entry to make necessary or agreed repairs. These rules cover rental agreements entered into after June 30, 2002, except a rent-to-own agreement entered into before July 1, 2008. Cautious course: hire and pay for repairs to the items you are responsible for, and if a tenant offers to do work, put any arrangement in writing as a one-time job you supervise and remain responsible for, not as a lease term.

title: Tenant Organizing Is Protected From Retaliation
bodyText: In Indiana, a tenant's organizing or becoming a member of a tenant's organization is protected activity. You may not respond to it by raising the tenant's rent, decreasing, ending or interfering with services to the rental premises, or bringing or threatening an action for possession, eviction or early termination of the lease. You may still decline to renew at the end of the term, raise the rent to comparable market rates at the end of the term (or during it if the lease allows), cut a service for all tenants equally where other law allows, and bring a possession case for listed reasons, such as unpaid rent not cured within the statutory or lease period, a lease violation that materially affects health or safety, a holdover after a fixed term, a case filed in good faith before the protected activity, or a good-faith move-in, major renovation or withdrawal from the rental market for at least six months at the end of the term. A lease term waiving these protections is void, and cities and counties may not adopt their own retaliation rules. The statute does not state its own remedy; Indiana courts decide how a tenant enforces it. Indiana has no statute giving tenants a right to meet in common areas, distribute literature door to door, or have the landlord recognize or bargain with a tenant organization, so those points are left to your lease and rules; apply any limits on common-area use or solicitation evenly, and not in response to organizing. State housing-finance programs may fund advisory services that help tenants form organizations in assisted housing.

title: No State Tenant Rights Statement to Attach or Sign
bodyText: Indiana has no state-agency statement or summary of tenant rights that you must attach to the lease, place as its first page, deliver at renewal or have each tenant sign or acknowledge, and nothing bars you from suing for rent or possession because you did not hand one out. There is no state summary for tenants who are victims of domestic violence, sexual offenses or stalking either; their protections apply whether or not they were told about them. Cities, towns and counties may not require one for privately owned rentals: under the state law limiting local landlord-tenant rules, they may not regulate disclosures about the rights and responsibilities of the parties unless the legislature authorizes it. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants. The pre-suit conditions in Indiana's tenant-duty and landlord-duty chapters concern the condition of the unit (a notice ending the tenancy is often still needed before a suit for possession, though the statute lists cases that need none, such as a lease for a set period that has ended; see the notice rows): before a tenant sues to enforce your statutory maintenance duties, or you sue to enforce the tenant's statutory duties of care, the side suing must first give notice of the problem and a reasonable time to fix it (if the tenant caused physical damage that you have already repaired, your notice instead specifies the repairs and documents their cost, and your notice is not needed once the tenant's occupancy has ended; see the repair notice and tenant remedies rows). A federally assisted program may require its own tenant materials; follow the program documents.

title: Tenant Cameras in Indiana: No Rental Rule; Surveillance and Interception Laws Apply
bodyText: Indiana has no rule on tenant-installed security cameras or video doorbells: no statute gives a tenant a right to install one or lets you forbid one, so the lease decides (an installation is also an alteration under any no-alterations clause). Indiana's criminal surveillance laws apply to everyone, you and your tenants alike. It is a crime to knowingly place a camera or other surveillance equipment that records while unattended on someone else's private property without the consent of the owner or tenant of that property. So do not put a recording camera inside a tenant's unit, and a tenant should not aim or place one on a neighbor's property; whether a tenant's doorbell camera in a shared hallway needs your consent as owner, the other tenants', or both, is for Indiana courts (this library has not reviewed those cases), so the cautious course is a lease rule requiring your written approval for any camera outside the unit and limiting its field of view to the tenant's own entry. Audio is stricter: recording the contents of other people's electronic communications (which include sounds transmitted in whole or in part by wire, radio or an electromagnetic or photoelectronic system), by someone who is neither a sender nor a receiver and without either's consent, is unlawful interception, a felony; a doorbell camera that records passersby's conversations risks that, so ask tenants to turn audio off for shared areas. Voyeurism laws also bar recording people in private settings. Since July 1, 2026, a homeowners association may not run automated license plate readers, or let anyone but law enforcement install one on association property; this does not reach an ordinary security camera that happens to capture a plate.

title: No Rent-Cap or Just-Cause Exemption Notice in Indiana
bodyText: Because Indiana has no statewide rent-increase cap, no just-cause eviction law and no tenant right to buy, there is nothing a property can be exempt from and no exemption notice to give. A lease statement that the property is exempt from rent control or just-cause rules has no legal effect in Indiana; leave it out. Two Indiana rules do vary by property type, and neither needs a notice in the lease: the ban on local rent regulation does not cover housing subsidized to provide reduced rents for low or moderate income tenants, and the residential landlord-tenant statutes do not apply to certain arrangements, such as transient hotel stays, employee housing tied to employment and occupancy by a buyer under a contract of sale (but not a lease with an option to buy signed after June 30, 2008), unless the arrangement was created to avoid those statutes (see the scope row).

title: No Tenant Protection Act Notice in Indiana
bodyText: Indiana has no tenant protection act of the California type, so there is no notice to put in the lease about rent-increase limits, just-cause eviction or a tenant's right to buy when you sell. Indiana has no statewide cap on rent increases, and under the state law limiting local landlord-tenant rules, cities, towns and counties may not regulate rents on privately owned property unless the legislature authorizes it. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants. Indiana does not require a reason to end a periodic tenancy or decline to renew, other than the bars on retaliation, discrimination and penalizing domestic violence victims (see the just-cause and retaliation rows). Tenants have no right of first refusal or opportunity to purchase when you sell; on a sale, written notice to the tenant is what relieves you of liability for later events, and you stay liable for the deposit for one year unless the buyer assumes it by notice to the tenant and you transfer the deposit (see the sale row). Do not add a California-style notice to an Indiana lease: it could be read as promising protections Indiana does not give.

title: Indiana's Landlord-Tenant Statutes Have No Expiry Date
bodyText: No part of Indiana's residential landlord-tenant law is set to expire on a fixed date: none of the chapters on deposits, tenant property, landlord and tenant duties, retaliation, protections for domestic violence victims, eviction filings or record sealing carries an expiration or automatic repeal clause, and no 2026 act amended any of them. Several rules apply only to rental agreements entered into or renewed after a past date (for example after June 30, 1999 for the landlord-tenant rights chapter, entered into (renewals are not mentioned) after June 30, 2002 for the tenant and landlord duties chapters, and after June 30, 2007 for the victim protections), which matters only for very old leases. Changes come by amendment, usually effective July 1 of the year passed, so review your Indiana lease each summer.

title: No Duty to Translate an Indiana Lease
bodyText: Indiana has no rule requiring you to translate a residential lease or a notice into the tenant's language, even if you advertised or negotiated in another language, and no rule saying which version controls if you sign a lease in two languages. That includes a lease back to a homeowner in a foreclosure rescue deal: Indiana's foreclosure rescue law requires written notice of the homeowner's rights but no translation. One related rule: a lease you record (for example, a lease longer than three years) that was signed in a foreign country, in a language other than English, must include an English translation before the recorder will accept it. Practical course: if a tenant does not read English well, offer a translation as a courtesy, state in the lease that the English version controls, and give the tenant time to have it read to them. A tenant who signs without understanding the terms can argue the lease was unconscionable under Indiana's consumer protection law, and federal fair housing law bars treating applicants differently because of national origin; neither question was reviewed here beyond the statutes. Federal lead rules add one language point: for housing built before 1978, the lead disclosure must be in the language of the lease (for example, Spanish if the lease is in Spanish).

title: Barring Non-Tenants Under Indiana's Criminal Trespass Law
bodyText: Indiana's criminal trespass statute lets you bar a non-tenant from your property, including common areas. A person who has no contractual interest in the property commits criminal trespass, a Class A misdemeanor, by knowingly or intentionally entering after being denied entry by you, your agent, or a police officer acting for you, or by refusing to leave after being asked to leave. You can deny entry by personal communication (oral or written), by posting a notice at the main entrance in a manner likely to come to the public's attention, by a court or hearing-authority order in certain nuisance and unsafe-building proceedings, or by purple paint marks on trees or posts placed to the statute's height and spacing rules. Entering a locked area without permission, or refusing to leave an area not open to the public when asked by police or your employee or agent, is also trespass. A repeat offense on the same property is a Level 6 felony. Limits matter. The entry and refusal-to-leave offenses reach only a person without a contractual interest in the property, so a tenant cannot be trespassed from the unit or the areas the lease gives them; the locked-area and non-public-area offense and the offense of interfering with another's possession carry no such limit, so a tenant who enters a locked area the lease does not give them, or refuses to leave a non-public area when asked, may commit trespass; a tenant who stays after the lease ends must be removed through eviction. The statute has no express exception for a tenant's guests or invitees, but whether you may ban a guest the tenant has invited, and how far a tenant's lease rights extend to guests in common areas, are for Indiana courts (this library has not reviewed those cases); the cautious course is a written no-trespass notice that names the person, states the reason, is given to both the person and the tenant, and is applied the same way to everyone, consistent with fair housing law. Police, firefighters and emergency responders on duty are not trespassers.

title: No Truth in Renting Act in Indiana
bodyText: Indiana has no Truth in Renting Act: there is no state statement of tenant rights you must distribute, no required notice in the lease telling the tenant that some terms may be unenforceable, and no list of forbidden lease clauses tied to a lease-wide penalty of the kind some states use. What Indiana does instead: it makes waivers of its main tenant protections void (security deposits, the landlord-tenant rights chapter, tenant and landlord duties, retaliation, protections for victims of domestic violence and similar crimes, and parts of the rules on a tenant's property after eviction); it voids a confession-of-judgment term and makes it a crime to knowingly have a tenant sign one, to keep one as its payee, or to try to enforce in Indiana another state's judgment based on one; and its consumer protection law reaches unconscionable lease terms. Leave void terms out of the lease. Including them does not make them binding and can support a consumer protection claim.

title: No Rule on Charging Parking Separately From Rent
bodyText: Indiana has no statute requiring parking to be offered or priced separately from rent, barring a separate parking charge, or limiting what you may charge for parking, and cities and counties may not regulate rents, lease terms or landlord fees. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants. You may include parking in the rent or charge for it separately; either way, state it in the lease. A separate parking charge paid to you under the lease counts as rent for Indiana's deposit law, which treats every payment under the rental agreement other than the deposit as rent. Local zoning may require a building to have a certain number of parking spaces; that is a land-use rule this library has not reviewed. The library's parking clauses cover where the tenant may park and assigned spaces.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: Indiana's consumer protection act covers leases of real property for personal, family or household use, so a landlord who regularly leases homes is a supplier under it. You commit an unconscionable act, treated as a deceptive act, if you solicit a tenant to sign a lease whose terms are oppressively one-sided or harsh, unduly limit the tenant's remedies, or set an unduly excessive price, and unequal bargaining power led the tenant to sign unwillingly or without knowing the terms. A tenant who signs a written lease is presumed, until shown otherwise, to know its terms. The act's enforcement is narrower for real property than for other sales: a tenant cannot bring the act's private damages suit or class action over a lease. The Attorney General can sue; for real property the act speaks of enjoining patterns of incurable deceptive acts (acts done as part of a scheme to defraud or mislead), and in that action a court may void or limit lease clauses that resulted from deceptive acts, order restitution, and, for a knowing violation of the unconscionability rule, impose a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per violation. The act does not reach a practice that state or federal law requires or expressly permits. Apart from the act, Indiana courts decide whether a lease term is unconscionable and unenforceable as a matter of contract law; this library has not reviewed those cases, or how courts read the act's real-property limits. Indiana has no statute letting a court revise a running lease because it has become excessively onerous, and no statute declaring any particular lease clause enforceable against an unconscionability challenge. The Uniform Commercial Code's unconscionability sections apply to sales and leases of goods, not to a lease of a home. Cautious course: keep fees, charges and remedy limits proportionate, explain unusual terms in plain words, and do not rely on terms that strip the tenant of remedies.

title: Leases Granted by a Life Tenant in Indiana
bodyText: Indiana has no civil-law usufruct, but its counterpart is the life estate, and Indiana has two statutes on leases granted by someone who owns property only for life. First, a conveyance by a tenant for life that tries to grant more than the life tenant has does not forfeit the life estate; it passes to the grantee whatever the life tenant could lawfully convey. Whether that statute governs a lease is not settled in its words, so the cautious reading is that a lease from a life tenant is secure only while the life estate lasts; Indiana courts decide whether, and on what terms, it continues after the life tenant dies. Second, if a life tenant who has leased the land dies on or after a rent due date, the life tenant's executor or administrator may recover the whole rent then due from the tenant; if the life tenant dies before the rent due date, the estate may recover the part of that rent that accrued before the death and the remainderman the part that accrued after. On the deposit, the owner of the dwelling unit when the rental agreement ends is bound by the deposit-return rules. If you hold only a life estate and lease the property, the cautious course is to tell the tenant in the lease that your interest ends at your death and to have the remainder owners sign the lease or a separate consent if the term may run past your lifetime. If you are leasing from someone who may hold only a life estate, ask, and check the recorded title. These rules apply the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: Limits on Rebilling Utilities to Tenants
bodyText: Indiana caps what you may collect when you rebill a utility bill to tenants. Electricity from a master meter: the statute lets you bill tenants through submeters in every unit (no statute or rule authorizes dividing the bill by formula), at the average cost per kilowatt-hour on your utility bill (including demand charges, taxes and other lawful charges, but not late-payment or disconnection penalties the utility charged you), and you may collect only what the utility charged you and no more; common-area electricity stays with you. Water and sewer you buy from a utility: if you bill separately, the total may not exceed what you paid the utility, less your own use, and the only extra charges allowed are a reasonable set-up fee, an administrative fee of no more than $4 a month and a returned-payment fee; you must give the required disclosure. If instead water or sewer is included in a flat rent or fee that does not itemize it, these billing rules do not apply. Indiana has no statute or rule on rebilling gas, and no rule that forbids passing master-metered electricity to tenants through a fixed amount in the rent. The Utility Regulatory Commission enforces the electric and water rules on tenant complaints and may order bills adjusted; the statute and rules read do not set a fine of their own. A lease term that sets a utility allowance and makes the tenant pay any excess is fine for a unit with its own utility meter whose account is in your name, but in a master-metered building it is a rebilling of the utility and must follow these rules, which for electricity means submetering; the cautious course there is to include the utility in the rent at a fixed amount.

title: Billing Tenants for Utilities Not Separately Metered
bodyText: No Indiana statute makes a lease term unenforceable just because it makes the tenant pay for a utility that is not separately metered to the unit. What you may charge depends on the utility. Water and sewer: you may simply include them in a flat rent or fee without itemizing them. If you instead bill tenants separately, the Utility Regulatory Commission's sub-billing rules let you charge either by submeter or by a reasonable allocation of your utility bill, such as a charge per unit spread by square footage, type of unit, number of occupants or estimated water use (for sewer, also estimated sewer flow); any other method must be fair and reasonable and must not produce a higher bill than those methods. You must first deduct your own use (personal or business use and common areas such as a laundry, pool, irrigation, fire sprinklers, grounds and common-area leaks), the total you bill may never exceed what you paid the utility, and the only extra fees allowed are a reasonable set-up fee, an administrative fee of no more than $4 a month and a returned-payment fee. You must give the required written disclosure, bill at a consistent frequency, show the required items on each bill (including that its due date is separate from the rent due date), give at least 17 days to pay before any collection action, keep bills for two years and let tenants inspect them. These rules do not apply to a single-family home that the utility meters directly. Electricity: Indiana's statute lets you bill tenants of a master-metered building for each unit's electricity through a submeter in every unit, under the submetering rules, and you may charge no more than the utility charged you; common-area electricity is yours. No statute or rule authorizes dividing an electric bill among tenants by formula, so the cautious course is to include electricity in the rent or submeter it. Gas: no Indiana statute or rule addresses billing tenants for gas that is not separately metered; the cautious course is to include it in the rent. Local governments may not regulate your lease terms or fees. This limit on local rules does not reach housing that receives government funds or benefits to provide reduced rents to low- or moderate-income tenants. See the water and sewer billing disclosure and the electric submetering rows for the lease language.

title: Utility Charges, Utility Deposits and the Security Deposit
bodyText: Indiana's deposit law names utility charges. You may apply the security deposit to utility or sewer charges that the tenant owed under the lease, that you paid and that the tenant did not pay, and you must list them on the itemized notice you send within 45 days. Indiana has no separate rule for a utility deposit that you, the landlord, collect: money you hold to secure the tenant's payment of utilities under the lease is part of the security deposit and is used and returned under the same rules; no statute requires it to be listed separately, though listing it in the lease avoids confusion. The deposit law also counts every payment made to you under the lease, other than the deposit, as rent, so utilities you bill under the lease are rent for deposit purposes; whether an unpaid utility bill is unpaid rent for the 10-day nonpayment notice is not settled by statute. If you bill tenants separately for water or sewer service, the Utility Regulatory Commission's rules let you collect unpaid bills by the same methods allowed for unpaid rent, but each bill's due date must be stated as separate from the rent due date. A city sewer utility may require owners, lessees or users to post a deposit of no more than three months' estimated average bills; it is refunded, less unpaid fees and penalties, once the depositor gives a notarized statement that the property was conveyed or disconnected, is forfeited if fees go unpaid for 60 days after service ends, and becomes the city's if unclaimed for seven years. A utility company's own customer deposit rules are not covered here.

title: No General Utility Disclosure or Lease Attachment
bodyText: Indiana has no general rule requiring you to give a tenant a utility disclosure or attach a utility addendum to the lease: no required statement of which utilities you or the tenant pay, of past or average utility bills, or of energy costs. Two specific statements are required when you bill tenants for utilities yourself. If you submeter electricity, every lease must clearly state that the unit is submetered, that bills are based on submeter readings, that common-area electricity is your responsibility, and the dispute procedure (use the electric submetering clause). If you bill tenants separately for water or sewer service you buy from a utility, you must give the water and sewer billing disclosure, in the lease, the first bill or a separate writing signed by the tenant, in type no smaller than the largest type in that document (use the water and sewer billing disclosure). Even without a rule, say in the lease which utilities each party pays: Indiana's ban on landlord utility shutoffs does not require you to pay for a service you did not agree to provide, so the lease is where that agreement is fixed.

title: No Right to Copies of a Tenant's Shutoff Notices
bodyText:
Indiana has no statute or Utility Regulatory Commission rule that lets you, as owner, authorize a utility to tell you when a tenant's service is about to be disconnected, or that lets a tenant name you to receive copies of shutoff notices. The disconnection rules require the utility to send its notice only to the customer who holds the account. Whether a particular utility will add a third party to an account voluntarily is up to that utility.

One narrow exception: where a sanitary district (a local sewer authority) sends a delinquency notice to a user who is a tenant, it must send a copy to the property owner at the owner's address on the county property tax records.

Separately, a city sewer utility's lien for unpaid fees on property occupied by someone other than the owner generally attaches only if the utility notifies the owner within 20 days after the fees become 60 days delinquent, so keep your mailing address in the county auditor's records current, or give the utility written notice of another address at which you want to receive these delinquency notices; a city storm water department's lien follows the same rule.

If you want to know about a tenant's past-due utility bills, put it in the lease: you may require the tenant to keep service on, to show proof of payment on request, and to give you a copy of any past-due or disconnection notice promptly. You may not shut off the tenant's utilities yourself.

title: No Shutoffs of Submetered or Sub-Billed Utilities
bodyText: If you submeter electricity, or sub-bill water or sewer, Indiana gives you no procedure for cutting off a tenant who does not pay. The utility disconnection rules bind the utility and its own customer, not you as a submetering owner, and the submetering rules contain no disconnection procedure at all. Indiana's landlord-tenant law forbids you, except under a court order, from interrupting, reducing, shutting off or causing the termination of a tenant's electricity, gas, water or other essential services; the only exceptions are an emergency, good-faith repairs and necessary construction. This applies to leases entered into or renewed after June 30, 1999, and any lease term waiving it is void. It does not apply to a unit the tenant has abandoned (rent unpaid and circumstances that would lead a reasonable person to conclude the tenant surrendered possession). The rule does not make you pay for a service you did not agree to provide. For unpaid charges, use ordinary collection: unpaid water or sewer sub-bills may be collected by the same methods the law allows for unpaid rent, after the 17-day payment period, and unpaid charges under the lease can be pursued with the deposit and in court. For submetered electricity, a tenant who disputes a bill may pay an amount equal to the six-month average while the complaint is reviewed, and may ask the Utility Regulatory Commission to review your decision. Because the utility can disconnect the whole building if the master-meter bill goes unpaid, keep that account current; letting it lapse could amount to causing the termination of your tenants' service. A tenant, in turn, may not shut off utilities if that would seriously damage the unit.

title: Utilities in the Landlord's Name: Shutoff Risks
bodyText: When a utility account for a rental is in your name (a master meter, or utilities you agreed to provide), the utility treats you as its customer. Indiana has no statute or Utility Regulatory Commission rule that bars a utility from disconnecting a building for your unpaid bill, requires the utility to notify each tenant before a building-wide shutoff, lets tenants pay your bill and deduct it from rent, or sets up a tenant receivership for unpaid utilities. The utility's disconnection notice goes only to the customer, and its residential protections cover service bought exclusively for residential purposes; whether a landlord's account for a rental building qualifies is not settled. Your tenants are protected through landlord-tenant law instead: except under a court order, you may not interrupt, shut off or cause the termination of a tenant's electricity, gas, water or other essential services (leases entered into or renewed after June 30, 1999; a waiver is void), and a tenant may seek an emergency court order. If the lease makes you responsible for a utility, letting service lapse can breach the lease. Where a heating system was on the premises when the lease was made, Indiana also requires you to keep it in good and safe working condition and sufficient to adequately supply heat at all times; whether a lapse in the fuel or power that runs it breaches that duty is for the courts. After notice and a reasonable time to fix a breach of your statutory duties, the tenant may sue for actual and consequential damages, attorney's fees, an injunction or other relief. Indiana courts may appoint a receiver under the general receivership statute when property or rents are in danger of being lost or materially injured; whether that reaches unpaid utilities has not been reviewed in this library. A tenant who opens service in the tenant's own name may not be disconnected for a previous occupant's unpaid bill. For city- or town-owned utilities, a non-owner occupant's charges are the occupant's if the utility's records show the occupant is responsible for them, they are not a lien, and the city may not require you to guarantee them. That rule does not cover sewage works under the municipal sewer statutes, consolidated-city utilities or a department of public utilities; for those sewage works a lien for unpaid fees can attach to your property after notice to you. If you own a building with four or fewer dwelling units, do not enroll in the water utility's lead service line program, replace the line yourself or respond within 45 days, and then block the utility's replacement, the utility may disconnect water to the property until you comply. An owner of a multi-family property with more than four units is outside that disconnection rule but, if it does not elect into the utility's program within 45 days of the request, must replace the line at its own expense. In a mobile home community, except where a utility may disconnect without notice, the owner and the state health department must get written notice at least 30 days before a water utility or sewer district sends its notice that the whole community will be disconnected from water, and for the health department's enforcement the community violates its duty to provide water from the date that disconnection notice is given. Keep owner-paid accounts current and give the utility your contact information.

title: When Utilities May Disconnect Residential Service
bodyText: Indiana's utility shutoff rules bind the utility, not you, and protect whoever holds the residential account: your tenant, if the service is in the tenant's name. They do not stop a utility from disconnecting for nonpayment; they set notice and timing limits. Electric and gas: from December 1 through March 15, an electric or gas utility (including city-owned and cooperative utilities) may not shut off residential service to a customer who is eligible for and has applied for the state's heating assistance program, and must keep service on while eligibility is decided. Since February 26, 2026, a privately owned or cooperative electric utility also may not shut off a customer who is eligible for and has applied for that assistance during the same calendar year on a day for which the National Weather Service has forecast (no more than 48 hours ahead) a heat index of at least 95 degrees for the customer's area, and the notice period is extended until a day when that heat index is not reached. Notice: an electric utility must give 14 days' written notice before disconnecting residential service for nonpayment, and any utility supplying energy or fuel must give 14 days' notice during the heating season (November 1 to April 1); a water utility must give 7 days' notice. A utility must postpone disconnection 10 days, renewable once, for a doctor's or health official's statement that disconnection would seriously threaten someone's health; may disconnect only between 8 a.m. and 3 p.m. and not just before a day its office is closed; may not disconnect a customer for a previous occupant's bill; and must offer a delinquent electric or gas customer a reasonable payment plan. Indiana has no general winter shutoff ban and no standing ban tied to a storm or declared emergency, though during a declared disaster emergency the governor may suspend state agency rules and allocate essential services, and during a disaster or energy emergency declared on its recommendation the Utility Regulatory Commission may temporarily alter utility service practices and orders, or suspend them with the utility's consent, so watch for emergency orders. Utilities may still disconnect at the customer's request or without notice for a hazard, a court or Commission order, fraud or tampering. For you: you may not shut off a tenant's utilities yourself, and the lease may require the tenant to keep tenant-paid utilities on and pay for them.

title: Putting Utilities in the Tenant's Name
bodyText:
Indiana has no statute or Utility Regulatory Commission rule that sets a deadline for a tenant to move utility accounts into the tenant's name, or that lets you cut off utilities left in your name when the tenant fails to do so.

Whether the tenant must open accounts is a matter for the lease; use the utility transfer clause, which requires the tenant to put tenant-paid utilities in the tenant's name by a date you choose and to reimburse you for the provider's actual charges for any period an account stays in your name.

Do not shut off service to force a transfer: except under a court order, you may not interrupt, shut off or cause the termination of a tenant's electricity, gas, water or other essential services, and that rule cannot be waived in the lease.

The same statute says it does not require you to pay for a service you did not agree to provide, but it does not say how those two parts fit together when an account is in your name, and Indiana courts would decide that; the cautious course is to keep the service on and collect what the tenant owes.

As the utility's customer you may ask the utility to stop service in your name on three days' notice, and you are not liable for service after three working days; do that only for a unit that is vacant, has been surrendered or has been abandoned. Utility charges the tenant owed under the lease that you paid can be taken from the security deposit and must be listed on the itemized notice.

When a non-owner occupant applies for service from a city-owned utility, the occupant must give the utility your name and contact information, and the occupant's charges are not a lien on your property.

title: No Indiana Incentive for Renting to Veterans
bodyText: No Indiana statute gives a residential landlord a tax credit, fee waiver, deposit guarantee or other incentive for renting to veterans or servicemembers, and none requires or regulates a veterans' rent discount or preference in private rental housing. Indiana's veterans' housing help runs through state grants to organizations that serve veterans, including programs to end or prevent homelessness, and through the state's housing first program, not through landlords. Indiana's civil rights law defines a discriminatory practice to include excluding a person from equal opportunities, or keeping a system that does so, because of status as a veteran; how far that reaches decisions about renting a home is decided by the civil rights commission and Indiana courts, which this library has not reviewed, so the cautious course is not to treat veteran status as a reason to refuse or set different terms (see `edu-fair-housing-in`). If you choose to offer a veterans' discount, apply it the same way to every eligible applicant and put it in writing. A separate Indiana lease disclosure applies to some property near military installations (see `military-installation-disclosure-in`), and federal protections for servicemembers on active duty, including early termination, are covered in `edu-statutory-early-termination-in`. These rules apply the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Water Heater Temperature Setting Rule
bodyText: Indiana has no statute requiring you to set a unit's water heater to a maximum temperature before each new tenant moves in, or otherwise limiting hot water temperature in a rental. Your landlord-tenant duty is about supply, not temperature: if plumbing is provided on the premises when the lease is made, you must keep it in good and safe working condition and sufficient to accommodate a reasonable supply of hot and cold running water at all times. Hot water temperature limits in Indiana's health rules apply to other settings, such as swimming pool facilities, youth camps and migrant labor camps; for a mobile home community, the health rules require the community's shared toilet and laundry buildings to keep hot water at a minimum of 120 degrees Fahrenheit. Water heater installation in new construction and alterations is governed by the state plumbing code (based on the 2006 International Plumbing Code) for buildings of three or more units, and by the residential code for single-family homes, duplexes and townhouses; Indiana's plumbing code amendments add no rental or turnover temperature setting, and the model code text, including any temperature-limiting rule for fixtures, is not reviewed here. As a safety practice, many landlords check that a unit's water heater is set at or below 120 degrees at turnover.

title: No Waterbed Law in Indiana
bodyText: Indiana has no waterbed law: no statute lets tenants keep a waterbed, lets you require waterbed insurance or a deposit, or sets installation standards. The lease decides. The library's Use of Property and Common Areas clause, which applies in Indiana, requires your written consent before a tenant keeps a waterbed or other water-filled furniture. If you consent, you may set conditions in writing, such as a liner, professional installation, or proof of renter's insurance covering water damage. Any extra deposit counts toward the security deposit, which Indiana does not cap, and damage a waterbed causes beyond ordinary wear and tear may be taken from the deposit under the deposit rules. A refusal or condition must be applied evenly, and a tenant with a disability who needs a water-filled mattress may be entitled to a reasonable accommodation.

title: No Window Guard or Security Bar Rule
bodyText: Indiana has no statute or state rule requiring you to install child window guards or window-opening limiters in a rental, to give a window-guard notice in the lease, or to disclose how security bars release. Window and emergency escape requirements for new construction and alterations come from the statewide building and residential codes, which adopt the model codes; Indiana's amendments read for this row do not add a window-guard or security-bar rule, and the model code text (including any rule on bars over bedroom escape windows) is not reviewed here. If you install bars or grilles on a window that serves as a bedroom emergency escape opening, the cautious course is to use bars that release from the inside without a key, tool or special knowledge, and to tell the tenant in writing how they release. Check local codes.

title: Which Indiana Notices Must Be in Writing
bodyText:
Indiana requires these notices and documents in writing.

From you: (1) one month's notice ending a tenancy at will; (2) at least 30 days' notice before you change the rental agreement, unless a written rental agreement provides otherwise; (3) the itemized list of deposit deductions with the amount due, within 45 days after the tenancy ends and possession is returned (you are not liable for it until the tenant gives you a mailing address in writing); (4) the names and addresses of the Indiana manager and the Indiana agent for notices, at or before the start of the tenancy; (5) notice to the tenant when you sell the property in a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser, or when a manager's management ends, which (unless otherwise agreed) is what releases you (or the manager) from liability for later events; after a sale you stay liable for the security deposit for one year unless the buyer gives the tenant notice that it has assumed that liability and you transfer the deposit to the buyer.

From the tenant: (6) the request that a protected tenant (a victim of domestic violence, sexual offenses or stalking with a qualifying order) make to have the locks changed, and the protected tenant's notice ending the lease at least 30 days ahead, with copies of the order and, for domestic violence or sexual assault, a recent safety plan recommending relocation; (7) the notice that a detector needs repair, which starts your seven working days to fix it; (8) the address in writing for the deposit refund; and (9) a complaint to you about your duty to keep the unit fit or about interference with access, possession or essential services, which is protected from retaliation only if it is made in writing (a complaint to a code enforcement agency is protected either way).

Also in writing: the tenant's acknowledgment at move-in that the unit has a working smoke detector, and a tenant's designation of a representative to act on the tenant's death or incapacity.

If you operate a mobile home community (at least five homes on leased lots used as principal residences), you must give each home owner written notice of an intended closure at least 180 days before the closure date; eviction for nonpayment or another violation of the tenancy, and enforcing your lien, are still allowed during that period, and failing to give the notice is a deceptive act under Indiana's consumer protection law.

Indiana's statutes do not say that a notice ending a month-to-month or year-to-year tenancy, or the 10-day notice for unpaid rent, must be written, but the service rules (handing it to the tenant, to a person living there, or attaching a copy to the premises) assume a paper notice, and the statutory forms are written; always give these in writing. Your notice of entry may be written or oral.

An email or other electronic record can satisfy a writing requirement only if both of you have agreed to deal electronically and the tenant can keep or print it; it cannot replace a delivery method the law specifies (see the notice method row).

Federal law adds two points: the federal electronic signatures law may also require the tenant's informed consent, given as that law describes, before an email can replace a written notice (whether Indiana's own electronic transactions law displaces that federal rule is unsettled and no court decision was reviewed, so the optional electronic notice clause includes the consent), and that federal law does not reach eviction notices for a tenant's primary residence.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Indiana follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (IC 26-1-3.1-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (IC 26-1-1-207(2)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Indiana's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (IC 32-31 searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Indiana's courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
